en: The Nectar-Ocean of the Essence of Devotional Love by Śrīla Śrīla [1].
The First Division: A Description of the Varieties of Devotion to the Lord [1.1].
General Devotion: The First Wave.
May the divine couple, Śrī Śrī Rādhā-Govinda, be victorious!

Victorious is the Moon, the beloved of Rādhā, whose form is the nectar of all aesthetic flavors, who obstructs the rows of stars with his spreading luster, and who is graced by the dark-complexioned Śyāmā.
I bow at the lotus feet of Lord Caitanya, that Hari, by whose inspiration I have been set in motion, though I am of wretched form.
May this ocean of the nectar of the rasa of devotion to my Lord, whose eternal body is the Temple of Rest, always bring joy.

I bow with reverence to those crocodiles among devotees who roam the nectar-ocean of the mellows of devotion, who have overcome the fear of the snare of time, and who do not seek the river of liberation.
May this ocean of the nectar of devotion to you, O Sanātana, surge forth for a very long time, blunting even the hardness of the submarine fire of the Mīmāṃsakas.

This presentation of the aesthetic sentiment of devotion (bhakti-rasa), which is the source of auspiciousness for the entire world, is being composed by me, though ignorant, for the delight of my friends. (RBhrs 1.1.6)
Of this ocean of the nectar of the rasa of devotion to the Blessed One,
four parts— beginning with the Purva (East)— will indeed be described in sequence.
In this first section, which defines the different types of devotion,
four waves (laharīs) are to be described in sequence.
The first is rich in general devotion; the second is endowed with spiritual practice;
the third is based on emotional disposition; and the fourth is characterized by pure love.
In this regard, first of all, in order to clearly explain its excellent distinction,
the definition of supreme devotion is set forth according to the opinion of the virtuous.
Devotion is the supreme practice of following Kṛṣṇa in a manner that is free from desire for anything else and unobstructed by [the pursuit of] knowledge, ritual action, and so forth. (RBhṛs 1.1.11)
As it is said in the Śrī Nārada-pañcarātra:
"Devotion is defined as the service of Hṛṣīkeśa by means of the senses, which is free from all limiting adjuncts (upādhi) and rendered pure through being directed toward Him alone. (RBhrs 1.1.12)
And in the third canto of the Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam (3.29.11–13): "That devotion which is unconditioned and uninterrupted toward Puruṣottama..."
Even when offered the states of residing in the same world (sālokya), possessing equal power (sārṣṭi), proximity (sāmīpya), having the same form (sārūpya), or even oneness (ekatva),
people do not accept them without my service.
That very [discipline] is declared to be the ultimate yoga known as bhakti-yoga.
The description of the excellence of the devotee found in the verse beginning with "sālokya" culminates in the definition [of devotion] through the manifestation of its purity. (RBhrs 1.1.16)

She is the destroyer of afflictions, the bestower of purity, and the creator of lightness for liberation; she is exceedingly difficult to attain, her essence being a special state of intense bliss, and she is the attractor of Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
In this regard, its quality of destroying the afflictions is as follows:
"The afflictions, however, are evil; their seed is ignorance, and thus they are threefold. (RBhṛS 1.1.18)
In that regard, sin is twofold: it may be uncommenced (aprārabdha) or it may be commenced (prārabdha).
In that regard, the quality of destroying even what has not yet begun [to bear fruit] is as stated in the Eleventh Canto (11.14.19): "Just as a well-kindled fire reduces fuel to ashes..."
Likewise, O Uddhava, devotion directed toward my own domain completely destroys all sins.
The power of removing even that which has already begun to bear fruit (*prārabdha-karma*),
as stated in the Third Canto (3.33.6):
"By hearing and chanting the names [of the Lord]..."
O Blessed One, since even a dog, by bowing down to you or even by remembering you at any time, immediately becomes fit for the Soma sacrifice, how much more so, then, from beholding you?
It is held that low birth alone is the cause for being unfit for the sacrificial rites;
and whatever sin constitutes the origin of that low birth, it is precisely that which has already been set in motion [as *prārabdha*].
And in the Padma Purāṇa: "The sin whose fruit has not yet begun, which is like a seed that is sprouting,
shall be dissolved in due course for those whose souls are devoted to Viṣṇu."
The destruction of the seed [of sin],
as stated in the sixth [chapter] (6.2.17):
"Those sins are purified by means of austerity, charity, vows, and so forth."
That heart of his was not born of unrighteousness, even through its service to the feet of the Lord.
The quality of removing ignorance,
as stated in the fourth [chapter] (4.22.39):
"By devotion to the play of the petals of whose lotus feet..."
The virtuous untie the tightly knotted accumulation of karma;
likewise, even ascetics whose minds are not yet emptied and whose streams of rebirth are blocked cannot do so. Therefore, resort to that Vāsudeva who is free from all conflict.
And in the *Pādma*:
"Devotion to Hari, accompanied by the sciences (*vidyā*), is unsurpassed;
it quickly burns away ignorance, just as a forest fire consumes a female serpent. (RBhrs 1.1.26)
Regarding the nature of the auspicious (*śubha*):
the wise have declared that the auspicious consists of delighting all the worlds, being beloved by them, virtuous qualities, happiness, and so forth. (RBhṛs 1.27)
In that regard, the quality of bestowing the two— namely, the delighting of the world and so forth—
is as stated in the Padma Purāṇa: "By whomsoever Hari is worshipped, by him the worlds are also gratified."
There, living beings—both mobile and immobile—take delight.
The bestowing of the six qualities and so forth, as in the fifth [chapter] (5.18.12):
"He who possesses unselfish devotion for the Blessed Lord..."
There, the gods abide together with all their virtues;
but for one who is not a devotee of Hara, how can there be great virtues,
as he runs outward after unreal desires?
The quality of bestowing happiness—happiness is indeed threefold: pertaining to the senses, pertaining to Brahman, and pertaining to the Lord. 1.30.
As it is stated in the Tantra:
"Through devotion to Govinda, there shall arise supreme and wondrous accomplishments, both worldly enjoyment and eternal liberation, as well as perpetual supreme bliss. (RBhrs 1.1.31)
As it is said in the *Haribhaktisudhodaya*:
"O Lord of Gods, I pray once more: may my devotion to You be firm—that creeper which bestows the fruits of the four aims of life up to liberation, and which grants happiness. (RBhrs 1.1.32)
Making liberation seem light— when devotion to the Blessed One has grown even slightly in the heart, the four aims of human life wither away on all sides like blades of grass.
As it is said in the Śrī-Nārada-Pañcarātra:
"All perfections such as liberation, as well as wonderful enjoyments, follow after the great goddess Hari-bhakti like her maidservants. (RBhrs 1.1.34)
Extremely difficult to attain— unobtainable even after a long time through a multitude of unattached practices;
and because she is [worshipped] by Hari and by Aśvadeva, she is thus twofold and extremely difficult to attain.
Among these, the first is as stated in the Tantra: "Liberation is easily obtained through knowledge; enjoyment [is obtained] through the merit of sacrifices and the like;
but this devotion to Hari is very difficult to attain even through thousands of such means. (RBhṛs 1.1.36)
The second [verse], as it appears in the *Pañcama-skandha* (5.6.18):
"O King, you are the lord, the guru, the sufficient protector, the deity, the beloved, and the head of the clan for the Yadus; where then is the servant among you?"
Let it be so, my dear; the Blessed Mukunda grants liberation to those who worship Him, but never indeed the yoga of devotion.
Even if the bliss of Brahman, whose essence is a particular intense joy, were multiplied by a factor of a hundred million (parārddha),
it would not equal even a single atom of the ocean of the bliss of devotion.
As it is said in the *Haribhaktisudhodaya*:

"O Teacher of the World, for me who am situated in the ocean of purity consisting of the bliss of direct perception of You, even the pleasures of Brahmā appear as mere puddles in a cow's hoofprint. (RBhrs 1.1.39)
Likewise, in the Bhāvārtha-dīpikā (on 10.88.11):
"Sporting with great joy in the ocean of the nectar of Your stories,
some fortunate ones regard even the four goals of human life as being like a blade of grass."
Śrī-kṛṣṇākarṣiṇī:
Having caused Hari, together with his circle of beloveds, to possess divine love, devotion brings him under its control; thus it is considered Śrī-kṛṣṇākarṣiṇī. (RBhrs 1.41)
As it is said in the Eleventh [Canto] (11.14.20):
"Neither yoga, nor Sāṅkhya, nor religious duty, O Uddhava, nor Vedic study, nor austerity, nor renunciation achieves Me as effectively as intense devotion unto Me."
And in the seventh [canto], in the words of Nārada (7.10.48): "O, you are most fortunate in the world of men; as sages, you approach this world while purifying it."
In whosever houses he dwells, the Supreme Brahman itself, though hidden, appears in human form.
The greatness of this devotion, which will be described in three ways below in sequence,
has been proclaimed in pairs by means of these six verses.
Furthermore:
Even a very slight inclination alone may lead to the realization of the true nature of devotion;
mere reasoning, however, certainly cannot, because it lacks a firm foundation.
Regarding this, it has also been stated by the ancients:
"Even an object established with great effort by skillful inferents may be demonstrated in an entirely different way by others who are more proficient. (RBhṛs 1.1.46)
Thus ends the first wave, on the general nature of devotion, in the first part of the *Śrī Śrī Bhakti-rasāmṛta-sindhu*.
Now begins the second wave.
That devotion is declared to be threefold: as the means (sādhana), as the state of being (bhāva), and as love (prema).
In that regard, devotional practice as a means (*sādhana-bhakti*) is that which is to be accomplished through action; it is designated as "means" because its state is something yet to be achieved.
However, the manifestation within the heart of that state which is eternally established constitutes its being "to be accomplished. (RBhrs 1.2.2)
That devotion was described by the celestial sage (Nārada) in the Seventh Skandha through a particular method.
As it is stated in the seventh [chapter] (7.1.31):
"Therefore, by whatever means possible, one should fix the mind upon Kṛṣṇa.
Thus, that method of practice is said to be twofold: the ritualistic (*vaidhī*) and that which follows from attachment (*rāgānugā*).
Among these, the *vaidhī* [type of devotion] is that wherein activity arises because one has not yet attained [the goal] through passion;
it is called *vaidhī* devotion because it occurs solely by means of the instruction of the scripture. (RBhṛS 1.2.6)
As it is said in the second [chapter] (2.1.6):
"Therefore, O Bhārata, the Blessed Lord, the Sovereign Hari, who is the Self of all, should be heard, celebrated, and remembered by one who desires fearlessness. (RBhrs 1.2.7)
And in the *Pādma*:
"Viṣṇu should be remembered constantly; he should never be forgotten.
All injunctions and prohibitions are merely servants to these two."
Thus, this injunction would be eternal with respect to all castes, stages of life, and so forth;
and although it is eternal, its fruit has been determined to be like that of the Ekādaśī fast and other such observances.
As it is clearly stated in the Eleventh [Book] (11.5.2–3):
"From the mouth, arms, thighs, and feet of Puruṣa, [the four castes] were produced along with the stages of life."
The four castes, beginning with the Brahmins, were born separately according to their qualities.
Those who do not worship this Lord, the manifest Person who is the source of their own selves, and who instead despise him, fall downward, deprived of their station.
And its fruit is stated in that very same place (11.27.49):
"Thus, by means of the paths of *kriyā-yoga* belonging to both the Vedic and Tantric traditions, a person worshipping Me on both sides attains from Me his desired perfection. (RBhrs 1.2.12)
And in the *Pañcarātra*:
"O celestial sage, whatever rite is prescribed in the scripture directed toward Hari, that alone is declared to be devotion; through it, supreme devotion shall arise. (RBhrs 1.2.13)
In this regard, the qualified candidate is one who, through some extraordinary good fortune, has developed faith in its practice;
he is neither excessively attached nor possessed of a spirit of detachment— such a person is qualified for this.
As it is said in the Eleventh Canto (11.20.28):
"For that person who, by chance, has developed faith in My stories and the like, and who is neither despondent nor excessively attached, the yoga of devotion bestows perfection. (RBhrs 1.2.15)
It is threefold: superior, middling, and inferior.
Among these, the best is as follows:
"He who is skilled in both the scripture and its application, who is in every way firm in resolve, and who possesses mature faith—he is considered the best qualified for devotion. (RBhṛs 1.2.17)
Among them, the middling [practitioner] is:
"He who is unskilled in the scriptures and so forth, yet possesses faith, is the middling one. (RBhṛs 1.2.18)
Among them, the youngest is he who possesses tender faith; he is called the youngest.
Among those four types of qualified practitioners mentioned therein in the Gītā and other texts,
[the Lord’s grace] falls upon whichever one He favors, or upon one who is dear to His devotee.
Having those various states extinguished, he becomes one who possesses the qualification for pure devotion—
just as Ībha, Śaunaka and others, Dhruva, and Caturānana.
As long as the demoness of longing for worldly enjoyment and liberation dwells within the heart,
how can there be the arising of the bliss of devotion here?
And even there, for those who especially do not desire the subtle state of liberation,
devotion— having captivated their minds and vital breaths— renders them people possessed of love.
And likewise, in the third [canto] (3.25.36):
"By means of those lovely limbs, their noble grace, smiles, glances, and charming speech..."
Devotion leads those whose minds and vital breaths have been captivated by Me to the subtle goal, even against their own will.
For these devotees whose minds are satisfied by the service of the lotus feet of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, there shall never arise a desire for liberation.
As it is said in that very same place, in the words of the illustrious Uddhava (3.4.15): "O Lord, who indeed [is equal] to those who partake of the lotus feet of Yours..."
O Infinite One, although [attainment] in these four goals is extremely difficult to find even here in this world, I do not choose them, being eager to serve the lotus-feet of Your Honor.
In that very place, in the words of Śrī Kapiladeva (3.25.35):
"Some, devoted to service at my feet and intent on my will, do not long for identity with me."
Those devotees who, having come together, praise my heroic deeds to one another; // RBhrs_1,2.27 //
In that very place (3.29.13):
"Even when offered—residence in the same world, equal power, proximity, identical form, or even oneness—people do not accept it without service to Me. (RBhrs 1.2.28)
In the fourth chapter, in the words of Śrī Dhruva (4.9.10):
"Whatever bliss belongs to embodied beings may arise from meditation upon Your lotus feet, or from hearing the narrations concerning Your devotees."
O Lord, let her not fall even from her own majesty in the realm of Brahmā, but rather from the celestial chariot as it tumbles, shaken by the sword of Antaka.
In that very place, in the speech of the illustrious Ādirāja (4.20.24):
"O Lord, I do not desire even that anywhere where the nectar of Your lotus feet is not present."
"Let that which has issued from the mouth of the Great One within my heart enter my ears; this is my boon."

In the fifth [canto], in the words of Śrī Śuka (5.14.44): "He who [renounced] his sons, kin, wealth, and wife— things difficult to abandon— as well as sought-after prosperity that is gazed upon with compassion by the best of the gods..."
The king did not desire that which was appropriate for the great, whose minds are devoted to the service of the Enemy of Madhu; even non-existence would have been insignificant [compared to that].
In the sixth canto, in the speech of Śrī Vṛtra (6.11.25):
"Neither the back of the celestial realm, nor the sovereignty of Brahmā, nor universal dominion, nor lordship over the netherworlds [is desired]."
O Perfect One, I do not desire the perfections of yoga or even liberation from rebirth, were I to be separated from You.
In that very place, in the speech of Śrī Rudra (6.17.28):
"All those who are devoted to Nārāyaṇa do not fear anything from any source;
they regard heaven, liberation, and hell as equal in their purpose. (RBhrs 1.2.33)
In that very context, in the speech of Indra (6.18.74): "Those who,
seeking the propitiation of the Blessed One, are free from desire for rewards—
even though they do not seek anything else— they are remembered as those skilled in their own true interest."

In the seventh chapter, in the speech of Prahlāda (7.6.25): "When He—the Infinite and Primordial—is satisfied, what is there that cannot be obtained? What need is there for those things here which are established by their own nature through the interplay of the modes?"
O Dharma and the others, what is the use of that which is devoid of virtue and yet craved by us, who delight in the essence while singing the praises of your feet?
In that very place, in the speech of Śakra (7.8.42):
"O Supreme One, our own portions have been recovered by You, our protector;
the lotus-heart of the Daityas, which was their abode, has been awakened."
O Lord, alas, how much of this is seized by Time for those who desire to serve you!
Is liberation not highly esteemed by them, or is it not [attained] through others than you, O Narasimha?
In the eighth [canto], in the speech of Śrī Gajendra (8.3.20): "Those who have indeed taken refuge in the Blessed One, the single-minded devotees, do not desire any object whatsoever."
Singing his most wonderful and auspicious deeds, they are immersed in an ocean of bliss.

In the ninth book, in the words of the Lord of Śrī-Vaikuṇṭha (9.4.67): "Those who are fulfilled by service to Me do not desire the fourfold [liberation] beginning with *sālokya* attained through such service; how much less anything else that is corrupted by time? (RBhrs 1.2.38).

In the *Śrī-daśama*, in the hymn by the wives of the Nāgas (10.16.37): "Neither the back of heaven, nor sovereignty over the whole earth, nor the position of Brahmā, nor lordship over the waters [is desired]."
Those who have taken refuge in the dust of his feet do not desire the perfections of yoga or even liberation from rebirth.
In that very same work, the *Śrī-Veda-Stuti* (10.87.21):

"Exhausted by the labor of circling the great ocean of the nectar of Your deeds, You who have assumed a physical form for the purpose of revealing the reality of the Self which is otherwise difficult to comprehend— "
O Lord, some do not even long for liberation, having abandoned their homes through association with the flock of swans that are Your lotus feet.

In the eleventh book, as spoken by the Blessed Lord (11.20.34): "The wise and steadfast devotees who are exclusively devoted to Me do not desire even liberation from rebirth, though it be offered by Me. (RBhrs 1.2.41)
Likewise (11.14.14):
"Neither the station of Brahmā, nor the abode of Mahendra, nor sovereignty over the whole earth, nor lordship over the netherworlds."
One whose self is offered unto Me does not desire the perfections of yoga or even liberation from rebirth as anything other than Me.
In the twelfth [chapter], in the words of Śrī Rudra (12.10.6): "The brahmin-sage desires no blessings whatsoever, nor even liberation;
he has attained supreme devotion to the immutable Supreme Person. (RBhrs 1.2.43)

And in the *Padma Purāṇa*, within the *Kārttika-māhātmya* (the *Dāmodarāṣṭaka*): "O Lord, I do not choose liberation, nor the limit of liberation, nor anything else here, even from You, the Sovereign of Boons."
O Lord, may this form of yours as a cowherd boy always remain undiminished in my mind; what need is there for anything else?
Just as You liberated the two sons of Kuvera while they were bound in physical form and made them bound by devotion,
so likewise grant me Your own loving devotion.
I have no attachment even to liberation, O Dāmodara.
And in the *Hayaśīrṣīya-śrī-nārāyaṇa-vyūha-stava*:
"O Lord who grants boons, I do not pray for dharma, nor for desire, nor for wealth, nor for liberation; I long only for servitude at your lotus feet."
In that very same place— though Viṣṇu repeatedly desired to grant him boons, he did not ask for liberation;
rather, he chose devotion alone— to that Prahlāda, I bow.
Salutations to that Hanumān, who, even when offered liberation by Viṣṇu as the son of Daśaratha obtained by chance, did not desire it without [the opportunity for] service.

For this very reason, the well-known statement of Śrī Hanumān is established: "I long for that which severs the bonds of worldly existence, not for liberation, wherein the distinction 'you are the Lord' and 'I am the servant' is dissolved. (RBhrs 1.2.49)
And in the *Śrī-Nārada-Pañcarātra*, in the *Jitante-stotra*:
"I have no desire whatsoever for virtue, wealth, pleasure, or liberation;
let my life be granted beneath Your lotus feet."
O Supporter of the Earth, I do not pray for liberation, nor for sālokya, nor for sārūpya;
for I desire your compassion, O illustrious one of noble vows.

Therefore, in the Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam (6.14.5): "O great sage, even among millions of liberated and perfected beings, one who is solely devoted to Nārāyaṇa and whose mind is perfectly tranquil is extremely rare."

And in the first instance, in the praise of the mother of Śrī Dharmarāja (1.8.20): "Likewise, for the purpose of prescribing the yoga of devotion for the pure-souled sages who are paramahaṃsas, how indeed may we women behold [the Lord]? (RBhrs 1.2.53).
In that very context, the Śrī-Sūtasamhitā states (1.7.10):
"Even sages who delight in the Self and are free from all bonds offer causeless devotion to the Wide-striding Lord; such are the qualities of Hari. (RBhrs 1.2.54)
Even if liberation of all five kinds, such as *sālokya* and the rest, is described here as something to be renounced, it is nevertheless not fundamentally incompatible with devotion (*bhakti*).
This [liberation] is superior in terms of happiness and sovereignty, and it is also superior in terms of loving service;
therein, liberation such as *sālokya* is of two kinds, but the former is not considered suitable for one who enjoys [the Lord's] service.
But those who are exclusively devoted to Hari, relishing the singular sweetness of love,
never at any time accept even the fivefold liberation.
Even among those, the most excellent are the single-minded devotees whose minds have been captivated by Govinda; for even the grace of the Lord of Śrī would not be able to steal away their hearts.

But according to the final conclusion (siddhānta), although there is no difference between the natures of Śrī Śiva and Kṛṣṇa, the form of Kṛṣṇa is elevated by aesthetic flavor (rasa); such is the nature of rasa.
According to the scriptures, it is heard that even a mere human being possesses the qualification for devotion; for,
by stating that the Māgha bath has universal qualification,
Vasiṣṭha cited devotion to Hari as an illustrative example with respect to the king.
As stated in the Padma Purāṇa:
"O King, all are indeed qualified for this devotion to Hari."
And likewise in the Kāśī-khaṇḍa: "Even the lowest-born in that kingdom, bearing the marks of the conch and discus,
having received Vaiṣṇava initiation, shone as if they were consecrated [brahmins]."
Moreover:
"A fault arises from the non-performance of the ancillaries of devotion;
this [fault] does not arise for those entitled to devotion from the non-performance of ritual acts. (RBhṛs 1.2.63)
"Expiation is not appropriate for an act prohibited by custom that occurs by chance;
this is the secret of the Vaiṣṇava scriptures, as held by those who know them. (RBhrs 1.2.64)
As stated in the eleventh [chapter] (11.20.26, 11.21.2):
"The steadfastness in each respective duty is proclaimed as a quality;
conversely, its opposite is a defect—this is the certainty for both. (RBhrs 1.2.65)
In the first [verse] (1.5.17):
"If, having abandoned his own duty, one worships the lotus feet of Hari but remains immature and then falls from that state..."
Wherever it may have been, what good fortune has accrued to him, and what purpose has been achieved by those who have followed their own dharma?
In the eleventh [chapter] (11.11.37):
"He who, having understood both the virtues and the faults of even his own duties as enjoined by me, abandons them all and worships me—he indeed is the most excellent of beings. (RBhrs 1.2.67)
In that very place (11.5.41): "O King, he is neither a servant nor a debtor to the gods, sages, spirits, kinsmen, men, or ancestors."
He who has gone for refuge with his whole being to Mukunda, the worthy refuge, having abandoned all other action.
In the Śrī Bhagavad Gītā (18.66):
"Having abandoned all duties, take refuge in Me alone.
I shall liberate you from all sins; do not grieve."
In the Agastya-saṃhitā:
"Just as injunctions and prohibitions do not approach one who is liberated, so too, O Rāma, they do not touch the devotee who practices according to the prescribed rule. (RBhrs 1.2.70)
In the eleventh [chapter] itself (11.5.42): "To His beloved devotee who worships at the base of His own feet, having abandoned all other states of being, Hari, the Supreme Lord..."
And whatever improper action has arisen in any way, he who is seated within the heart shakes it all off.
In the *Haribhaktivilāsa*, the limbs (*aṅga*) of this devotion number in the hundreds of thousands;
nevertheless, those that are well-known are here pointed out according to my understanding.
In this context, the definition of a subsidiary (aṅga) is as follows:

whether it consists of several distinct subordinate parts or is itself a single entity, an action that is performed solely for the sake of devotion is called a subsidiary by the learned. (RBhṛs 1.2.73)
Now, the auxiliary practices (aṅgas):
taking refuge at the feet of the Guru; from that, receiving instruction on the initiation of Kṛṣṇa and so forth;
serving the Guru with full confidence; and following the path of the virtuous.

Inquiring about the true Dharma, renouncing wealth and other possessions for the sake of Kṛṣṇa, and residing in places such as Dvārakā or in the vicinity of the Gaṅgā and other sacred sites; RBhṛs 1.2.75.
In all worldly transactions, acting in accordance with the facts as they are;
honoring the day of Hari; and showing reverence for the Dhātrī tree, the Aśvattha, and so forth.
Among these ten limbs, there may be the nature of an undertaking.
The renunciation of attachment is far removed from people who are averse to the Blessed One;
it consists of not being bound by disciples and the like, and the absence of exertion in great undertakings and the like.
The avoidance of the study of many texts, artistic skills, and of exposition and debate.
Even in worldly affairs, there is no meanness, nor being subject to the sway of grief and the like.
Contempt for other deities, causing no agitation among living beings, and ensuring the non-arising of faults known as "service" [to others]. // RBhrs_1.2.81 //
Intolerance toward offenses such as hatred or blasphemy directed at Kṛṣṇa and His devotees constitutes the practice of these ten [vices] by way of their opposites.
Although all twenty limbs serve as gateways for entry into this [state],
the three beginning with taking refuge at the feet of the Guru are declared to be the primary ones.

One should maintain steadfastness regarding the Vaiṣṇava marks, the syllables of Hari’s name, and the remains of His offerings (nirmālya) and so forth; and before Him, one should perform the tāṇḍava dance and prostrate like a staff.

Rising to meet [the teacher], following after him, moving when he moves, standing still when he stands, circumambulating, honoring, serving, singing his praises, proclaiming his virtues, and reciting his names.
Proclamation, the recitation of hymns, the tasting of the food offering and the water for the feet,
the fragrance of incense, garlands, and so forth, the touching, and the beholding of the glorious Form.

The hearing of the *ārātrika* festival and other such rites, the beholding of His well, remembrance, meditation, as well as servitude (*dāsya*), friendship (*sakhya*), and self-surrender (*ātma-nivedana*).
The surrendering of one’s own beloved, all activity for his sake,
seeking refuge in every way, and service to his followers.
His tulasi plants, scriptures, Mathurā, Vaiṣṇavas, and so forth—
along with all such opulent materials— are celebrated as a great festival through the assemblies of the virtuous.
There is a particular eagerness for vigor, especially on occasions such as the anniversary of one's birth;
there is especially faith and delight in serving the feet of the Śrī-mūrti.

The savoring of the meanings of the Śrīmad-Bhāgavata together with connoisseurs occurs naturally through association with a virtuous person who is kind-hearted and whose disposition is of the same nature as one's own.
The chanting of the Name and residing within the sacred circle of Śrī Mathurā.
This group of five limbs, which was previously described,
is proclaimed here once again for the sake of understanding its complete preeminence.
Thus are the meditations upon the body, the senses, and the internal organ.
There are sixty-four [systems] individually, according to the divisions of the *sāṅghātika* and so forth, following the sequence.
Now, an illustration of these [categories] is being set forth according to the consensus of the ṛṣis.
1. Among these, taking refuge at the feet of the Guru is as stated in the eleventh [chapter] (11.3.21):
"Therefore, one who desires to know the supreme good should take refuge in the Guru."
One who is proficient in verbal knowledge and in the Supreme Brahman, and who takes refuge in tranquility.
2. Instruction on initiation by Śrī Kṛṣṇa and so forth, as stated in that very same work (11.3.22):
"There, one who regards the guru as his own self and as the deity should learn the duties of the devotees of the Lord."
But Hari, the Self and the giver of the self, is pleased by those who follow with sincerity and without guile.
3—Service to the guru with full confidence, as it is said in that very same place (11.17.27):
"One should know me as the teacher; one should never disregard me."
One should not feel resentment toward the Guru with the thought that he is merely mortal, for he embodies all the gods.
4. Following the path of the virtuous;
as it is said in the Skanda Purāṇa:
"That path which is free from affliction should be sought as the cause of all that is auspicious."
By which the virtuous of old set out, having attained their ascetic toil.
And in the *Brahmayāmala*:
"Devotion to Hari that is exclusive [of other deities], when devoid of the injunctions of the Vedas, Smṛtis, Purāṇas, and Pañcarātra, leads only to calamity. (RBhrs 1.2.101)
This exclusive devotion appears so because of a lack of inquiry;
in reality, however, it is not thus, since it is observed to be contrary to the scriptures.
5. Inquiry into the True Dharma, as stated in the Nāradīya:
"The desired goal of all these is accomplished very soon."
Those whose minds are resolute for the sake of awakening to the true Dharma.
6. The renunciation of enjoyments and so forth for the sake of Kṛṣṇa, as stated in the Padma Purāṇa: "For you who have renounced enjoyments at the proper time, dedicating them to Hari..."
Established in the world of Viṣṁu, she remains unperturbed by prosperity and awaits [her time].
7—Dwelling in Dvārakā and other places;
as stated in the Skanda Purāṇa:
"For a year, or for six months, or for a month, or even for half a month."
All the men and women dwelling in Dvārakā possess four arms.
By the word "etcetera," the abode of Puruṣottama is also included, as stated in the Brāhma [Purāṇa]:
"Oh, how great is the majesty of this sacred field (kṣetra), extending ten yojanas in every direction!"
Where those dwelling in heaven behold all [beings] as indeed four-armed.
Dwelling in the Ganges and other such places,
as described in the first [chapter] (1.19.6)— "She who indeed [is adorned] with shimmering, auspicious tulasī... and so forth.
Whose water-channel is enriched by the dust from Kṛṣṇa’s feet— what dying person would not serve that river which purifies both worlds along with their lords?
8— Adaptation to one's actual needs,
as stated in the Nāradīya:
"One who knows the purpose should accept only so much wealth as would suffice for his own maintenance."
In cases of excess or deficiency, one falls away from the ultimate truth.
9. The honor accorded to Hari’s day, as stated in the Brahma-vaivarta Purāṇa: "It pacifies all sins and likewise bestows ultimate merit."
The remembrance of Govinda and fasting on the Ekādaśī day [bring great merit] for men.
10. Reverence for the Dhātrī, Aśvattha, and others, as stated in the Skanda Purāṇa:
"The Aśvattha, Tulasī, Dhātrī, cows, the earth, brāhmaṇas, and Vaiṣṇavas..."
When worshipped, saluted, and meditated upon, they destroy the evil of human beings.
11. Now, the abandonment of those who are averse to Śrī Kṛṣṇa, as stated in the Kātyāyana-saṃhitā: "Better is dwelling within the cage of the flames of the sacrificial fire."
Nor [should one endure] the calamity of living among people who are averse to the thoughts of Śauri.

And in the *Viṣṇu-rahasya*: "I consider embracing even serpents, tigers, and aquatic creatures to be better than association with those who are like thorns— those who serve various deities while professing to worship the One God alone."
12–14— The triad beginning with "not binding oneself to disciples," as in the seventh [chapter] (7.13.8): "One should not bind oneself to disciples, nor should one study many books."
One should not employ explanatory discourse, nor should one ever undertake any undertakings.
15. Lack of meanness even in worldly dealings, as stated in the Padma Purāṇa:
"Whether food, clothing, or the means of subsistence are unobtained or lost..."
Having become firm-minded, one should remember Hari alone with the intellect.
16—Being under the sway of grief and so forth;
as it is said in that very same [text]:
"He whose mind is overwhelmed by states such as grief, indignation, and the like..."
How could there be any possibility of the manifestation of Mukunda therein?
17. Ignorance regarding other deities, as stated in that very same [text]:
"Hari alone is to be constantly worshipped, the Lord of all lords of the gods."
The others, such as Brahmā, Rudra, and so forth, are never to be held in contempt.
18. Not causing agitation to living beings;
as it says in the Mahābhārata:
"He who is compassionate does not agitate people, just as a father [does not agitate] his son."
For one who is thus purified, Hṛṣīkeśa quickly becomes gracious toward him.
19. The avoidance of offenses against service and the Name, as stated in the *Vārāha-purāṇa*: "O Earth, those offenses against my worship which are proclaimed by me..."
These, however, must always be avoided with great effort by one who follows the path of Viṣṇu.
And in the *Pādma*:
"Even one who has committed every offense is liberated if he takes refuge in Hari;
whereas he who commits offenses against Hari is like a man of dust with two feet. (RBhṛs 1.2.119)
The basis of one's name may at times be such that one transcends [suffering] merely by means of that name;
yet, due to an offense against a friend who bears one's name, one indeed falls low.
20. Intolerance toward their censure and so forth;
as stated in the Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam (10.74.40):
"Hearing the censure of the Blessed Lord, or that of people devoted to Him..."
Furthermore, he who does not depart from it also goes downward, fallen from his meritorious deeds.
21. Now, regarding the wearing of Vaiṣṇava marks, as stated in the Padma Purāṇa: "Those who have a garland of tulasī and lotus seeds clinging to their necks..."
Those whose upper arms are marked with the conch and discus,
or those who bear shining vertical sectarian marks (*ūrdhva-puṇḍra*) upon the surface of their foreheads—
those Vaiṣṇavas quickly purify the world.
22. Retaining the syllables of the Name;
as stated in the Skanda Purāṇa:
"The forehead marked with the syllables of Hari’s name and adorned by the Gopī-mṛḍa [tilaka]..."
The fierce soldiers of Yama shall not touch one who wears a garland of tulasī upon his chest.
And in the *Pādma*:
"One should mark the body with the syllables of the name of Kṛṣṇa using sandalwood paste and so forth;
having become a purifier of the world, one shall attain his world. (RBhrs 1.2.124)
23. Wearing the remains of offerings (*nirmālya-dhṛti*); as it is said in the eleventh [chapter] (11.6.46):
"Adorned with the garlands, perfumes, garments, ornaments, and unguents used by you..."
We are your servants who eat the remnants; may we conquer your illusion.
And in the Skanda Purāṇa: "O Sage Nārada, he whose body touches the floral offering (nirmālya) removed by Kṛṣṇa becomes liberated from all diseases as well as from sins."
24. First, the *tāṇḍava* dance, as described in the *Dvārakā-māhātmya*: "He who dances with a joyful soul through many emotional states (*bhāvas*) out of devotion..."
He burns away his sins even throughout hundreds of Manvantaras.
Likewise, in the words of Śrī Nārada: "By the frequent clapping of hands before the Lord of Śrī while He dances, all the birds of sin residing within the body are made to fly away. (RBhrs 1.2.128)
25—Prostration like a staff; as it is said in the Nāradīya: "Even a single prostration made to Kṛṣṇa..."
It is not equal to the ten purificatory baths (*avabhṛtha*) of the horse-sacrifice (*aśvamedha*).
One who has performed ten horse-sacrifices returns to birth;
but one who bows to Kṛṣṇa does not return to further existence.
26. Rising up to meet [the guest], as described in the *Brahmāṇḍa-purāṇa*:
"Seeing Janārdana approaching ahead, mounted upon his vehicle..."
A man who rises [to greet] casts off all sin.

27. Following in procession (*anuvrajyā*); as stated in the *Bhaviṣyottara Purāṇa*: "Whether going by chariot, or at the side, behind, or in front, all—even those starting from the lowest castes—become equal to Viṣṇu himself."
28. Movement according to the place—his place is both a sacred site (tīrtha) and a home; his movement therein is just like [the movement] at that sacred site.
In another Purāṇa:
"Only those two feet of Hari are praiseworthy which travel to sacred pilgrimage sites (tīrthas), for they are capable of delivering one from the desert wilderness of saṃsāra."
And regarding the abode (*ālaya*), as stated in the *Haribhaktisudhodaya*:
"The wise person of great devotion, entering the abode of Viṣṇu for the sake of seeing Him, shall never again enter the prison of his mother’s womb. (RBhrs 1.2.134)

29. Circumambulation (*parikrama*): As it is said in that very same place—“He who turns back again while circumambulating Viṣṇu, for him that very turning back will not occur again within worldly existence (*bhava*). (RBhṛs 1.2.135)

And in the *Skanda Purāṇa*, in the *Caturmāsya-māhātmya*: "O foremost of brahmins, by four circumambulations, the entire world of moving and non-moving beings has been traversed; that is equivalent to visiting sacred pilgrimage sites and so forth. (RBhrs 1.2.136)

30. Now, regarding worship (arcanam): Worship consists of the presentation of ritual offerings (upacārāṇām) preceded by the completion of preliminary rites such as purification (śuddhi) and ritual placement (nyāsa), performed with the recitation of mantras. RBhrs_1.2.137 //
Thus, as stated in the tenth [chapter] (10.81.19):
"For men, the worship of His feet is the root of both heaven and liberation, of all prosperities on the earth of the netherworld, and of all supernatural perfections. (RBhrs 1.2.138)
And in the *Viṣṇurahasya*:
"Those men on earth who perform the worship of Śrī Viṣṇu go to the eternal, supreme abode of Viṣṇu’s bliss. (RBhrs 1.2.139)
31. Service (*paricaryā*):
Service, however, consists of attending upon [the teacher] and the preparation of requisites and so forth;
likewise, it includes worship with various items such as umbrellas and musical instruments. (RBhrs 1.2.140)
As it is said in the Nāradīya: "He who stays in the temple of Hari for even a moment or half a moment goes to the supreme abode; how much more so those who are devoted to his service? (RBhrs 1.2.141)
As it is said in the fourth [chapter] (4.21.31):
"The inclination toward service at whose feet purifies the impurity of the intellect accumulated over all births for ascetics..."
It destroys instantly while increasing day by day,
like a river flowing from the big toe of one's foot.
There may indeed be various ancillary elements for worship and service;
however, they have not been written down here out of fear of making the book too voluminous.

32. Now, regarding song, as it is stated in the *Laiṅga*: "A Brāhmaṇa who sings incessantly of the supreme one called Vāsudeva attains the same world as Hari (sālokya); his singing of Rudra would be even more meritorious. (RBhṛs 1.2.144)
33. Now, regarding *saṃkīrtana*: "The loud proclamation of the Name, pastimes, qualities, and so forth, is indeed *kīrtana*. (RBhrs 1.2.145)
In that regard, there is the chanting of the name,
as stated in the Viṣṇudharma:
"He in whose speech the auspicious name 'Kṛṣṇa' proceeds..."
O Indra among kings, millions of great sins are reduced to ashes.
The glorification of divine pastimes (*līlā-kīrtana*), as in the seventh [canto] (7.9.18): "I am that very person of my beloved friend, the Supreme Deity..."
O Nṛsiṃha, by chanting Your playful stories sung by Viriñca,
one is quickly liberated from the material qualities and crosses over all difficulties through association with the *haṃsas* who dwell at the abode of Your two feet.
The glorification of virtues,
as in the first [chapter] (1.5.22):
"For this is the fruit for a man of his austerity, or of his sacred learning..."
The meaning of the well-performed sacrifice and the well-spoken hymn, when offered with an enlightened mind, has been determined by the seers to be unswerving: namely,
the description of the qualities of the Lord of Excellent Fame.
34. Now, as for recitation (*japa*): the easy pronunciation of a mantra is designated as *japa*.
As stated in the Pādma [Purāṇa]:
"O King, this mantra 'Salutation to Kṛṣṇa' accomplishes all aims;
for devotees who recite it, it bestows the fruits of heaven and liberation. (RBhrs 1.2.150)
35. Now, as for *vijñapti* (informal communication), as stated in the *Skānda*: "Whatever communication is made by speech directed toward Hari..."
By that very [means], the bolt on the door of liberation has been removed for you; thus, liberation has been granted to you.
"Consisting of earnest prayer, characterized by a sense of wretchedness, and filled with longing—such is the various petition addressed to Kṛṣṇa described by the wise. (RBhrs 1.2.152)
In that regard, it consists of longing,
as stated in the *Pādmapurāṇa*: "Just as [the desire] of young women for a youth, and of youths for a young woman..."
Just as the mind finds delight in that, may the mind find delight in you.
The awakening of dejection,
as in that very same place:
"There is no one equal to me in sinful nature, nor is there anyone else so guilty."
Even in the face of such a lapse, I feel shame; what can I say, O Supreme Person?
Consisting of intense longing,
as it is said in the *Śrī-Nārada-Pañcarātra*: "O Lord of the Universe, when will You, endowed with Śrī, speak with Your profound voice?"
With a fly-whisk held in your hand, you shall say to me, "Do it thus."
Or as it is said:
"O Lotus-eyed One, when shall I, weeping and chanting Your names on the banks of the Yamunā, perform the *tāṇḍava* dance? (RBhṛs 1.2.156)
36. Now, regarding the recitation of hymns (stava-pāṭha): The wise have proclaimed the Gītā, the Stavarāja, and other such hymns.
As it is said in the Skanda Purāṇa:
"Those whose tongues are adorned by the multitude of jewels that are the hymns of praise to Śrī Kṛṣṇa are to be saluted by sages and Siddhas, and are to be venerated by the gods."
And in the *Nārasiṃha*:
"He who praises Madhusūdana with hymns and eulogies before the Lord,
being liberated from all sins, shall attain the world of Viṣṇu."
37. Now, the tasting of the food offering (*naivedya*), as stated in the *Pādma*: "The food offering is grain mixed with *tulasī*."
He who constantly eats what has been especially sprinkled with the water from the feet before Murāri obtains the merit of ten million times ten thousand sacrifices.
38. Now, the tasting of the water for the feet (*pādyāsvāda*), as it is said in that very same [text]:
"For those who have neither charity nor oblations, neither Vedic study nor worship of the gods..."
They too, having drunk the water from his feet, attain the supreme goal.
39. Now, regarding the fragrance of incense, as it is said in the *Haribhaktisudhodaya*:
"The smelling, on all sides, of the remains of the incense offered to Hari..."
For those bitten by the serpents of existence, this ritual of nasal administration (nasya) removes the poison.
Now, regarding the fragrance of the floral offering (*mālya-saurabhya*),
as it is said in the *Tantra*:
"When the fragrance of Hari’s floral offering has entered the cavity of the nose..."
The confinement within the cage of evil immediately comes to dissolution.
And in the *Agastya-saṃhitā*: "O ascetic, the smelling of incense, flowers,
and other articles that have been offered is declared here to be the purification of the infinite sense of smell."
40. Now, regarding the touching of the Śrī-mūrti, as stated in the Viṣṇudharmottara: "Having touched the abode of Viṣṇu, one becomes pure, endowed with faith."
Completely liberated from the bonds of evil, one shall obtain all desires.
41. Now, regarding the vision of the Śrī-mūrti, as stated in the Vārāha-purāṇa: "O Vasundharā, those who behold Govinda in Vṛndāvana..."
They do not go to the city of Yama; they go to the destination of those who have performed meritorious deeds.

42. Regarding the viewing of the *ārātrika* lamp, as stated in the *Skānda*: "Tens of millions of sins of killing Brahmins, tens of millions of sins of approaching those who should not be approached..."
The face of Viṣṇu, together with its nocturnal splendor, burns by its mere light.
Regarding the viewing of the festival,
as stated in the *Bhaviṣyottara Purāṇa*:
"Those who behold Keśava seated upon the chariot, even with mere curiosity..."
All the hosts of deities become outcastes and the like.
By the word "etcetera" (ādi), the vision of worship is intended, as stated in the Āgneya-purāṇa:
"He who, with devotion, beholds Hari as one who has been worshipped or is currently being worshipped... (RBhrs 1.2.169).
43. Now, regarding *śravaṇa*: *śravaṇa* is the hearing of [the Lord’s] deeds, qualities, and so forth. (RBhṛs 1.2.170)
In that regard, there is the hearing of the Name;
as it is said in the *Garuḍa*:
"It is the sole remedy for one whose movements have perished after being bitten by the serpent of saṃsāra."
Upon hearing the Vaiṣṇava mantra "Kṛṣṇa," a person shall indeed be liberated.
The hearing of his life-story,
as in the fourth [canto] (4.29.41): "In that [place],
the great sound of the deeds of the slayer of Madhu resounded..."
O King, those who drink from the rivers flowing everywhere with the remainder of nectar, their thirst quenched by holding them firmly to their ears,
are not touched by hunger, thirst, fear, sorrow, or delusion.
Hearing of the qualities [of the Lord],
as stated in the Twelfth [Canto] (12.3.15):
"But that which is the recitation of the qualities of the One of Excellent Fame..."
That which destroys inauspiciousness is constantly sung;
one who desires pure devotion to Kṛṣṇa should listen to that very [song] perpetually and repeatedly.
Then, regarding that glance of his, as it is said in the tenth book (10.14.8):
"He, observing your compassion with great care..."
Experiencing the ripening of what was done by oneself,
you who live while offering salutations with heart, speech, and body at the state of liberation— you are the heir to that inheritance.
Now, as for memory:
"Memory is said to be a connection with the mind in whatever manner it may occur. (RBhṛs 1.2.175)
As it is said in the Viṣṇu Purāṇa (5.17.17):
"I go for refuge to that unborn, eternal Hari, by the mere remembrance of whom one becomes a vessel for all auspiciousness."
And as it is said in the Padma Purāṇa:
"Salutations to that Self of Consciousness, by remembering whose name at the time of departure or even while not departing, the flood of sins of men is instantly destroyed. (RBhrs 1.2.177)
Now, regarding meditation (dhyāna):
meditation is the thorough contemplation of form, qualities, play, service, and so forth. (RBhṛs 1.2.178)
In that regard, the meditation on form (*rūpa-dhyāna*) is as stated in the *Nārasiṃha*:
"Meditation on the pair of the Lord’s feet is declared to be free from duality."
Even for the wicked, that which is beneficial is ordained through association with others.
Meditation on the qualities [of the Lord],
as stated in the Viṣṇudharma:
"Those who always perform the recollection of Hari's qualities with devotion..."
Having exhausted the flood of their impurities, they enter the abode of Hari.
Meditation on the Divine Play,
as described in the *Padma*: "All the essences of sweetness and all that is most wondrous."
Meditating upon the charming deeds of Hari, one is liberated.
Meditation on service,
as stated in another Purāṇa:
"Always serving Hari with mental offerings."
Others attained him directly, though he is inaccessible to speech and mind.
Now, regarding service (dāsya):
service is the offering of one's actions; it is also, in every way, the performance of his personal attendance (kaiṅkarya).

Regarding that, the first [type] is as stated in the Skanda Purāṇa: "Even natural action, when dedicated to the Lord, becomes the dharma of a devotee; how much more so, then, action that is intentionally offered? (RBhṛs 1.2.184).
"O Blessed One, one's own natural duty and the performance of recitation, meditation, worship, and so forth—this twofold service has been offered to Kṛṣṇa by the Vaiṣṇavas. (RBhrs 1.2.185)

For one whose faith is weak, it is said that their qualification for ritual action is very slight; some declare that such a person's devotion consists solely in offering themselves as a servant to Hari.
Second, as stated in the *Nāradīya*:
"He whose effort toward service to Hari is performed through action, mind, and speech in all states whatsoever, is called one liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*). (RBhrs 1.2.187)
Now, regarding friendship:
trust and the conduct of a friend—friendship is said to be of two kinds.
Among these, the first is as stated in the Mahābhārata:
"O Govinda, this is my vow: your devotee never perishes."
Thus, remembering again and again, I sustain my vital breaths.
Likewise, in the eleventh [chapter] (11.2.53):
"Even for the sake of the prosperity of the three worlds, his memory remains unimpeded; he is sought after by the gods and others who have not yet conquered their own selves."
He who does not waver even for half a moment from the lotus feet of the Blessed One is indeed the foremost of Vaiṣṇavas.
Mere faith is the cause of one's qualification for devotion to Him;
however, this specific kind of conviction [is required] regarding Keśava as a subordinate factor.
The second [type], as stated in the *Agastya-saṃhitā*:
"Some, devoted to service, lie in palaces; they look upon him as if he were a human being, and interact with him like kinsmen. (RBhrs 1.2.192)
Its state of being an auxiliary to passion arises from its independence from the path of ritual injunction;
and by means of these two paths, the joy of friendship is considered to be accomplished.
Now, regarding the offering of oneself, as it is said in the Eleventh [Book] (11.29.34):
"When a mortal has abandoned all ritual actions..."
Having offered himself and being desired by me,
he who attains immortality is indeed fit to become one with my own self.
Scholars establish two meanings for the word "self" (ātman):
some [hold it to be] the embodied being who is the locus of the "I-notion," while others [hold it to be] the body which is the object of the "mine-notion."
In that regard, the embodied soul is as described in the *Yāmunācārya-stotra* (verse 49): "Whether I possess any quality whatsoever in my body and so forth, or am of such a nature [as I may be],"
Therefore, here I am, surrendered this very day by me at your lotus feet.
As it is said in the *Bhakti-viveka*:
"Just as one would not worry about protecting a sold animal, so too, having surrendered the body to Hari, one should desist from its protection. (RBhrs 1.2.197)
Because of their difficulty, these two— the rare [acts of] offering friendship and self-surrender—
attain the status of being worthy of accomplishment only for certain steadfast individuals.
Now, regarding the offering of one's own beloved,
as it is said in the Eleventh Canto (11.11.41):
"Whatever is most desired in the world, and whatever is exceedingly dear to oneself..."
One should offer each of those to me; that conduces to infinity.
Furthermore, all activity for that purpose is as stated in the Pañcarātra:
"O Sage, whatever action is performed, whether worldly or Vedic,"
One who desires devotion should perform that very practice which is conducive to the service of Hari.
Now, regarding the taking of refuge, as it is said in the *Haribhaktivilāsa* (11.677):
"Declaring with one's speech, 'I am yours,' and likewise realizing it with one's mind..."
Residing in that state, he who has sought refuge rejoices with his body.
And in the Śrī-Nārasiṃha Purāṇa:
"O God of gods, Janārdana, I have come to you for refuge.
I deliver from suffering that person who has thus sought refuge.
53—Now, regarding the service of those [deities]:
Tulāsya; as stated in the Skanda Purāṇa:
"She who, when seen, pacifies the accumulation of all sins, and when touched, purifies the body..."

Salutations to that Tulasī, who is saluted by all diseases as their dispeller, who terrifies Death himself when sprinkled, who brings about proximity to the Blessed Lord Kṛṣṇa when planted, and who, when placed at His feet, bestows the fruit of liberation. RBhrs_1,2.203 //
And likewise in that very same place:
"The auspicious *tulasī* is seen, touched, meditated upon, praised, saluted, lauded, planted, served, and constantly worshipped."
Those who worship the goddess Tulasī nine times every day dwell in the abode of Hari for thousands of crores of yugas.
54—Now, regarding the scripture (*śāstra*): here, "scripture" is defined as that which expounds devotion (*bhakti*).
As it is stated in the Skanda Purāṇa:
"Those men in this world who listen to and recite the Vaiṣṇava scriptures are blessed; Kṛṣṇa is pleased with them. (RBhrs 1.2.207)
But those men who honor the Vaiṣṇava scriptures in their home become liberated from all sins and are praised by the gods.

(15) Caturaḥ—One who performs four [tasks] simultaneously is called *catura*. (RBhṛs 2.1.86)
For example:
"By the arrangement of female pigeons, he [the cowherd] [resembles] a herd of cows;
by the rippling of his sidelong glances, he [resembles] a group of cowherd girls."
Gladdening his friends with his prowess in most wonderful battles and bestowing fearlessness upon them, Hari shone forth.
(16) Dakṣa: One who acts swiftly even in what is difficult to perform is designated as "dexterous" (dakṣa).
As it is said in the *Śrī-daśama* (10.59.17):
"O best of the Kurus, whatever weapons and missiles were hurled by the warriors,
Hari cut them down with his own sharp arrows, shooting one for each weapon-bearer."
Or as it is said:
"O remover of sins, join with me and perform a dance together"—
thus desiring to fulfill the prayer of all the gopīs.
He displayed such lightness in the grace of his movement that they saw him even more clearly, as if he were right by each of their own sides.
(17) Grateful: One should be grateful, being one who recognizes services and other deeds performed [for oneself]. (RBhṛs 2.1.91)
As it is said in the Mahābhārata: "This debt has grown so great that it will not depart from my heart—that Kṛṣṇā cried out 'Govinda! to me while I was living far away. (RBhrs 2.1.92)
Or as it is said:
"Reflecting deeply on his past devotion, Śauri took the maiden and offered great honor to the one who bears the bear-marked crest."
A virtuous person would not forget even a small favor done for them in any way; how much less so one who is the crest-jewel at the very peak of the assembly of the virtuous?
(18) *Sudṛḍhavratas*:
one whose vows and observances are true is a *sudṛḍhavratas*.
In that regard, one who is true to his promise,
as it says in the *Harivaṃśa* (2.68.38)—
[note: this verse is not found in the critical edition]— :
Neither the hosts of gods and gandharvas, nor the rākṣasas,
nor the asuras, nor even the yakṣas and pannagas are able to thwart my vow.
O Sage, you are indeed capable; let it truly be so for you.
Or as it is said:
"Having playfully rendered the son of Ākhaṇḍala (Indra) and Pāṇḍu (Arjuna) devoid of the *apārijāta* tree, the enemy of Kaṃsa..."
Fulfilling his own vow,
he made Satyabhāmā and Kṛṣṇā happy.
The vow of truthfulness is as follows:
"O Kṛṣṇa, while performing the difficult task of lifting up the mountain, you revealed your own vow: 'My devotee shall not suffer. (RBhrs 2.1.97)
(19) One who knows the proper place, time, and recipient—such a person performs the appropriate action for each respective occasion. RBhṛs 2.1.98.
For example:
"In the three worlds, there is no other time equal to the autumnal moonlight; nor is there anywhere a place for play equal to Vṛndāvana."
Reflecting that no lotus-eyed girl among the young women of Vraja could possibly be her equal,
my mind repeatedly became filled with longing for the rasa of the Rāsa festival.
(20) The Eye of the Treatise—
He whose action conforms to the treatise is called "the Eye of the Treatise."
For example:
"The eye of the enemy of Kaṃsa became, as it were, a scripture for the perception of the truth."
But having taken only the lotus-eyes from the multitude of young women, // RBhrs_2,1.101 //

(21) *Śuci*—purity—is said to be of two kinds: the purifying (*pāvana*) and the pure (*viśuddha*). The purifying is that which destroys evil; the pure is that which has abandoned all defects. (RBhṛs 2.1.102)
In that regard, he is the purifier;
as it is said in the Padma Purāṇa:
"O treasure-house of virtues, worship him who is sincere and the purifier of all purifiers."
The mind of one who is colored by faith is exceedingly devoted to the crown of the One of Excellent Fame;
for alas, even the mere radiance of the sun that is His name, arising within the cavity of the heart,
destroys the mass of darkness that is great sin.
It was pure, as follows:
"Alas! There is neither deceit nor violence in Acyuta; nor indeed is there any lack of nobility in Satrājit."
O Srimanta, how can you now so vainly desire to forcibly establish friendship with the Kaustubha?
(22) One who has mastery is said to be self-controlled and one who has conquered the senses.
As it was said in the first [chapter] (1.11.37): "Even Madana was defeated by those women through their modest glances and their pure, lovely smiles that betrayed their unrestrained passion."
Bewildered, they dropped their bows— those most excellent women who, by means of their deceits, had been unable to disturb his senses.
(23) Steadfast means one who acts until the arising of the fruit; such is "steadfast."
Just as Murāri did not experience weariness while wandering through the forest,
nor did he consider the calamity of entering the cave of the bears.
Having brought back the very jewel, he entered the city;
for indeed, the exertion of those with resolute minds culminates in the attainment of results.
(24) The Tamed One—
He is tamed who can endure even unbearable hardship that is appropriate for his practice.
For example:
"Though his limbs were tender, Hari—whose teeth were like those of a goat—endured even the hardship of living with his teacher through sincere devotion; he was not [merely] this [ordinary being]."
Alas, the nature of those who transcend the world is exceedingly difficult to fathom; when reflected upon, it spreads a certain wondrous thought within the mind.
(25) One who is of a patient disposition (*kṣamāśīla*) is proclaimed to be one who endures offenses.
As it is said in the *Māgha-kāvya* (*Śiśupālavadha*, 16.25):
"Keśava gave no reply to the King of Cedi, even though he was cursing him."
A cloud does not utter the cry of a jackal,
nor does a lion produce the howls of a jackal.
Or as it is said in the *Stotraratna* (60) by the teacher of the Yamunā:
"O best of the Raghus, O Kṛṣṇa, that you became such [a friend] to a crow when he bowed down to you, and that you were compassionate toward Caidya..."
O deluded one, you have offended Him in every birth; tell me, what transgression is there that is beyond His forgiveness? He is the bestower of union [with Him]. (RBhrs 2.1.113)
(26) Profound—That which has an intention difficult to awaken is said to be "profound. (RBhṛs 2.1.114)
For example:
"In Vṛndāvana, even though Hari is being intensely worshipped with hymns of praise by Varātri, he is not able to be known by Brahmā, whether he be angry or pleased. (RBhrs 2.1.115)
Or as it is said:
"Even though Hari was intoxicated by the wine of his love for the youthful Rādhā, he was recognized as being without change of state by Rāma, who was well-versed in such matters. (RBhrs 2.1.116)
(27) One who possesses fortitude is full of aspiration and remains steadfast even when faced with causes of agitation.
Among these, the first is as follows:
although the Enemy of Kaṃsa intensely cherished fame, he nevertheless accepted the renown of having slain the Lord of Magadha.
Did he himself bestow incomparable fame upon Bhīma?
For what is there that those endowed with superhuman virtues need not possess?
The second, as follows:
[the praise] of one who was censured by the son of Damaghoṣa, and [the censure] of one who was praised by the sages with agitation.
In the assembly of the Rājasūya sacrifice, no sign of agitation whatsoever was perceived in him by the lords of the earth.
(28) Equanimous—
one who is free from attachment and aversion is called "equanimous" by the wise.
As it is said in the Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam (10.16.33):
"Punishment is indeed appropriate for this one who has committed an offense;
Your incarnation is for the purpose of subduing the wicked."
Since you look with an equal eye even upon the sons of your enemies, you bestow self-restraint as a fruit that is truly commendable.
Or as it is said:
"O best of the Yadus, even an enemy, if he is pure, is to be honored by you; even a son, if he is wicked, is to be punished."
Furthermore, for the Lord of all, who is free from partiality, it is impossible for your conduct ever to be inconsistent.
(29) The Generous One— He who is a hero in giving is called "the generous one" (vadānya).
For example:
"By the slayer of Kaṃsa, the desires of all seekers were rendered futile through the complete fulfillment of their wishes."
Out of a sense of shame, as it were, the wish-fulfilling gem, the cow of plenty,
and the tree of paradise resort to Dvāravatī.
Or for example:

"Those whose inner apartments consist of a thousand women filled with sixteen [qualities], and who likewise possess wives numbering one hundred and eight, shine on all sides surrounded by that same number [of attendants]."
Who could be equal to him who daily bestowed upon each one of them calves that were still nursing, adorned with ornaments, and born from their first pregnancy, all at once?
(30) Dhārmikaḥ—
one who performs and causes others to perform dharma is called dhārmika.
Just as you, O Lord of Gopas, increased the strength of the protected bull with its four feet, so did you cause it to grow.
Moving about at his own will throughout the three worlds, he forcibly devoured whatever things were tainted by unrighteousness.
Or as it is said:
"While the lords are being incessantly drawn away by you through the expansive displays of your sacrifices,"
O Mukunda, the host of deities with beautiful brows, being distressed,
bows down to your ninth incarnation.
(31) A hero— one who is energetic in battle, a warrior, and skilled in the employment of weapons.
Among these, the first is as follows:
Having plunged into the lake of the vast battle, he performs the practice of sporting within the forest of his enemies' lotuses.
You throb with trunk-like trembling arms;
O destroyer of evil, you possess the grace of a lordly elephant.
The second is as follows:
"In the terrible host of Jarāsaṃdha’s Akṣauhiṇīs, in an instant,
not a single person was seen there who was not bitten by Hari’s weapons, which were like serpents."
(32) Karuṇa: One who cannot endure the suffering of others is called compassionate (karuṇa).
For example:
"Of kings who were themselves blinded by the dense masses of the darkness of suffering within the prison of the Lord of Magadha, whose depths were unfathomable..."
Today, I bow to that friend of the lotus-like feet of the Joy of the Yadu clan, who, out of compassion, fashioned eyes filled with bliss for the multitude.
Or as it is said:
"To him whose splendor was consecrated by the falling tears from his eyes, and who had swallowed up his own manifestation due to the surging waves of intense haste..."
Salutations for the grace of the Blessed One, who comes instantly under the sway of remembrance, by the son of the celestial river (Gaṅgā) while he was lying upon his bed of arrows at nightfall.
(33) Mānyamānakṛt—one who honors those worthy of honor, such as teachers, brahmins, elders, and so forth, is a *mānyamānakṛt*. (RBhṛs 2.1.135)
For example:
"Having bowed to the lotus-feet of the guru,
and likewise to his father and elder brother, he then remained prostrate."
Thus Hari, with folded hands and with words, [spoke] to the elders of the Yadus, beginning with my own grandfather.
(34) *Dakṣiṇa*:
One whose conduct is gentle and characterized by good character is called *dakṣiṇa* by the wise.
For example:
A servant does not see even the faults of his masters,
and he regards even the slightest service rendered as manifold.
Even toward the malicious, this Supreme Person, whose mind is stainless through his virtuous conduct, manifests no malice.
(35) The Disciplined One—He who is said to be "disciplined" is one who has abandoned arrogance. (RBhṛS 2.1.139)
As it says in the *Māgha-kāvya* (13.7): "O King, here is a sight [of him] from afar as he wishes to alight from his chariot with haste."
Having himself first descended, Hari distinguished his own humility with great agitation.

(36) *Hrīmān*— one who, when the secret of the god of love is known by others, or when praise is being offered, experiences contraction due to modesty (*śālīnatva*) is called *hrīmān*. (RBhṛs 2.1.141)
As it is said in the *Lalitā-Mādhava* (9.40):
"While Mount Govardhana trembles slightly from the shaking of his hand out of fear of being gazed upon by the region of the breasts of the cowherd girls as they raise them up..."
Victorious is the Enemy of Madhu, who, his face bowed in humility upon seeing Rāma with a smiling countenance before him, had his praise commenced by all the cowherds who were afflicted by fear.
(37) Protector of those who have come for refuge—one who protects those who have sought refuge is a protector of those who have come for refuge. // RBhrs_2,1.143 //
Just as this lord of the Yadavas, upon seeing Induvati suddenly approaching him even though she had committed an offense in this battle, cast aside his fear of the fever of anger— so too should you.
(38) The enjoyer who is happy— untouched even by the scent of suffering— shall become truly happy.
Among these, the first is as follows:

"The burden of your jewel-ornaments, which cannot be obtained even by the King who subdues wealth through his royal conduct, and the triple symphony at your gate, which is difficult to attain even for the wielder of the thunderbolt in a dream."

O Best of the Yadus, in this world, who else besides you is a true enjoyer, possessing by your side women as weighty as Gaurī, endowed with many digits of the moon, and whose every limb is lovely? 2.1.146.
The second [example] is as follows:
"He knows not of decline, nor of withering, nor of absorption in the duties of his own home; he knows not of terror, nor of trembling, nor indeed of any affliction whatsoever."
In the forest of Vṛndāvana, Hari sports incessantly and most intensely with beautiful women who have fully embraced their friends, the god of love.
(39) The devotee-friend (*bhakta-suhṛt*) is considered to be of two kinds: the one who is well-served and the kinsman of the servant (*dāsa-bandhu*). // RBhrs_2,1.148 //
Among these, the first is as stated in the *Viṣṇudharma*:
"With merely a single leaf of *tulasī* and a handful of water, He who is affectionate toward His devotees sells His very self to His devotees. (RBhrs 2.1.149)
The second [verse], as in the first (1.9.37):
"Abandoning his own scripture, he has leaped down from his chariot to undertake my true proposition."
With his feet placed upon the chariot, he rushed forward like Hari against a moving elephant, his upper garment trailing behind as he went to slay him.
(40) Subjugated by love—one who is subjugated by mere dearness is one who would be subjugated by love. (RBhṛs 2.1.151)
As it is said in the Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam (10.80.19):
"Exceedingly delighted by the touch of the limbs of his dear friend, the brahminical sage,
the lotus-eyed Lord, being filled with joy, shed tears from His eyes."
Or as it is said in that very same place (10.9.18):
"Seeing the exhaustion of his own mother, whose limbs were perspiring and whose braided hair and garlands were disheveled, Kṛṣṇa was moved by compassion and bound himself. (RBhrs 2.1.153)
(41) Sarva-śubhaṅkaraḥ—
he who acts for the benefit of all shall be Sarva-śubhaṅkara.
For instance:
"The sages have achieved their purpose through amusements, and all the righteous have attained their ends by the destruction of the wicked."
And by crushing their bodies in battle, what was not made wholesome for whom by Hari? Even the wicked.
(42) *Pratāpī*: one who possesses majesty; one who causes distress to enemies through the manifestation of prowess; one who enjoys renown. RBhrs_2,1.156 //
For example:
"O Kṛṣṇa, the world is scorched by the heat of your majesty."
The darkness of the caves became a refuge for the owls of the terrible asuras.
(43) Kīrtimān— one who is renowned for stainless virtues is celebrated as "Kīrtimān."
For example:
"Even while leading your fame— the kinsman of the night-lotus— toward whiteness on all sides by means of moonlight,"
O delighter of Nanda, how indeed did you fashion the three worlds, which are permeated by devotion to Kṛṣṇa?
Or as it says in the *Lalitā-Mādhava* (5.18):
"Terrified, Girijā leaves Rudra when she does not see his dark throat;
seeing it white, she throws down her garment, while he, clad in blue, is struck with wonder."
Thinking it to be milk, Yamī, longing for water, cooks the water from the Ābhīras while Nārada plays the lute to the song of Dāmodara’s glory.
(44) One who wins the affection of the world: The wise know that one who wins the affection of the world is a worthy vessel for the affections of people. (RBhṛs 2.1.161)
As it was said in the first [skandha] (1.11.9):
"O lotus-eyed one, whenever you departed for the Kurus or the Madhus out of a desire to see your friends..."
In that regard, O Acyuta, for one deprived of you, a single moment would be like ten million years, just as it is for us who are deprived of the sun for our eyes.
Or as it is said:
"The truthful blessing 'Victory! Victory! Victory! resounds from the sages, and the deep, sweet-sounding chorus of the praise of the host of gods has appeared."
A great clamor of the city women resounded on all sides out of joy;
for who among them did not feel devotion toward Hari upon the stage?
(45) Taking refuge in the virtuous—
He who sides exclusively with the good shall be one who takes refuge in the virtuous.
For instance:
"O Puruṣottama, had you not descended into this world for the welfare of the earth..."
I do not know what the fate of virtuous people would have been had they fallen into the midst of the circle of the Vikaṭāsuras. Alas!
(46) Captivating the minds of throngs of women—
captivating the minds of throngs of women, he is the enchanter of the multitude of beauties.
As it is said in the Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam (10.90.26):
"Even when merely heard, He forcibly draws away the minds of women; how much more so for those who behold Him, He who is widely traversed and widely glorified!"
Or as it is said:
"O Mādhava, you are a magnet, and the race of women is surely made of iron;
she runs hither and thither wherever you wander for sport. (RBhrs 2.1.168)
(47) Sarvārādhya: He who is worthy of worship by all and is honored foremost by everyone is called Sarvārādhya.
As it was described in the first [chapter] (1.9.41):
"In the assembly hall of King Yudhiṣṭhira’s Rājasūya sacrifice, which was crowded with hosts of sages and the best of kings..."
Worthy of honor, worthy of being beheld, this Self has appeared within the range of my vision.
(48) *Samṛddhimān*: he who possesses great prosperity is one who is "endowed with abundance" (*samṛddhimān*).
For example:
"Fifty-six crores of those born in the Yadu lineage worship you,
and these eight treasures rain down all manner of wealth upon you."
And the inner apartments shine forth, marked by nine auspicious signs of a palace;
O Subduer of Mura, beholding such splendor, who would not be filled with wonder?
Or as it is said in the *Kṛṣṇakarṇāmṛta*:
"The wish-fulfilling gem is the foot-ornament of women;
the trees of love are the trees of the gods."
In Vṛndāvana, the wealth of Vraja is indeed a multitude of wish-fulfilling cows; oh, what an ocean of bliss is this splendor!
(49) *Varīyān*: he who is the most preeminent among all is called *varīyān*. RBhrs_2,1.174 //
For example:
"O Brahman, sit here for a moment on the seat before me with the enemy of Pura; O Lord of the Gods, remain silent; O Lord of Waters, enough with your flatteries; stay far away!"
"Why do these hosts of gods repeatedly raise such a clamor at the gate?
Alas, even now no opportunity for the Lord of Dvāravatī has yet arisen."
(50) Īśvara:
Īśvara is proclaimed to be twofold: independent and one whose command is inviolable.
In this regard, independence is as follows:
Kṛṣṇa showed favor even to the serpent Kāliya, who had committed an offense, by indeed marking him with His footprints.
Not even for Brahmā, though he praises him with a vision [of truth], does this one— whose conduct is independent and who is lauded by the Vedas— bestow a reward not previously earned.
His command is difficult to transgress,
as stated in the third [chapter] (3.2.21):
"But he himself, being without equal or superior, is the Lord of the three."
Having attained all desires through the splendor of sovereign self-rule,
the soles of his feet were honored by the tips of the crowns of the long-enduring world-protectors as they brought him tribute.
Or as it is said:

"When the multitude of creators issues commands for the sake of creation upon a new host of universes, and the host of Rudras, being instructed, brings about destruction when [the universe] is worn out by time."
O Enemy of Kaṃsa, those guardians who are portions of yourself provide protection to the youth; under your command, all the lords of the cosmic eggs reside in every direction.
Now, (51) "one who has attained the true nature of the eternal"—one who has attained the true nature of the eternal is one who has brought under control the effects of *māyā*. // RBhṛs 2.1.180 //

As stated in the first [chapter] (1.11.39): "This is the sovereignty of the Lord; even while abiding in primordial nature, he is not joined with its qualities because his self is eternally established in that [nature], just as the intellect, though resting upon it, is not joined with it. (RBhṛs 2.1.181)
(52) The Omniscient One— He who knows all objects, including those residing in the minds of others and those separated by space, time, and so forth, is called "Omniscient. (RBhrs 2.1.182)
As it was said in the First Canto (1.15.11):
"He who, having come to the forest, protected us from the unbearable hardship devised by our enemy Durvāsas— he who eats ten thousand [mouthfuls] at a time..."
For, having consumed the remnants of his vegetable food, he considered the three worlds satisfied while his entire assembly remained submerged in water.
(53) Ever-new (*nitya-nūtana*):
That which, although being experienced at all times, produces wonder as if it were never before experienced by its sweetnesses, is called "ever-new. (RBhrs_2,1.184)
As it was said in the first [chapter] (1.11.34):
"Even though he stands at her side or has gone into her private presence, nevertheless, for her, his pair of feet are ever new."
Who would cease at every step from that path,
even if wavering, since Fortune never abandons it?
Or as it says in the *Lalitamādhava* (1.52):
"O fair-faced one, piercing the multitude of stones that are the virtues of the noble body [of Kṛṣṇa] with the strokes of the sharp, long chisel of your sidelong glances..."
What unprecedented being is this who, like Viśvakarman, simultaneously covers the courtyard with hundreds of thousands of emerald jewels?
(54) With limbs dense with existence, consciousness, and bliss— he whose form is a mass of consciousness and bliss.
For example:
"When the fivefold afflictions have gradually come to an end,
that supreme bliss of Brahman spontaneously flashes forth."
Wasting that away, who is this dark being in human form appearing before me as a mass of fragrance?
As it is said in the *Brahma-saṃhitā*, in the *Ādi-puruṣa-rahasya* (5.51):
"The splendor of Him, the Source, manifests as the entire array of manifestations, from the earth onwards, differentiated within millions upon millions of cosmic eggs."
I worship that Govinda, the primordial Person, who is Brahman—partless, infinite, and the essence of all beings. 2.1.189.
Therefore, by the Śrī-Vaiṣṇavas, who point to all the Śrutis and Smṛtis,
that Brahman is proclaimed to be the manifestation (vibhūti) of the Blessed Lord.
For instance, in the *Yāmunācārya-stotra* (verse 14):
"That which is within the scope of the cosmic egg, and those ten successive layers of enclosures..."
The qualities (guṇas), primordial matter (pradhāna), the person (puruṣa), the supreme state, and the Brahman beyond the highest— these are Your manifestations.
(55) "Served by all accomplishments":
one who is served by all accomplishments shall have all accomplishments under his own control.
For example:
