"The eight great supernatural powers (mahāsiddhis), beginning with atomization (aṇimā), though surrounded by ten accomplished female companions, find no opportunity at the gate of Kṛṣṇa. (RBhrs 2.1.193)
(56) Now, inconceivable great power—
such as being the agent of divine creation and so forth, the deluding of Brahmā, Rudra, and others,
and the destruction of the *prārabdha* karma of devotees— is what constitutes the state of inconceivable power.

In that regard, his authorship of the divine creation and so forth is as follows: "At first, the Lord was accompanied only by his shadow; then, with part after part of himself, he fashioned the bodies of calves, infants, and others, and subsequently extended among them the state of having many and four arms."

Then, being praised by the Vṛttas, Tattvas, and other [Vedic hymns] that are free from worldly desires, the Soul of All—who is clearly served by the entire universe—manifested; I take refuge in that Lord.
It deludes even Brahmā, Rudra, and the others; as it is said: "Alas! Even the Grandfather was deluded in his childlike play, and even Śambhu was overcome in battle."
By whom— the enemy of Kaṃsa— were those gods, including Mahendra and others like you, defeated today before him?
The destruction of the *prārabdha* karma of a devotee is as described in the Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam (10.45.45):
"The son of the guru, who had been brought here bound by his own past actions..."
"Bring him here, O Great King, placing my instruction foremost."

By the word "etcetera" (ādi), even the accomplishment of the impossible is included— namely, that the Lord himself, though devoid of birth, became the son of the cowherd chief, his form fitting perfectly within the embrace of a pair of arms.
Although he has manifested many forms, this Lord, who is of a single nature and possesses inconceivable, infinite power, delights my intellect.
(57) "The embodiment of ten million cosmic eggs"—
rich with countless world-eggs, he is the embodiment of ten million cosmic eggs.
Thus has the all-pervasive majesty of this venerable form been proclaimed.
As it is said in that very same place (10.14.11):
"Where am I, whose body is seven spans in length, encased within the jar-like cosmic egg enveloped by darkness, the mahat-tattva, ego, space, wind, fire, water, and earth?"
And what is the greatness of you, whose movement through countless cosmic eggs and atoms, and whose path through the wind, is as subtle as a single pore of your hair?
Or as it is said:
"This universe, enriched by the principles (tattvas), marked by the abodes of the hosts of gods, studded with fifty crores of yojanas upon the earth, and filled with the netherworlds (pātālas)..."
Even the Creator has seen but a single compartment of that Vṛndāvana which contains tens of thousands of millions of such universes; who is capable of praising it for you?
The seed of the lineage of incarnations is called the "incarnator" (*avatārī*). // RBhrs_2.1.202 //

As it is said in the *Śrī-Gītagovinda* (1.16): "While He retrieves the Vedas, sustains the worlds, upholds the earth, shatters the demon [Jalandhara], deceives Bali, and effects the destruction of the Kṣatriyas..."
Salutations to you, Kṛṣṇa, who performed ten deeds: conquering the son of Pulastya, wielding the plow, extending compassion, and causing the barbarians to faint.
(59) The giver of the state of one whose enemies are destroyed— He who grants liberation to those whose enemies have been slain is the giver of the state of one whose enemies are destroyed.
For example:
having brought about defeat, frothing at the mouth, bondage, fear, and death—
O you who wear a crest-jewel, although you are the giver of liberation (pavarga), you are the bestower of destruction (apavargada) upon your enemies.
Or as it is said:
"O Murāri, the faction of the enemies of the gods has been engaged in battle on all sides by you in a wondrous manner."
Having not divided the hosts of enemies, yet creating dissension among friends, one goes to the immortal state.
(60) Atmārāma-gaṇākarṣī—
this term *ātmarāma-gaṇākarṣī* indeed has a self-evident meaning.
For instance:
"O Mādhava, how is it that the great medicine of your divine play, having smelled me—a full-fledged paramahaṃsa—has, alas, made me a deer and rendered me thirsty for the lake? (RBhrs 2.1.208)
Now, regarding the four uncommon qualities— (61) *līlā-mādhurya* (the sweetness of playful grace)—
as described in the *Bṛhad-vāmana*:
Although I possess many various enchanting pastimes,
I do not know what my mind would be like upon remembering the Rāsa dance.
Or as it is said:
"May the beautiful life-story of the Lord of Lakṣmī shine forth here, as well as that of the multitude of His incarnations who bring joy to the world."
Although it increases the multitude of wonders even for Hari himself, the essence of the rāsa-līlā nevertheless bears a certain astonishment within my heart.
(62) The superiority of the beloved through love,
as in the *Śrī-daśama* (10.31.15):
"That you wander in the forest during the day..."
To those who do not behold you, even a moment stretches out like an eon;
yet for those who gaze upon your beautiful face with its curly locks, the eyelashes act as a barrier to their eyes, making them dull.
Or as it is said:
"O Enemy of Evil, even that multitude of nights of Brahmā passed in Your company like half a moment."
Alas! Even half a moment in separation from the cowherd girls became like a multitude of Brahma-nights.
(63) The sweetness of his flute,
as in that very same place (10.33.15): "Having perceived that at every libation, the lords of the gods..."
Led by Śakra, Śarva, and Parameṣṭhin, the sages,
with their necks and hearts bowed down, fell into dejection, as they remained uncertain of the truth.
Or as it says in the *Vidagdhamādhava* (1.26):
"Obstructing the clouds, repeatedly causing Tumburu to experience supreme wonder,
making those headed by Sanandana disappear from his meditation, and leaving even the Creator (Brahmā) in a state of astonishment— "
The sound of the flute wandered everywhere, inciting Bali with its series of eager notes, causing the lord of serpents to reel, and shattering the walls of the cosmic eggshell.
(64) The sweetness of His form,
as described in the Third Canto (3.2.12)—
that which is suitable for His mortal pastimes through His own yoga—
Displaying the power of illusion, he took hold of it;
it was a source of wonder, the supreme state of his own excellence in fortune, with its limbs adorned by ornaments.
And in the Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam (10.29.40):
"O dear one, what woman in the three worlds would not be bewildered by Your sweet-toned, long-drawn, and resonant melody, and thus fail to follow the path of the Noble Ones?"
And beholding this form, the good fortune of the three worlds,
the cows, the twice-born, the trees, and the deer all bore horripilation.
Or as it says in the *Lalitamādhava* (8.34): "This unprecedented, most weighty flood of sweetness, which produces such wonder, manifests within me."
Alas! Beholding this very one, even I, with a greedy mind, desire to enjoy him impetuously, just like Rādhikā.
In this world, only a mere indication of the qualities of Kṛṣṇa has been shown— he who is an ocean of all various wonderful and auspicious virtues.
And as it is said in the Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam (10.14.7):
"Who indeed is capable of measuring Your qualities, O Soul of the modes, who have descended for the welfare [of the world]?"
Or by those well-fashioned celestial palaces measured out in due time,
the dust of the earth, the mist, and the light of the sun were [rendered] in the sky.
Although he possesses eternal attributes, wears a forest garland, and is the crest-jewel of all leaders,
his [manifestation] is dependent upon his devotees.
Its threefold nature is also written down here.
Hari is threefold— as the Most Perfect (pūrṇatama), the More Perfect (pūrṇatara), and the Perfect (pūrṇa)—
and he is designated in drama by such terms as "the Best," "the Middling," and so forth.
One whose entire qualities have been manifested is considered by the wise to be "most full" (pūrṇatama);
one who manifests not all [qualities] is "more full" (pūrṇatara); and one who reveals only a little is "full" (pūrṇa). // RBhrs_2,1.222 //
The state of being the most perfect (pūrṇatama) was manifested in Gokula;
the state of perfection (pūrṇatā) and the state of being more perfect (pūrṇatara) were manifested in Dvārakā, Mathurā, and other places.
Furthermore, he may be of four types: the noble-minded (dhīrodātta), the playful (dhīralalita), the one named calm (dhīrapraśānta), and likewise the haughty (dhīroddhata).
For Padmanābha, who is the locus of manifold qualities and activities,
the fourfold [Vedas] are indeed not contradicted due to His various diverse divine sports (līlā).
Among these, the *dhīrodātta* (noble and self-controlled) is:
profound, modest, patient, compassionate, firm in his vows, free from boastfulness, with hidden pride, and possessing great fortitude. (RBhrs 2.1.226)
For example:

"His laughter strikes down the pride of those who consider themselves heroes; he is a leader who has fulfilled his vow in the rescue of the distressed; and his resolute form is like that of a lofty mountain in its uprooting [of obstacles]."
Even though I have committed great offenses against you, seeing you repeatedly restrained by sweet praise, my mind and speech— whose heart is difficult to fathom— do not stir.
The general qualities such as profundity and so forth that are proclaimed here are for the purpose of demonstrating their preeminence among these [Buddhas].
For this quality of being noble and steadfast was proclaimed by the ancients regarding the scion of Raghu;
it is likewise observed in Kṛṣṇa, according to the devotion of each respective devotee.
The *dhīra-lalita* (the steadfast and playful) is clever, in the bloom of youth, and skilled in jesting;
the *dhīra-lalita* is generally free from anxiety and remains under the influence of his beloved. (RBhrs 2.1.230)
For instance—
by means of words that revealed her boldness in the arts of love during the night, he placed Rādhikā,
whose eyes were contracted with shame, before his friends.
Having reached the pinnacle of expertise in the playful art of painting makaras upon the blossoms of her breasts,
Hari makes his youth fruitful by sporting with her in the forest grove.
In Govinda, the quality of *dhīralalita* (the brave-and-graceful) is clearly manifested;
those learned in drama generally cite the god whose banner bears the sea-monster (*makaradhvaja*) as the exemplar here.

The "steadfast and tranquil" (dhīra-śānta) is one whose nature is tranquility, who endures afflictions, and who is discerning; endowed with qualities such as discipline, he is declared to be "steadfast and tranquil."
For example:
"With a form sweet through discipline, with eyes slow, moist, and bright, and revealing all principles of policy through the artful nuances of his speech..."
Proclaiming the Dharma here in the presence of the Son of Dharma,
the enemy of Kaṃsa is beheld like the Lord of the Twice-born himself.
Yudhiṣṭhira and the others are proclaimed by the wise as being steadfast and tranquil.
The *dhīroddhata* (the haughty hero) is described by the learned as one who is envious, egoistic, deceitful, irascible, fickle, and boastful. (RBhrs 2.1.236)
For example:
"O sinful Lord of the Yavanas, Dardura! Turning back this very moment, you must now establish your dwelling somewhere within the hollow interior of a blind well!"
With the mere upward glance of my eyes, the cosmic egg has been reduced to ashes; before me I am awake as the serpent Kṛṣṇa, here named Kṛṣṇa, for the sake of assisting you.
The *dhīroddhata* (bold and haughty) hero is described by the learned as Bhīmasena and others.
Although these qualities, such as parsimony and the like, are perceived as defects,
they are considered virtues here because they possess a particular kind of playfulness.
Or for example:
"Spreading the illusion of clouds bowed down by the weight of water,
this terrible mass of thunderous noise, having raised its hand-barrier of beautiful lightning..."
O Śrīdāman, you deer-like one! Behold me, Kṛṣṇa, standing right here before you—difficult to restrain and the vanquisher of others; accept defeat on this very field of battle.
Although some qualities mentioned here are mutually contradictory,
none of them would be impossible in Hari, because of His absolute and unbounded sovereignty.
And so it is said in the Kūrma Purāṇa:
"He is non-material and yet subtle, both gross and subtle in every respect;
he is declared to be colorless yet everywhere dark-blue, with eyes red at the corners."
Due to his possession of sovereign power (*aiśvarya*), the Blessed One (*bhagavān*) is designated by a term whose meanings appear contradictory.
Nevertheless, faults in the Supreme should never be imputed in any way whatsoever;
yet these qualities, even if they appear contradictory, are to be gathered from everywhere.
And in the Mahāvārāha [Purāṇa]:
"All the bodies of that Supreme Self are eternal and everlasting;
they are devoid of loss or gain, and are never born of *prakṛti*."
They are an accumulation of supreme bliss and consist of pure consciousness in every respect;
all are filled with all virtues and entirely free from all defects.
Also in the Vaiṣṇava Tantra:
"The body of the Blessed One is free from the eighteen great defects;
it consists of all sovereignty and has the nature of truth, consciousness, and bliss. (RBhrs 2.1.246)
The eighteen great defects, as stated in the Viṣṇuyāmala:
delusion, drowsiness, confusion, astringent taste, and intense lust;
Longing, intoxication, and envy; violence, weariness, and fatigue.
Untruth, anger, longing, apprehension, universal delusion, inequality, and dependence on others— these eighteen defects have been proclaimed.
Thus, among all the incarnations,
the fullness of sweetness in the son of Vraja’s lord, who descended even from that [highest state], has been perfectly proclaimed.
And so it is said in the *Brahma-saṃhitā*, in the *Ādi-puruṣa-rahasya* (5.59):
"Depending upon the duration of even a single exhalation of Him,
the lords of the cosmic eggs born from the pores of His skin continue to live."
He is Viṣṇu, the Great One, of whom this is a particular manifestation;
I worship Him, Govinda, the Primal Person.
Now, eight types of human beings are celebrated, renowned for their virtuous qualities; they are the varieties of *sattva* characterized by auspiciousness and adornment. (RBhṛS 2.1.251)
Beauty, gracefulness, sweetness, auspiciousness, stability, splendor, charm, and magnanimity—
these are the varieties of the quality of goodness (sattva) pertaining to persons.
In that regard, *śobhā* (beauty):
where compassion toward the lowly, rivalry toward those superior in merit, heroism, enthusiasm, dexterity, and truthfulness become manifest—that they know as *śobhā*. 2,1.253.
For example:

Desiring to bring about the destruction of heaven, He observed the slaughter on the land of Vraja; then, perceiving the lowly ones through excessive rain, waves of compassion arose within Him toward the enemies of Namuci and others.
Seeing no one equal to himself here who could serve as a worthy recipient for his own wrath,
may Hari, true to his promise, lift up the great mountain to delight his kinsmen.
Vilāsa (Gracefulness):
A gait as deep as that of a bull, a steady gaze,
and speech accompanied by a smile— where these are present, it is called vilāsa.
Just as one who,
having cast his gaze upon an ill-behaved woman in the arena of wrestlers,
shakes the earth with the display of his prowess like an elephant.
At the commencement of the speech, the lotus-eyed one moved across the high stage area, washing the space around the platform with the fragrances of his smiles.
Sweetness—
this sweetness occurs where there is desirability of movement and so forth.
For example:
"Seated upon the excellent bank, creating a hanging garland that sways and lingers by means of the *kadamba* trees which desire to provide support..."
When the deer-eyed daughter of the Sun has first entered the path of the sacred ford, the enemy of Madhu casts his sidelong glance upon her.
Auspiciousness—
auspiciousness is considered to be the very state of being a locus of trust for all the worlds.

For example: "The Dānavas [thought], 'There is no injustice against Hara,' and the gods, being addicted to their sports, were heedless, thinking, 'Kṛṣṇa is our protector'— thus the bolts on the doors were removed."
"He knows that devotion"— thus thinking, O Viśvambhara, who among those with bowed heads and free from anxiety have not sought refuge at the pair of Your feet?
Steadfastness— steadfastness is the lack of wavering from one's resolve, even when beset by obstacles.
For example:
even when Śiva is adverse and possessed of pain,
and Śivā is naked and without parts.
Mukunda indeed lopped off the arms of Vindhyāvalī’s son.
Tejas—The wise proclaim that *tejas* is the state of penetrating all minds. (RBhṛs 2.1.263)
As it is said in the Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam (10.43.17):
"He was a thunderbolt to the wrestlers, the best of men to other men, Cupid incarnate to women, a kinsman to the cowherds, a punisher of the wicked kings, and a child to His own parents."
To the ignorant, he was the death of the Bhoja king; to the yogis, he was the supreme reality;
to the Vṛṣṇis, he was known as the supreme deity. Thus understood, the arena has departed along with his elder brother.
For example:
"Lustre is defined by the wise as the inability to endure contempt and the like. (RBhṛs 2.1.265)
For example:
When Kaṃsa, the enemy of the universe, being enraged, wished to inflict manifest punishment upon Nanda and Ānakadundubhi in the arena before them, he reviled them.
Casting his gaze upon that couch—which was like a messenger for the association with the unchaste woman that is Death, the enemy of the gods—he leaped about; behold, Acyuta stretches forth!
The Lalita (graceful) style: they know that to be Lalita wherein the gestures abound with the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*).
For example:
"The connoisseur, his soul agitated, impetuously fashioned with his left hand a playful dolphin upon the bud-like breasts of Rādhā."
While the jackal shrieks harshly and haughtily from the left, Kṛṣṇa laughs and, with his hair standing on end, adjusts his lower garment.
Magnanimity—
causing the offering of oneself and so forth is what is celebrated as magnanimity.
For example:
"Who here could be more generous than Puruṣottama, by whom even his own self is given away to one who possesses nothing and is devoid of qualities? (RBhṛs 2.1.270)
Although these qualities of the hero, such as steadfastness and the like, are common [to other characters],
they are nevertheless mentioned again because of certain distinctions from what preceded.
Now, his companions are proclaimed as follows: Garga and others were his companions in dharma; Yuyudhana and others in battle; and Uddhava and others likewise in counsel. (RBhrs 2.1.272)
Now, as for the devotees of Kṛṣṇa:
those whose inner hearts are permeated by his being are called devotees of Kṛṣṇa.

The qualities beginning with "one whose speech is truthful" and ending with "possessed of modesty," which have been described [as belonging] to Kṛṣṇa, should be understood by the wise as existing in his devotees.
Those practitioners are proclaimed to be of two kinds: the aspirants and the perfected ones.
In that regard, the practitioners (*sādhakas*)—
those in whom passion has arisen, who have properly attained freedom from obstacles,
and who are fit for the direct realization (*sākṣāt-kṛti*) of Kṛṣṇa— are proclaimed as *sādhakas*. (RBhṛs 2.1.276)
As stated in the Eleventh [Chapter] (11.2.46):
"He who practices love toward the Lord, friendliness toward those dependent on Him, compassion toward the ignorant, and equanimity toward enemies—he is the middling [yogin]. (RBhrs 2.1.277)
Or as it is said:
"O wise one, even though drenched by the shower of tears born from the river of news concerning the Blessed One, the fire of worldly existence still persists; therefore, enough with your anxiety."

In the sky of the heart, the emergence of the dark cloud that is Kṛṣṇa is clearly perceived as most proximate through the torrent of the compassionate rain that removes the longing for immortality, amidst the intense dancing of the broad hairs of the body.
Those practitioners who are equal to Bilvamaṅgala are thus proclaimed.
Now, the Siddhas:
those who have not recognized any afflictions whatsoever, whose actions are always centered on Kṛṣṇa, and who are devoted to tasting the bliss of constant love—they are the Siddhas. (RBhrs 2.1.280)
The Siddhas are of three kinds: those who have attained perfection, those who are perfected, and those who are eternally perfected.

In that regard, those who have attained accomplishments (siddhi) are of two kinds: those who have attained accomplishments through spiritual practices (sādhana) and those who have attained them through his grace (kṛpā).
In that regard, those who have attained perfection through spiritual practice are as described in the third [skandha] (3.15.25):
"And they go by following the lead of the Bull among Sages (the Lord)."
For those Yamas, whose conduct is to be longed for, are far above us;
their limbs are made to bristle with joy as they shed tears of agitation from their mutual passion for recounting the great fame of their Lord.
Or as it is said:

"Those for whom the waves of affliction have been swallowed up by the power of devotion, who feel even a sense of aversion toward liberation and the like— though they have already offered salutations to them— whenever such persons cast even a glance [at worldly things]..."

We pay homage again and again to those fortunate ones, whose hearts are blossomed with the festival of the expansion of love, whose cheeks are washed by tears of joy, and who are covered in horripilation.
Mārkaṇḍeya and others are said to have attained their perfections through these means of accomplishment.
Now, regarding those perfected through compassion,
as stated in the Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam (10.23.42–43): "They have no Vedic sacraments, nor do they reside with a guru."
There is no austerity, no inquiry into the self, no purity, and no auspicious rites.
Moreover, even though we possess the refinements of ritual purification and the like, firm devotion has not arisen within us toward Kṛṣṇa, the one of supreme renown, the Lord of the lords of yoga.
Or as it is said:
"The Guru had no expertise whatsoever in the constraints of ritual service, nor was there even a scent of the slightest exertion in his performance of spiritual practices."
You have attained the fulfillment of your purpose through the stream of the nectar of devotion to the lotus feet of Mukunda, which is sought after by the illustrious Paramahaṃsas.
Kṛpā, Siddhā, Yajñapatnī, Vairocanī, Śukā, and others [are the yoginīs].
Now, regarding the eternally perfected ones (nitya-siddhas):
they have attained supreme love for Kṛṣṇa that is millions of times greater than their own selves;
all these eternally perfected ones possess the quality of eternal bliss, just like Mukunda himself.
As it is stated in the *Pādma* [Purāṇa], in the dialogue between the Blessed Lord and the goddess Satyabhāmā:
"Then, at the request of the gods beginning with Brahmā, I came to the earth; all those attendants were likewise born along with me."
For all these Yādavas, O beautiful lady, are indeed my own attendants;
they are always dear to me, O Goddess, and possess qualities equal to mine.

And so it is said in the Śrī Daśama: "Oh, what fortune! Oh, what fortune for Nanda Gopa and the inhabitants of Vraja, that their friend is the Supreme Bliss, the perfect, eternal Brahman! (Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam 10.14.32)
In that very place (10.26.13):
"O Nanda, this affection for your son is difficult for all of us inhabitants of Vraja to relinquish;
how could it also be innate in him toward us?"
"How could his innate affection for us have arisen from the thought, 'He is my eternal friend'? And thus, their state of being eternally beloved was established.
Thus, for this reason, the cowherd women of the Yādavas are said to be eternally beloved;
their worldly-like activities are like the divine pastimes of the Enemy of Mura.
For it is said in the *Pādmottara-khaṇḍa*:
"Just as Lakṣmaṇa and Bharata, and just as Saṅkarṣaṇa and the others,
so too are they born from their own world by His own will."
Furthermore, by that very [means] they go to that supreme, eternal state;
for the Vaiṣṇavas, there exists neither the bondage of karma nor rebirth.
The fifty-five qualities of the enemy of Kaṃsa that have been described in sequence,
as well as others such as the granting of success (*siddhi*) to those who have attained perfection (*siddha*), are considered [to be present].
The devotees are said to be of five kinds: the peaceful ones, those such as the sons of servants, friends, the group of gurus, and beloveds. (RBhrs 2.1.300)
Now, the excitants (uddīpanas): "Those which kindle the emotion are declared to be the excitants;
they consist of the qualities, activities, and ornaments of Śrī Kṛṣṇacandra. (RBhrs 2.1.301)
The fragrance of his smiling limbs, the bamboo flute, the horn, the anklets, and the conch;
the footprints, the sacred field, the *tulasī*, the devotees, and the day of his birth—these and others [are his manifestations].
In that regard, the qualities:
"The qualities are said to be of three kinds, based on body, speech, and mind. (RBhṛs 2.1.303)
Among those, the physical [qualities] are: youth, beauty, form, physical softness, and so forth.
Although these qualities, such as those pertaining to the body and so forth, are in fact its very own nature,
they are nevertheless described as "excitants" (uddīpana) by accepting a distinction [between them].
Therefore, for that [rasa] in its essential nature, there can indeed be only the state of being an object of perception (ālambanatā);
whereas ornaments and the like can only serve as excitants (uddīpanatva).
And these possess the nature of being objects of focus, as well as the quality of being stimulators.
In that regard, *vayaḥ* (age)—it is threefold, namely: childhood (*kaumāra*), middle childhood (*paugaṇḍa*), and youth (*kaiśora*).

Childhood (*kaumāra*) lasts until the end of the fifth year; adolescence (*paugaṇḍa*) extends up to the tenth; youth (*kaiśora*) continues until the sixteenth year, and beyond that, one enters full maturity (*yauvana*).
In that affectionate sentiment (*vatsala-rasa*), the state of childhood (*kaumāra*) should be described according to propriety;
the state of early youth (*paugaṇḍa*) [should be described] when there is a connection with various sports and the like toward a beloved.
The excellence of this youthfulness is indeed radiant;
nevertheless, because it generally conforms to all aesthetic sentiments (*rasa*), it is illustrated here in due order.
The first, the middle, and likewise the remainder—youth is thus threefold.
Among these, the first [sign] is as follows:
an indescribable brilliance of complexion and a lovely reddish glow in the corners of the eyes,
along with the manifestation of the line of body hair, occur when the first stage of youth has arrived.
Likewise:
"A certain whiteness steals away the splendor of great Indra’s jewels from her limbs;
a slight reddish luster enters, as it were, into the corners of her eyes."
O friend, the fine line of hair on the body of the wearer of the forest garland grows faintly, while a fresh splendor now flashes upon his form.
The attire of the preeminent dancer consists of the Vaijayantī garland, the crest-jewel, and so forth;
the sweetness of the flute, and the splendor of the garments constitute his equipment here.
As it is said in the Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam (10.21.5):
"He wore a crest of peacock feathers upon His head, the finest dancer’s form, with *karṇikāra* flowers on His ears, a garment tawny like gold, and the Vaijayantī garland."
Filling the holes of his flute with the nectar of his lips, he whose fame is sung by the hosts of cowherds entered Vṛndāvana, which is delightful with his own footprints.
The hardening of the tips of the nails, the arching of the eyebrows like a drawn bow, the staining of the teeth with red powder—such are the gestures [of the *khaṭakāmukha*]. (RBhṛS 2.1.317)
For example:
"The pair of eyebrows of the one whose enemies are dancing away is like a new bow of the bodiless [Kāma];
the row of his sharp nails at the tips is like a line of arrows sharpened on a whetstone."
O friend, what woman would not tremble at the sight of him, whose radiant row of teeth shines red upon his body? (RBhṛs 2.1.318)
That state of being deluded is as follows: rendered infatuated, they are not capable of making an effort themselves through anything unpleasing,
nor do they dare even to open their mouths toward any person whatsoever.
Having seen those news of Mādhava, which were smiling with fresh sweetness,
they today offered three handfuls of water-libations even to their own lives.

Now, regarding the middle [stage]: "When one has reached the middle [of youth], there is a certain splendor of the two thighs and the arms, as well as of the chest; and there is the first sweetness of form in the state of adolescence. (RBhrs 2.1.320)
For example:
"He longs for a pair of thighs like the trunks of elephant tusks,
and his chest desires friendship with the jeweled door-panels of Garuḍa."
Even his pair of arms desires to bring reproach upon the class of door-bolts at the onset of Keśava’s fresh youth.
A face rich with the charm of a smile, eyes tremulous with playful grace,
and a song that enchants the three worlds— such is the sweetness described here.
For example:
"Her eyes are rippling with the practiced skill of the god of love's arts; her lotus-face is beautiful with lips lovely through the play of an upturned smile."
When the sprout of Hari’s youth began to blossom, there arose an indescribable sweetness, accompanied by music that mocked the vows of steadfast noblewomen.

The expansion of the essence of cleverness, the great festival of sporting in the groves, the commencement of the *rāsa*-pastimes and so forth, and the excellence of gestures and the like—[these constitute the nature of the Lord]. (RBhrs_2.1.324)
For instance:

"In some places with footprints of visible lac-dye, in some with fallen peacock-feather ornaments rolling about, in some with couches from which the waist-bands have slipped, and in others with heaps of scattered forest-grove flowers— "
The forest of Vṛndāvana most highly proclaims the multitude of Govinda’s playful pastimes, its sandy banks shimmering with the beauty of the circles formed by the dancing herds of calves.
Its power of delusion is as follows:
revealing from afar the fire of Māra within the sun-gem of the heart, casting aside the moon of Dharma, and spreading a veil of passion on all sides.
Alas, O friend! How shall we find protection? The swift sun of sweetness, burdened with its weight, rises in the dark cloud of Kṛṣṇa, causing the water-lily of awakening to close its buds.
Now, as for the remainder:
when the final stage of youth has arrived, the limbs certainly bear an excellence even greater than before, beginning with the manifestation of the three folds [of the waist]. (RBhṛS 2.1.327)
For example:
[He] whose pair of arms crushes the undertaking of the jeweled pillars of Indra, and who seizes the radiance of the boulders on the slopes of the emerald mountain;...

I meditate upon the Destroyer of Asuras, whose three folds of skin mock the shadows of the ripples of the slender Yamunā, and whose thighs are as firm as the trunk of a plantain tree in the grip of passion.
Its sweetness is such— for instance:
"O Lord, whose bodily splendor is capable of subduing the sweetness of the five arrows [of Love],
which has shaken the fortitude of women, and which is the abode of the play of supreme arts..."

O young woman, behold the one clad in yellow robes, whose emerging youthfulness is radiant, and who has eclipsed the brilliance of the *khañjarīṭa* bird with the wondrous charm of the corners of his eyes.
This alone is called the "fresh youth" of Hari by the wise.
In this place, the Gokula goddesses possess the entirety of their inner being;
they engage in unprecedented festivals of amorous play and other such delights according to the arts of Kandarpa.
For example:
"In one place he quarrels with his beloveds; in another, he sends love-letters by means of parrots; in another, he makes preparations for a playful tryst."

In some places, possessing the sixfold policy of the arts of love, he sows dissension among her friends; in other places, the King of the Grove seeks an alliance, while elsewhere he governs the supreme kingdom of erotic passion.
Her state of enchantment was such that—
whispered from ear to ear by her female friends in solitude, the process of praising the messenger,
the skill in deceiving her husband, and the rehearsal for her departure to the grove at night; *niśi* (at night).
O Kṛṇa, today the host of Gaurīs is being made to recite their vows by you, who are heavy with youth: deafness to the words of elders and pricking up the ears for the sound of flutes.
Although the very nature of the Leader (netṛ) is described here as being in his youth (*kaiśora*),
it is nevertheless considered an excitant (*uddīpana*) because of the manifestation of various forms. (RBhṛs 2.1.334)
In some cases, even in childhood, there is a manifestation of fresh youthfulness;
however, because it is not carried by an intense aesthetic flavor (*rasa*), it has not been cited by those who know *rasa*.
Now, regarding beauty:
beauty consists in the arrangement of the limbs in their proper manner.
For example:
"Your face is long-eyed; your chest is as full as a slope of emerald;
your pair of arms is beautifully curved with the luster of pillars; and your pair of sides..."
O enemy of Kaṃsa, whose heart would not be captivated by this lotus-eyed woman— her waist so slender, and her hips so enchanting with their broad, rippling curves?
Now, regarding form (rūpa):
that by which an ornament is adorned is called form.
For example:
"O fair-limbed one, the series of Kṛṣṇa's ornaments— the jeweled earrings and so forth— have attained contact with his body for the sake of its adornment."
She was not able to perform that task even in the slightest degree; on the contrary, she herself became profusely adorned.
Now, regarding softness (*mṛdutā*):
softness is said to be the inability to bear even the touch of something delicate.
For example:
"Alas! How delicate is the body of this youth, possessing the loveliness of a fresh cloud;
even from contact with a new sprout, his limbs wither away. (RBhṛs 2.1.341)
The wise should understand that those qualities which have been described in the section on the Hero (nāyaka)— whether verbal or mental— are precisely what constitute the excitants (uddīpana) here.
Action—
action consists of pastimes such as the *rāsa* dance, as well as the slaying of the wicked and so forth.
Among those, the *rāsa* [pastime] is as follows:
[the glory] of Him whose splendor was beheld by Rambhā and other celestial nymphs as He was rendered helpless by the theater of love through the embraces of the dancing cowherd women.
O Śrī Puṇḍarīkākṣa, expert in the playful tāṇḍava dance, the sweetness of you who long for the rasa of the commencement of the rāsa dance draws our hearts from every side.
The slaying of the wicked,
as in the *Lalitamādhava* (9.50):
"Śambhu leads the bull into the interior of the caves of Mount Mandara."
Where even one who was languid yet gracefully shaking his head [in defiance], saying "Ah,
observe this curiosity!", that Hari crushed that wicked bull-like demon, who was a portent of ill-fortune arising from a mere fragment of sport.
Now, regarding adornment: it has been stated that adornment consists of clothing, ornaments, decoration, and so forth.
Regarding his clothing there:
resembling the rays of the rising sun, saffron, or yellow orpiment, the fourfold age [manifests] as the predominant garment; thus the clothing of Hari is of three kinds.
In that context, "yuga" refers to the lower garment together with the upper wrap; this is declared to be the form of the *yuga*.
As in the *Mukundāṣṭaka* (verse 3) of the *Stavāvalī*: "Wearing upon his hips a yellow garment that delights with the splendor of a mass of gold, and over that a fresh red one; thus he appears."
May Mukunda bestow upon me the fulfillment of the longing of my eyes, as if he were to apply to my beloved’s face a pleasing hue imbued with passion.
The group of four:
the group of four consists of the shawl (kañcuka), the turban (uṣṇīṣa), the waistband (tundabandha), and the inner garment (antarīyaka).
For example:
"With a smiling face, his body adorned with the beauty of a reddish garment, and his limbs covered by a golden, radiant, and long tunic..."
Wearing a reddish turban and a variegated lower garment,
the enemy of Kaṃsa brings us great joy at this grand festival.
"Abundant" (bhūyiṣṭha)—
the wise have described it as being mostly multicolored, consisting of many pieces, and suitable for the various costumes and actions of actors. (RBhṛS 2.1.352)
For example:
"Resplendent with a clearly manifested arrangement made as appropriate by cloths that were both uncut and cut, white, tawny, blue, and crimson..."
This Mādhava, possessing the luster of the king of young camels and adorned with abundant colors, brings intense joy to me, O lady with thighs like those of a young camel.
Now, regarding *ākalpa* (adornment): the binding of hair, ointments, garlands, various decorative marks, betel, amusements, lotuses, and so forth— this is proclaimed as *ākalpa*.
The *jūṭa*, *kavarī*, *cūḍā*, and *veṇī* are types of hair-binding.
*Pāṇḍura*, *karbura*, and *pīta* are considered the three kinds of *ālepa* (smearing).
A garland (*mālā*) is of three kinds: the *vaijayantī*, the jewel-garland (*ratnamālā*), and the forest-wreath (*vanasraj*).
Varieties of this [garland] are considered to include the *vaikakṣaka*, the *apīḍa*, the *prālamba*, and so forth.

The forehead mark (*viśeṣaka*) may likewise be variegated with yellow, white, and red, richly adorned with designs of crocodile patterns; other [ornaments] should be inferred by the wise for themselves.
For example:
With his moon-like face radiant with betel, displaying a stainless braid of hair,
and beautiful with the splendor of a well-polished smear of saffron shining from the parting of his locks;
O friend, today Mādhava, with his high chest adorned with a golden garland, his fingers shining with leaf-patterns upon his forehead, and the dark luster of his body, pours joy into my eyes.
Now, regarding ornamentation:
the crown, earrings, necklace, the catuṣkī, bracelets,
armlets, keyūras, anklets, and so forth, are called the jewel-ornaments.
For example: "A variegated girdle, an incomparable crown, earrings with captivating diamonds,
a necklace of bright pearls, a spotless bracelet, and a footstool as beautiful as the moon."
The lovely waves in the flood of sweetness and the anklets— by these very limbs of the Enemy of Evil (Śiva),
the entire collection of ornaments is adorned, yielding further beauty.
This forest adornment made of flowers and the like is said to consist of forehead marks (tilaka) produced from minerals, as well as leaf-designs, creepers, and so forth.
Now, as for the smile,
as it is said in the *Kṛṣṇakarṇāmṛta* (99):
"With streams of the essence of unbroken nirvāṇa..."
Victorious are your cool smiles, which have shattered all other internal aesthetic sentiments and are like oceans of nectar overflowing without restraint.
Now, the fragrance of the limbs, as follows: This river of perfume, flowing everywhere,
causes the bodies of even the sages— who are otherwise beyond compare— to thrill with horripilation.
I believe that during the eclipse, the enemy of Madhu—
the ocean of faultless fragrance— entered the land of the Kurus for his diversion.
Now, the lineage: He who,
by force of his meditation, shatters the supreme state of the Paramahaṃsa family, and who, being of unsteady character, reviles the sweetness of the nectar [of liberation].
Victorious is this sound of the flute of the slayer of Kaṃsa, which repeatedly proclaims the burden of the command of Kandarpa.
This [flute] is of three kinds: the *veṇu*, the *muralī*, and the *vaṃśikā*.
Regarding that, the flute: the flute known as *pāvikā* should be twelve finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) in length;
it is measured by the thumb in thickness and is provided with six holes. (RBhṛs 2.1.366)
The muralī is two cubits in length, provided with mouth-holes,
equipped with four sound-holes, and produces a beautiful resonance. (RBhrs 2.1.367)
Vaṃśī:
The eight holes, beginning with the *tārā*, have a measurement of half a finger-breadth (*ardhāṅgula*) apart from one another;
then, at a distance of one and a half fingers, there is the mouth-opening (*mukha-randhra*), which is likewise one finger-breadth wide.
The head is four finger-breadths and the tail is three finger-breadths;
that flute is known by the wise as having nine holes and measuring seventeen finger-breadths.
If the distance between the aperture of the *tāra* and the mouth [of the *nāda*] should be ten finger-breadths,
it is explained as "Great Bliss" (*mahānanda*) and likewise as "Deluding" (*saṃmohinī*).
If that [flute] is between the Sūrya [note], it is considered an attractor;
if the Vaṃśī is between the Indra [note], it is then called Ānandinī.
This beloved of the cowherds is renowned as Vaṃśulī;
she is threefold, being respectively made of jewels, gold, and bamboo.
Now, regarding the horn:
A horn made from the buffalo's horn, with its upper and lower ends bound in gold, its middle shimmering with a lattice of jewels, is known by the name *Mandra-ghoṣa*. (RBhṛs 2.1.373)
For example:
Tārāvalī was bitten by the serpent of the flute, whose venom is the playfulness of the stars.
Having drunk the milk from the horn, the horned animal increased its poison twofold at will.
Now, regarding the anklet (nūpura), as it is said: "O friend, having heard the sound of the anklet of Aghamardana, [she] was filled with profound agitation."
Alas, though my eyes were restless with longing, I did not look outward today, for my elders stood before me.
Then Kambu said:
"But Kambu, when it spirals to the right, is called Pāñcajanya."
For example:
"This one, who revels in the slaughter of the embryos of the wives of the enemies of the immortals,
brings joy to the multitude of women in the city of the third heaven."
The sound of the king of conchs, whose splendor is inflamed by Mādhava, wanders through the midst of the world, causing a multitude of horripilation to arise.
Now, regarding the footprints, as it is said in the Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam (10.38.26):
"His agitation increased by the joy of seeing them..."
With his hair standing on end and his eyes filled with the shimmering moisture of love,
he leaped down from the chariot and fell prostrate before them,
exclaiming, "Aha! These are the dust-particles of my Lord's feet!"
Or as it is said:
"Friends, Hari has clearly reached the bank of the Yamunā by this path; observe!"
This row of feet, marked with banners, thunderbolts, goads, and lotuses, captivates my two eyes.
Now, regarding the field (*kṣetra*):
behold— alas, the sight of the lands where Hari sports, which possess exceedingly rare splendor, remains far away.
Even the mere name "Mathurā," as it enters the path of our ears, delights our minds.
Now, regarding Tulasī,
as it is said in the Bilvamaṅgala:
"O garland upon the head of the lotus-eyed one!"
O Tulasī-mañjarī, I beg a small favor of you:
please awaken me, who long for refuge at the lotus feet of the Charioteer of Pārtha.
Then there is the devotee,
as described in the Fourth Canto (4.12.21):
"Having recognized those two as servants of the Supreme Gopī..."
Rising up, his composure forgotten by his agitation,
he bowed with palms joined in reverence, chanting the names of the Slayer of Madhu, while mentioning the two foremost among the Pārshatas.
Or as it is said:
"Having placed the serpent-like arm of Subala upon your lofty shoulder, you shine in the courtyard with a smile and glancing sidelong looks."
Tell me, where is that beloved friend of yours who sprinkled our pair of eyes with waves of nectar? Where does he now abide?
Now, regarding that day:
"Though there be many wonderful festival days for the Blessed One, the blessed eighth day of the month of Bhādrapada in the dark fortnight gladdens my heart. (RBhrs 2.1.384)

Thus ends the first wave, concerning the *vibhāvas* (excitants), within the general exposition of the aesthetic flavor of devotion (*bhakti-rasa*) in the southern division of the illustrious *Bhakti-rasāmṛta-sindhu*.
Southern Division [2.2].
The second wave is called *anubhāva*.
For *anubhāvas* are the indicators of the internal mental states (*bhāvas*);
they are said to consist primarily of external transformations and are designated by the name "the radiant" (*udbhāsvara*). (RBhrs 2.2.1)
Dancing, rolling about, singing, shouting, contorting the body,
uttering the sound "huṃ," yawning, excessive breathing, disregard for the world,
drooling, loud laughter, as well as reeling, hiccupping, and so forth.
These are declared to be of two kinds according to their literal names: "cool" (*śīta*) and "throwing" (*kṣepaṇa*).
The "cool" types consist of singing, yawning, and so forth; those termed "throwing" consist of dancing and so forth.
In that regard, as for dancing:
"Having beheld the moon-like face of Hari, which scatters the nectar of its skill with the flute, [the dancer] trembles."
Hara performed a frantic dance to the sounds of the ḍiṇḍimas of Gaṇeśa during the counting.
It is rolled back,
as in the third [case] (3.1.32):
"Is the wise man living well and free from disease?"
Śvaphalka’s son was a devotee who had taken refuge in the Blessed One; his fortitude shattered by love, he rolled about in the dust of the path marked by Kṛṣṇa’s footprints.
Or as it is said:
"Intoxicated by fresh passion, your limbs rendered helpless, she has become mad upon catching the fragrance of the forest garland."
Rolling on the hard ground of the cow-pen, that fair-limbed woman caused her body to be scarred.
As in the song: "With her heart blended with the splendor of passion, she performs a new song of your virtues."
O Lord of Gokula, today that [power] turns the stones— the friends of Rādhikā— into water.
Crying out, as it were— just as he who was transformed by the chanting of Hari's names cried out, so now has Nārada cried out.
Soon, out of fear that he was a lion among men,
the demons who had been held by him dissolved away.
Or as it is said:
"O King of Vraja, O Joy! Like an elephantine trunk agitated by a plaintive cry (kāku) that has been accepted."
Today, Sundarī, her heart made restless by the flute, cried out here again and again.
Bending the body, as follows:
When the sage, the lute-player, was delighted in his heart by the joyful lute-playing upon the name of Kṛṣṇa, [he performed this].
Violently crushing some indistinct form with his body, he tears apart the entire sacrificial thread.
The sound of *huṃ*, as follows: "When Śaṅkara’s mind was bewildered by the sounds of the flute, the resonance of his *huṃ* cry [arose] in heaven."
Even while repeatedly destroying the host of Dānavas, he always made the assembly of the virtuous ever new.
Yawning, as for example:
"When this full moon, the repository of digits, rises before us in this expansive forest of night-lotuses..."
O lotus-like woman, your lotus-face undergoes a yawn; oh, how wonderful!
The stage of breath, as follows:
When the cloud of the variegated cloth has appeared,
the female cātaka bird named Lalitā experiences an increase in her thirst.
Seeing him, who had the form of a dark cloud and was driven by the gale-like wind of his sighs, she was agitated.
Disregard for worldly concerns, as stated in the *Śrī-daśama* (10.23.41):
"Aha! Behold how even women [are devoted] to Kṛṣṇa, the teacher of the world!"
He who pierced the bonds of death known as "the home," which have an endless nature.
Or as it is said in the *Padyāvalī* (73): "Let people criticize us however they wish; indeed, we do not concern ourselves with such talkative folk."
Intoxicated by the wine of the nectar of Hari,
let us roll upon the ground, dance, and enjoy ourselves.
Salivation, as follows:
"I suspect the sage has fallen into distress, bitten by the serpent of passion;
for from the mouth of this motionless man, saliva is trickling forth. (RBhrs 2.2.16)
Aṭṭahāsa: This aṭṭahāsa is distinct from ordinary laughter; it arises from the distraction of the mind. (RBhṛS 2.2.17)
For example:
"I suspect that for a long time the creeper of devotion has blossomed on the bank of the heart of a servant of Keśava."
By which the heaps of *aṭṭahāsa* blossoms fall tremulously upon the surface of his snout.
Whirling, as for example:
"Surely the enemy of Agha (Śiva) must be creating a whirlwind under the guise of his blowing upon you, O Muralī."
Otherwise, O friend, why does this sound cause you to reel, making the lotus-eyed women of Vraja also whirl?
Hiccough:
"O daughter, do not prepare the medicine; cast away this excessively agitated hair.
Why do you vainly suspect inauspiciousness toward your dear friend?"
Agitated by the transformation of love for Hari, she repeatedly cries out, "O dear-eyed one!
Hari! and thus today she produces a great burden of hiccuping.
Other [signs] such as the blooming of the body and the emergence of redness may also occur;
however, because they are extremely rare, they have not been mentioned here.
Thus ends the second wave, on the Manifestations (anubhāvas), within the General Description of the Flavors of Devotion (bhakti-rasa) in the Southern Division of the *Śrī-Śrī-Bhakti-Rasāmṛta-Sindhu*.
Southern Division [2.3].

The third wave, known as *sāttvika*, is that state where the mind is pervaded by emotions related to Kṛṣṇa, whether directly or through some mediation; this is called *sattva* by the wise. (RBhrs 2.3.1)
Whatever entities have arisen from this *sattva* are of the nature of *sattva*;
they are considered to be of three kinds: smooth, oily, and likewise rough. (RBhrs 2.3.2)
Among them, the "affectionate" (snigdha) are considered to be of two kinds: those characterized by sattva, which are further divided into primary (mukhya) and secondary (gauṇa).
Among them, the primary ones are as follows:
through the primary passion (*rati*) directed toward the *ākrāmas*, these [devotees] are the primary *sāttvika*s;
the wise should recognize that their connection with Kṛṣṇa here is indeed direct.
For example:
"She who, with teeth that mock the kunda flower, joyfully creates excellent garlands of kunda for Mukunda..."
Due to the passion for music, the lute-player’s limbs became motionless.
This is the primary pillar; in this manner, perspiration and the others should also be understood by you.
Now, as for the secondary [sentiments]: they are called secondary because they are attained through the primary sentiment of love (rati), by means of that which has become secondary;
here, the connection with Kṛṣṇa occurs through some degree of mediation.
For example: "When,
in ancient times, Puruṣottama was led away from the city like a rain-cloud for his own eyes, which were like cātaka birds..."
With her face flushed crimson, the mistress of Gokula reproaches the king with a faltering voice.
These two—change of color and change of voice—are secondary [indications].
Now, as for those that are smeared (digdhāḥ):
through the assault upon the mind by emotions inseparable from the two types of passion (rati).
If, when passion has arisen in people, those who follow after passion are smeared with poison.
For example:
"Having observed Pūtanā here at night, with her formidable limbs rolling about in the interior of the house..."
With trembling limbs and a distressed mind, the Queen of Vraja searches for her son.
Because it follows upon passion, this trembling is called "poisoned" (digdha).

Rough [devotion] arises in some people who are devoid of love, through joy, wonder, and so forth, produced by hearing news of the Lord’s sweet and marvelous deeds; such devotion is merely nominal. (RBhṛs 2.3.12)
For example:
"Even though he reveals his own heart here through his actions— which are devoted solely to the means of enjoyment and devoid of even a scent of passion— "
At that moment, her body became thrilled with horripilation from the sweet songs of Mādhava’s amorous play, which filled her with joy.
This is the "rough" [type] characterized by horripilation:

"The wise have described this rough [state] as horripilation arising from the absence of sexual pleasure; it occurs previously in those such as seekers of liberation who have practiced sexual union. (RBhṛs 2.3.14)
The mind, becoming solidified, casts its own formidable self into the vital breath;
but the vital breath, undergoing transformation, thoroughly agitates the body.
At that time, these states such as paralysis (stambha) and others arise within the body of the devotee.
Stupefaction, perspiration, horripilation, change of voice, trembling, change of color, tears, and fainting—these eight are known as the *sāttvika* [emotions]. (2.3.16)
The vital breath sometimes relies upon the four elements, earth and the rest;
at other times, being its own master, it moves everywhere within the body.
The vital breath (prāṇa), when situated in earth, produces stiffness; when resting in water, it causes tears;
when abiding in fire, it brings about perspiration and discoloration; and when supported by space, it leads to dissolution.
Remaining in its natural state, it sequentially undergoes the distinctions of mild, moderate, and intense intensity;
in this regard, it manifests these three: horripilation, trembling, and change of color.
Because they cause agitation both externally and internally,
the wise have clearly declared their nature to be that of "passions" (bhāva) and their status as "manifestations" (anubhāva).
Among those, paralysis (*stambha*)—paralysis arises from joy, fear, wonder, despondency, or indignation.
In that state, there is an absence of speech and other faculties, immobility, a sense of emptiness, and so forth. (RBhṛS 2.3.21)
In that regard, [the state] arising from joy is as described in the third [chapter], verse 2.14:
"Of her, whose laughter and dance were overflowing with passion..."
Having received honor through his playful glances,
the women of Vraja stood as if their tasks were unfinished, their minds following him with their very sight.
Out of fear— for example:
"Before me stood a circle of wrestlers resembling mountains, more precious than even the highest life."
Beholding her son, the mother’s eyes grew dim and, alas, her limbs became motionless.
Out of wonder, as it is said in the *Śrī-daśama* (10.13.56): "Then, with his eleven senses paralyzed by an intense surge of curiosity,
Brahmā remained silent before that splendor, like a young girl standing before her mother."
Or as it is said:
"As the dark child gazed at the cloud-kissing mountain held in his hand, the assembly of those dwelling in the cow-pen became as if fixed in a painting. (RBhrs 2.3.25)
From despair, as for example:
"Seeing Acyuta entering the belly of the Dānava Bakasodara..."
The host of gods, their minds despondent,
clearly appears like a painted canvas in the sky.
Out of indignation, as for example:
"O pitiless son of Kṛpī, you wish to discharge your arrows before the enemy of Mura."
Though eager to retaliate against his enemy, the monkey-bannered one was rendered motionless for a moment by his rage.
Now, perspiration:
perspiration is that which causes moisture in the body and is born from joy, fear, anger, and so forth. (RBhṛs 2.3.28)
In that regard, out of joy, for example: "O lovely-eyed one, why do you display such cleverness here, casting aside the heat of the sun?"
Having previously seen the lotus-eyed one,
you have become perspiring and pierced by the god whose weapon is flowers.
Out of fear, as for example: having reviled Hari, who was disguised as Abhimanyu, with bold words out of curiosity—
In an instant, Raktaka, his true form revealed, became agitated and his body broke out in a sweat.
From anger, for example: "Seeing Śakra causing excessive rain due to the destruction of the sacrifice, Garuḍa became enraged."
Even as he stood above the clouds, drops of water from the cloud fell upon his limbs at that time.
Now, regarding horripilation (romāñca):
This horripilation indeed arises from wonder, joy, enthusiasm, fear, and so forth;
it is the bristling of the body hairs, and in that state, there are such things as the touching of the limbs.
In that regard, it is due to wonder, as follows:
seeing the three worlds within his mouth as he yawned, the child became filled with bashfulness.
This wife of the lord of the cowherd settlement became one whose slender body was covered with buds formed by her body hairs.

Out of joy, as it is said in the *Śrī-daśama* (10.30.10): "O Earth, what penance have you performed, that you shine with the hair on your limbs standing on end from the festival of touching the feet of Keśava?"
Was it born from the foot, or from the stride of the wide-striding one (Urukrama), or perhaps from the embrace of the one in the form of a boar?
Through enthusiasm, as for example:
At the commencement of the sport of crushing sins, the body of Śrīdāman, desiring to fight, thrilled with horripilation, took delight in the battle. (RBhṛ 2.3.35)
Out of fear, as for example:
having beheld there before him Puruṣottama, who bears the universal form and possesses a wondrous appearance.
Arjuna, his face instantly parched, took refuge in a body covered with formidable bristles.

Now, the variation of voice (svara-bheda): A disorder of the voice arising from despondency, astonishment, indignation, joy, fear, and so forth, is called *vaisvaryam*; this produces such conditions as stammering (*gadgadikā*). (RBhṛS 2.3.37)
In that regard, due to despondency, as for example:
"O Queen of Vraja, Hari himself [is coming] from the chariot ahead"— thus she spoke with her words half-faltering.
It is said that the friend of that fawn-eyed woman was made to weep by her as she relaxed even toward her teacher out of shame.
Out of wonder, as it is said in the *Śrī-daśama* (10.13.64):
"Then, rising slowly and wiping his eyes, he gazed at Mukunda with his neck slightly bowed."
With palms joined in reverence, humble, and composed,
he spoke with a trembling voice in faltering words.

Out of indignation, as it is said in that very same place (10.29.30): "To Kṛṣṇa, who was speaking as if he were someone other than their beloved, they— having renounced all desires for the sake of that [goal]— "
Wiping their eyes, which were impaired by weeping,
those who were devoted spoke with voices somewhat faltering due to agitation.
Out of joy, as it says in that very same place (10.39.56–57): "With the hair on his body bristling and his eyes moistened by his inner emotion..."
Resorting to courage, the Sātvata praised Him with a faltering voice,
bowing his head in humble devotion and slowly joining his palms in reverence.
Out of fear— for instance,
having heard my words, "Bestow the flute upon you," the careless man became intensely pale with distress.
Immediately, O Mukunda, his throat became choked with a heavy sob, and by this [sob], that bird was lost.
Now, regarding trembling (vepathu): Trembling, caused by fear, indignation, joy, and so forth, produces a shaking of the limbs. (RBhṛ 2.3.43)
In that regard, [there is fear] through terror, as for example:
"Beholding Śaṅkhacūḍa, whose prowess was increased and whose arms were outstretched with the desire to seize [him]..."
Crying out, "O son of the king of Vraja!", Rādhikā was overcome with a surge of trembling.
Through indignation, as follows:
Agitated by the insult directed at Kṛṣṇa, Nakula, like the king of mountains during an earthquake, suddenly trembled with indignation as if the earth were shaking. (RBhṛs 2.3.45)
With joy, as follows: "O cursed one, why do you laugh? See, I am trembling now with fear;
ward off the son of Vraja-pati as he approaches so restlessly! (RBhṛs 2.3.46)
Now, regarding change of color (*vaivarṇya*):
"Change of color is a transformation of the complexion resulting from despondency, anger, fear, and so forth;
in this context, those who know the internal states have proclaimed such things as squalor and emaciation. (RBhṛs 2.3.47)
In that regard, due to despondency, as for example:
"O Kṛṣṇa, O divine sage, Gokula, having now turned all its people white through separation from you, bears the illusion of being Śvetadvīpa. (RBhrs 2.3.48)
Out of anger, for example:
"Seeing before him the brothers of Kaṃsa with weapons raised, as he was about to attack the enemy of Kaṃsa..."
The face of that Śrī-bala, as he grew angry, shone like the rising moon, O friend.
Out of fear— for instance:
when the Vraja clan was protected by the slayer of Baka after he had effortlessly cast aside a great mountain.
The blackness appearing on the face of the enemy of Bala expressed the fear that had arisen in his mind.
In dejection, whiteness is said to appear; sometimes there is a yellowish-grey or blackness.
In anger, however, redness appears; in fear, blackness or sometimes whiteness.
A distinct redness is observed in some cases even during an excess of joy;
however, because it is not universal, no example of this has been provided here.
Now, regarding tears: tears are the outflow of water from the eyes caused by joy, anger, dejection, and so forth.
Tears born of joy are cool, while those arising from anger and the like are hot.
In all cases, there is the cleansing away of agitation of the eyes, passion, and so forth.
In this regard, regarding joy (*harṣa*), for example:
The lotus-eyed one loudly praised that bliss which rained down a flood of tears provoked by the sight of Govinda. (RBhṛs 2.3.54)
Out of anger, as it is said in the *Harivaṃśa* (2.66.24):
"From her two eyes flowed water born of affectionate anger,
like dew-drops from the petals of a lotus."
Or as it is said:
"The face of Bhīma, desiring to effect the slaughter of the Lord of the Cedis, shone with tears flowing from it and reddened by rage."
Like the orb of the moon, its face rising and sprinkled with drops of water, as if seized by the glow of twilight.
Regarding despondency, as it is said in the *Śrī-daśama* (10.60.23):
"With her well-formed foot, possessing the crimson splendor of her nails,
she scratches the ground while shedding tears darkened by collyrium."
She stood with her face cast downward, her breasts stained with saffron, her speech stifled by extreme sorrow.
Now, dissolution (pralaya):
Dissolution is the cessation of activity and cognition due to pleasure and pain;
in this state, the external manifestations (anubhāvas) are said to be falling to the ground and so forth. (RBhrs 2.3.58)
In that regard, by means of bliss, as follows:
"Beholding Hari approaching unexpectedly from amidst the thicket of creepers, a woman of Vraja shone with her limbs motionless, her mind devoid of cognition. (RBhrs 2.3.59)
Through suffering, as it is said in the Śrī Daśama (10.39.15):
"And others, whose entire mental functions had ceased through meditation upon Him,
did not perceive this world, as if they had entered their own spiritual realm."

For although all entities are indeed characterized by *sattva* because they have *sattva* as their root, nevertheless, because these [entities] have *sattva* alone as their fundamental basis, they are designated as "sāttvika."

Due to the gradation of *sattva*, there would be a gradation in the agitation of the vital breath and the body; from that very cause, there would be a gradation among all those characterized by *sattva*.
Those that are smoky, those that are blazing, those that are radiant, and those designated as intensely radiant—
these fourfold types of *sāttvika* [fires] reach an ever-increasing intensity.
That [increase] may be threefold: by its pervasion over a long duration of time, by its pervasion of many limbs, and likewise by excellence in its own nature. Thus, increase is of three kinds.
In that regard, [the practice] is appropriate for those very [limbs] excluding the eyes and the voice;
for these extend over many limbs, and they possess a certain distinctiveness in those two [respects].

In that regard, tears cause the eyes to become vacant and produce a pale whiteness; likewise, they bring about a distinct variety and peculiarity in the pupils. Furthermore, when there is a change in the quality of the voice, it results in brokenness, faltering, agitation, and so forth.
Brokenness, displacement of the place, and stiffness—this is the state of the constricted throat;
while agitation consists of being low, high, hidden, or lost.
Those of a sattvic nature generally remain smoky and rough;
however, all those who are smooth generally fall into these four categories.
In great festivals and the like, or in noble assemblies, dances, and so forth, they shine with exuberance; though harsh in some respects, they are pleasing to someone.
The supreme state is delight (*rati*), which is the cause of the wonder of universal bliss;
for without it, these [other states] cannot serve as the basis for such wonder.
In that context, "smoking" (dhūmāyita) refers to those states which are either non-dual or accompanied by a second;
they are considered "smoking" because they are slightly manifest and thus capable of being denied.
For example:
"As the priest listened to the fame of the Enemy of Sin— which destroys all evil— he became one whose tears were sparse, mingled with the tips of his eyelashes."
The sacrificer bore his lotus-face with its cheeks and hair bristling from joy, and its nose slightly perspiring.
Now, the "Blazing" (jvalita):
when two or three [breaths] move simultaneously into a clearly manifest state, they can only be suppressed with great difficulty; thus they are known as "Blazing. (RBhṛs 2.3.73)
For instance:
"The hand, trembling with agitation, is unable to grasp the *guñjā* berry;
the eyes, filled with tears, cannot quickly discern the peacock feather."
O friend, your thighs have become so rigid with exhaustion that you cannot even take a step,
now that the sound of the flute has reached your ears from the forest.
Or as it is said:
"O friend, with faltering voice and out of shame, I somehow suppressed my tears; immediately, my trembling was also concealed."
Even though the bamboo grove in the mountain valley resounded with sounds produced by the skillful gestures of my attendants, passion still took hold within my mind.
Now, regarding the *dīpta* [breaths]:
"When three, four, or five distinct [breaths] occur simultaneously, and cannot be restrained, they are called *dīpta* by the wise. (RBhṛs 2.3.76)
For instance:
"He did not apply his skill to lute-playing for long, being overwhelmed by trembling; he was not able to offer verses of praise, his speech being choked by a faltering voice."
The sage was unable to look upon the enemy of Madhu as he stood shimmering before him; his form became helpless, with tears flowing from his eyes.
Or for example:
"Why do you shed tears? Why do you vainly scatter the pollen of flowers? Why do you tremble with horripilation? And why do you cry out against the cold wind?"
"O friend, do you loathe wandering in the forest because of a stiffness in your thighs?
O Rādhā, you speak of the torment of love through a faltering voice that betrays your condition."

Now, regarding the "flaming" (uddīpta): those [seeds] which have manifested at one time—whether five or six, or all of them—having ascended to the highest excellence, are celebrated as "flaming. (RBhṛS 2.3.79)
For example:
"Today she perspires, trembles, and with her limbs covered in horripilation, she assumes stillness; she laments distractedly with plaintive cries and withers away with her intense heat."

The people dwelling in the cowherd settlement are moistened by the waters rising from their eyes, yet they immediately faint again and again due to separation from that one clad in yellow garments who sports so wildly.
When these [qualities] become intensely ignited within the Great State (mahābhāva),
they all indeed reach the supreme limit where the sattvic emotions (sāttvika) are fully sustained.
Furthermore:
Now, the fourfold appearances of the sattvic [emotions] (sāttvikābhāsas) are described here.
Those who appear as passion likewise appear as sentient beings;
yet these excellent ones are devoid of sentient beings and are contrary [to appearances], just as previously described.
Among those, the first [category] consists of those headed by the seeker of liberation (mumukṣu), because of the semblance of passion (raty-ābhāsa) previously described.
For example:
A certain resident of Vārāṇasī, recounting the deeds of Hari in an assembly of ascetics, his hair standing on end, drenches both his cheeks with tears. (RBhṛs 2.3.85)
Now, regarding the states arising from the appearance of *sattva*:

when an appearance of joy, wonder, and so forth arises in a heart that is naturally lax, it is called the "appearance of *sattva*"; from that, the states arising from the appearance of *sattva* [occur].
For example:
"Even as an aged Mīmāṃsaka listened to the account of Kṛṣṇa’s amorous dalliance, his body broke into horripilation, his mind becoming as if thrilled. (RBhrs 2.3.87)
Or as it is said:
"How can I describe the sweetness of your profound eloquence, which rains down a continuous flow of the nectar of Mukunda’s deeds?"
For even those who do not seek that goal and are seekers of sensual pleasures, upon hearing of the victory of the Lord from his mouth, shed streams of tears for a moment.
Now, even in those devoid of spiritual essence—
whose inner hearts are naturally slippery and who are intent on such practice—
tears, horripilation, and the like may sometimes occur even without the appearance of true spiritual essence. (RBhṛ 2.3.89)
For example:
"As he listened to the deeds of Hari, indeed, states such as pleasure and pain did not arise in his heart;
because of his lack of attachment, how could tears flow incessantly? (RBhṛs 2.3.90)
In those whose minds are by nature lax or indeed slippery, a semblance of sattva generally arises in the assembly.
Now, regarding those who are hostile: "Hostile" refers to those other than one's own well-wishers—namely, Kṛṣṇa's enemies—who act out of anger, fear, and so forth. (RBhṛs 2.3.92)
In that regard, [anger] is as follows; for example, in the *Harivaṃśa* (2.30.63)
— {Critical Edition, 76.16}:—
Then, with his lips quivering and the surface of his lower lip blood-red,
Kaṃsa’s face, through its fury, acted like a crimson sun.
Out of fear, just as a wrestler, seeing Kṛṣṇa on the arena with his face withered, perspired with beads of sweat upon his forehead.
As the Goddess of Liberation approached him directly before him, he offered her with great reverence as if it were water for washing her feet.
Or as it is said:
"While the Purāṇa was being recited before him,
having heard [the account], Kaṃsa experienced an excess of fear."
At that time, his inner mind was agitated and his face was withered on all sides.

Although there is no purpose whatsoever in describing what merely resembles the sattvic qualities, nevertheless, a general direction has been shown for the sake of discerning the true sattvic qualities.
Thus ends the third wave, the *sāttvika-laharī*, within the general exposition of the aesthetic flavor of devotion (*bhakti-rasa*) in the southern division of the *Śrī-Śrī-Bhakti-Rasāmṛta-Sindhu*.
[2.4] Now begins the fourth wave, known as the *vyabhicārin* (transitory moods).
Now, those thirty-three states which are called transitory (vyabhicārin) are described;
they move specifically and directly toward the permanent emotion (sthāyin).
These transitory states (vyabhicārin) are to be known by their indications through speech, limbs, and disposition;
they are called "transitory" because they move along with the course of the dominant emotion (bhāva).
Emerging and submerging in the stable ocean of nectar like waves,
they cause it to swell and attain its very same nature.
Despair, despondency, wretchedness, exhaustion and fatigue, intoxication and pride, suspicion, terror, agitation, insanity, epilepsy, and likewise disease; RBhS 2.4.4.
Delusion, death, laziness, dullness, shame, and dissimulation; memory, as well as reasoning, reflection, intelligence, and fortitude; joy and eagerness. (RBhṛs 2.4.5)
Austerity, envy, fickleness, sleep, slumber,
and wakefulness— these are declared to be the transitory mental states (vyabhicāribhāvas).
In this context, (1) *nirveda*—
the self-contempt fashioned by great suffering, separation [from the beloved], envy, or the discernment of the virtuous— is what is here called *nirveda*.
In this case, there are anxiety, tears, pallor, dejection, sighing, and so forth.
In that regard, there is great urgency, as follows: "Alas! What is the use of us maintaining these wretched bodies, which yield fruitless results of merit?"
Come, O wife, let us forcibly offer ourselves as oblations into the fire of poison in the Kāliya lake.
Through separation, as for example:
"Because of the lack of attachment to the sweetnesses of Mādhava,
[the spring] has become sapless, having failed to flower."
Alas! In Vṛndāvana he withers away; from where does that meritless bee Subala draw his breath?
Or as it is said in the *Dānakelikaumudī* (20):
"Let my ears be sufficiently deafened, since they have not heard the chatter of Mādhava."
O friend, he was indeed not seen by those two eyes as they gazed upon him, nor were these two eyes seen by him.
Out of envy, as in the *Harivaṃśa* (2.67.11) [in the critical edition,
Appendix 29], the speech of Satyādevī:
If she was indeed to be praised by Nārada in your presence,
why was this unfortunate person made to repeat her praises there?
Through the discrimination of the real, as it is said in the Śrī-daśama (10.51.47):
"O unconquerable one, this time of mine has passed fruitlessly."

For a king whose pride is swollen by the glory of sovereignty, who perceives himself as merely mortal, and who is attached to his children, wife, treasury, and lands through endless anxieties; // RBhrs_2.4.12 //
Some say that the Sage first spoke of inauspiciousness and then designated this [state] as the primary stable emotion (sthāyin), calling it "the peaceful" (śānta). (RBhṛS 2.4.13)

Now, (2) Despair (*viṣāda*): Dejection is a state of remorse arising from the failure to obtain what is desired, the non-achievement of an undertaking already begun, misfortune, or even from one's own transgressions and the like. (RBhṛs 2.4.14)
In this regard, there is also the investigation of the means and the companion, as well as reflection, weeping, lamentation,
sighing, discoloration, dryness of the mouth, and so forth.

In this regard, [suffering] arises from the non-attainment of the desired, as follows: "My body has reached old age, my speech has become powerless, and this activity of my mind has entered a path of failing memory."
O Destroyer of Sins, may the moon of your vision remain far away;
alas, even the opportunity for me to practice devotion has not been attained.
Because the work already commenced is not accomplished, as for example: "Today, indeed, flowers were gathered by me with effort in a dream, and a forest garland was fashioned from them."
Alas, as soon as she was placed within the heart of Mukunda,
that sleep instantly ceased.
Regarding misfortune, for example:
"How was my son brought to the city by Maya?
Why was he not seized and kept at home?"
Alas!
On this very day, the eclipse-demon Rāhu seeks to afflict the moon that has already been eclipsed.
Due to offense, as it is said in the *Śrī-daśama* (10.14.9):
"O Infinite One, O Supreme Self, even though You are the primordial Lord and the master of illusion, I have seen Your ungenerous nature toward me."
Having spread out my illusory power (māyā), I desired to behold the extent of my own majesty, as if wishing to see how great a flame is within the fire.
Or as it is said:
"Having seized the Syamantaka jewel, I went to the terrible-faced Antaka;
what crossing could I have made, or would I not have been cast into the Vaitaraṇī? (RBhṛs 2.4.20)

Now, (3) Dainyam—dejection: it is a lack of vigor caused by suffering, fear, transgression, and so forth; it produces flattery, languor, dejection, anxiety, physical numbness, and the like. (RBhṛs 2.4.21)
In that regard, concerning suffering, as it is said in the *Śrī-daśama* (10.51.57):
"For a long time here, afflicted by misfortune and tormented by regrets..."

O Giver of Refuge, O Supreme Self, I have somehow attained peace and am now endowed with the six qualities that satisfy all thirst; protect me, who have approached Your lotus feet— the feet which grant fearlessness, truth, and freedom from sorrow, O Lord!
Out of fear, as in the first [chapter] (1.8.10):
"O Lord, O All-pervading One, this arrow of heated iron rushes at me;
let it burn me as it pleases, O Protector, but let my embryo not be destroyed. (RBhṛs 2.4.23)
On account of an offense,
as it is said in the Śrī-daśama (10.14.10):
"Therefore, O Acyuta, forgive me, who am born of the mode of passion."

"Indeed, this one who, being ignorant, considers himself a lord separate from You, whose eyes are blinded by the darkness of the pride of birth— this one is to be pitied by me, for he has found a protector."
By the word "first" is meant even out of shame, as in that very same passage (10.22.14): "O sir, do not do this; you are the beloved son of Nanda-gopa."
We know you, O worthy one of Vraja; give us garments, for we are trembling!
Now, (4) *mlāni* (depression):
Vitality (*ojas*), which consists of the essence of the moon (*soma*), produces strength and nourishment in the body;
however, from its depletion due to mental anguish, excessive passion, and so forth, depression (*glāni*) is considered to be a state of being breathless.
It causes trembling of the limbs, numbness, discoloration, emaciation, and wandering of the vision, and so forth.
In that regard, by way of fatigue, for example:
"With her forearms radiant with jeweled bracelets that were spinning [from dancing], and her lips set in motion by the fame of the Enemy of Mura (Kṛṣṇa) within the assembly..."
Churning the pot of curd with her tremulous eyes,
she became indifferent to the weight of her exhaustion for the sake of Kṛṣṇa.
Or as it is said:
"Gathering a beautiful mass of flowers in order to weave an incomparable forest garland,"
In the difficult forest, the deer-eyed woman became momentarily weakened by the burden of exhaustion.
By way of an illustration:
she is devoid of the blending of aesthetic flavors (rasas), and with her life-force diminished, the swan has flown away.
O Mādhava, today your mother has withered away from separation from you,
like a lake dried up by the heat of summer.
As described in the *Rasa-sudhākara* (2.13ff):
"Exhausted at the end of their dalliance despite her greatest efforts, she was laid upon the bed by Kṛṣṇa."
Taking his hand in her own,
she reached the porch, which was made joyful by the moonlight.
Now, (5) fatigue (*śrama*): exhaustion arising from travel, dancing, sexual pleasure, and so forth, is called fatigue.
It is accompanied by sleepiness, perspiration, rubbing of the limbs, yawning, labored breathing, and the like. (RBhṛS 2.4.31)
Now, as for the journey:
