the queen of the king of Vraja followed her son, who had committed an offense, into the midst of the cow-pen's courtyard.
With the binding of her locks slipping loose,
her limbs became drenched with drops of perspiration.
Of dancing and so forth, as for example: surrounded by friends whose mouths were eager for music, he performed a graceful movement of the limbs, spreading and swaying his necklace.
Or Rāma, having begotten Nanda’s son through ignorance, performing tāṇḍava dances upon the riverbank.
From the *Śrī-daśama*:
"O dear one, out of compassion, He lovingly wiped their faces with His most peaceful hand as they were exhausted from excessive dalliance. (10.33.20)
Now, (6) intoxication (*mada*):
Intoxication is an exhilaration that robs one of discrimination; it is considered to be of two kinds:
that arising from the drinking of wine, and that born from the intensity of the transformations of love.
It causes stumbling in gait, faltering of speech, rolling of the eyes, redness [of the face], and so forth.
In that regard, the state of drinking honey is as described in the *Lalitamādhava* (5.41):
"Where indeed did the king-ants, tormented [by the heat], dissolve into the hole?"
"I am indeed Hari; will he not cast his wrath upon me, the cosmic egg?
"O deer of Śacī’s house, why do you laugh? Thus shouting, the wielder of the plow (Balarāma) rises before him, his crest-jewel shaking from the intoxication of his pride.
Or as it was said by the ancient *Puruṣottamadeva*:
"Bha-bha! The earth is spinning; la-la! The moon is falling;
kṛ-kṛ! O Kṛṣṇa, speak quickly; ha-ha! Are the Vṛṣṇis laughing?"
May Haladhara, who, while speaking with words faltering from intoxication as he sat in his drinking vessel, cried out "Sisīdhu! Mu-mu-muñca me! Pa-pa-pa-pāna-pātre!", bring you prosperity.
The best [type of person] lies down from intoxication; the middling laughs and drinks;
the lowest cries out at will, speaks rudely to people, and weeps.
Intoxication is also said to be of three kinds, distinguished by the categories of "young" and so forth;
it has not been described here in detail because it is not very useful for this context.
Arising from the weight of the transformations of the bodiless god [of love], as follows:
having first beheld the son of the Lord of Vraja, her eyebrows are arched; she wanders about, laughs, weeps, and hides her face.
She prattles on repeatedly and bows to her friend; look, Vrinda, this Gandharva maiden is blinded by the intoxication of fresh passion! (RBhrs_2.4.40)

Now, (7) pride (*garva*): Pride is defined as the slighting of others due to being the supreme repository of good fortune, beauty, youth, and virtues, as well as through the attainment of desired objects and the like. (RBhṛs 2.4.41)
In this context, there are sarcastic remarks, feigning the inability to provide an answer, gazing at one's own limbs, concealment, and not listening to the words [of others]. (RBhṛs 2.4.42)
In that regard, by way of good fortune, as it is said in the *Śrī-Kṛṣṇakarṇāmṛta* (3.93):
"O Kṛṣṇa, you have gone away having forcibly raised your hand; what is so wonderful about this?"
If you depart from my heart, I shall reckon your manliness.
By virtue of her physical beauty and youth— for example:
"Whose naturally sweet form, having been enjoyed, caused even the splendor of her youth to become exceedingly blessed."
O Kṛṣṇa, how can this friend of mine cast her glance upon you, who have been enjoyed and then released by hundreds of the women of Vraja?
By way of quality, for example:
"Let the cowherds weave garlands at will with fragrant flowers that possess great beauty."
But Kṛṣṇa, filled with wonder, will place my garland, along with my longing, before him in his heart.
By virtue of having the most excellent refuge,
as stated in the Śrī Daśama (10.2.33):
"O Mādhava, Your devotees are never [overcome] anywhere."
Those who have bound their friendship to you do not fall from the path;
protected by you, O Lord, they wander fearlessly upon the crests of the hosts of obstacles.
By the attainment of what was desired, as follows:
"O Lord of Vṛndāvana, having obtained your supreme grace, my mind is delighted and I am repeatedly uplifted."
Even today, my heart does not hope for the compassion of the Lord of Vaikuṇṭha, which is sought through the functioning of the desires of sages.
Now, (8) apprehension (*śaṅkā*): that which is the imagining of one's own misfortune arising from one's own offense such as theft, or from the cruelty of another, is designated as apprehension.
In this state, there occur emaciation, discoloration, gazing in the directions, dejection, and so forth.
And therein, by way of theft— for example:
"Then the Lotus-born [Brahmā], with deceit, while carrying off the multitude of children along with their calves..."
About to vanish, he gazes upon the eight directions with his eight restless eyes.
Or as it is said:
"Alas, because I went far away, having concealed the Syamantaka jewel which was yielding wealth..."
Even now, that very same blameworthy deed pierces my heart, robbing it of its peace.
On account of an offense, for example:
"O Lord of Śacī, you have been stained in the cowherd settlement of Nanda ever since you caused the rain to fall."
Listen to what is beneficial for you: having sought refuge in Kṛṣṇa, enter without hesitation into the splendor of Indra.
By the cruelty of another, as in the *Padyāvalī* (331):
"It does not spread my intense anguish in such a way..."
There is separation from his companion, the moon of cowherds;
his dwelling is in the city of the Lord of the Danujas, surrounded by the bitter circles of the Asuras.
But for excellent women, suspicion born of timidity may cause fear.
Now, (9) *trāsa* (fear):
*Trāsa* is an agitation in the heart caused by the terrible roars of fierce creatures as violent as lightning;
it produces horripilation, trembling, paralysis, dizziness, and so forth, in one who stands nearby seeking support. (RBhrs 2.4.54)
In that regard, by means of lightning, for example:
"Struck instantly in the eyes by a dense flash of lightning, a certain cowherd child cried out, 'O Kṛṣṇa, protect me! (RBhrs 2.4.55).
By his terrible power, as for example: when the enemy of the gods, having approached not far away, transformed himself into a bull before the cowherd women.
Mistaking it for Kṛṣṇa, she whose limbs were trembling quickly embraced the tamāla tree and became motionless.
With a fierce roar, such that Yaśodā, hearing the thundering of the wolves manifest in every direction— a calamity reaching the very path of her ears— [was struck with fear].
She long gazed at her own son, who was as clever as four Yāmas and who moved about with the grace of four eyes.
A sudden trembling of the limbs accompanied by agitation of the mind is called *trāsa* (terror).
*Bhaya* (fear), which arises from the deliberation of what precedes and follows, is distinct from *trāsa*.
Now, (10) *āvega* (agitation): that which is a perturbation of the mind is *āvega*, and it is of eight kinds:
caused by the beloved, the unloved, fire, wind, rain, portents, and the roar of an elephant. (RBhṛs 2.4.59)
When arising from something pleasant, there is horripilation, conciliation, agitation, and so forth;
but when arising from something unpleasant, there is falling to the ground, wailing, wandering, and so forth.
In the fire-born [type of ophthalmia], there is wandering of the gaze, trembling, closing of the eyes, lacrimation, and so forth;
in the wind-born type, there is obstruction, rapid movement, wiping of the vision, and so forth.
That born of rain causes running, holding up an umbrella, and contracting the limbs; in that of an omen, it causes discoloration of the face, astonishment, loss of appetite, and so forth.
In the *gaja* [mudrā], there is trembling, fleeing, fear, looking over the shoulder, and so forth;
it causes the enemy to seize armor, weapons, and the like, and to retreat.
Here is an example arising from the sight of the beloved:
"Beholding her son returning from Vṛndāvana, the mistress of Gokula, her breasts overflowing with milk, became agitated and covered in horripilation. (RBhrs 2.4.64)
That which arises from hearing what is dear,
as stated in the *Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam* (10.23.18):
"Having heard that Acyuta had arrived, they who were constantly eager for his sight [welcomed him]."
With their minds drawn by that story, they became filled with wonder.
Born from the sight of the unpleasant, as for example:
"What is this? What is this? What is this loud noise?"—thus she speaks, reeling from the roar of a terrible sound.
At night, seeing the son of Pūtanā, Yaśodā wanders about in a state of agitation.
Born from hearing what is unpleasant, as for example: "Hearing that her son had fallen into the midst of two lions on the riverbank, she stood with upturned eyes."
The queen of the Ābhīras, her heart pierced by agitation, did not know what ought to be done.
Born from fire, as it were—
our intellect was born from the distracted [mind] of all our friends; seeing that jewel which protects life, the cow [the earth] sought it with reverence as it remained deep within the dense forest.
Behold, O Lord whose crest is adorned with peacock feathers: the fire, emitting a harsh and unbroken roar, drinks up the waves of water from the celestial ponds with its long-reaching flames.
Born of wind, as for example:

when the comet initiated by the dust-clouds— possessing a mass of valor that crushed the huts of the vast forest— attained the behavior of a master of the *tāṇḍava* dance upon the many arms of the towering branches of the *bhāṇḍīra* tree.
In a mass of wind that scatters the peaks of dried cow-dung, amidst gravelly ground resounding with splashing sounds,
and seeing no son upon the earth, the wife of the Lord of Vraja wanders about in great distress.
Regarding the rainy season, as described in the *Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam* (10.25.11):
"Due to the excessive downpours and fierce winds, the cattle became trembling;
the cowherds and cowherd girls, afflicted by the cold, went for refuge to Govinda."
Or as it is said:
"In this cow-pen, showers of rain fall in every direction, equal to the trunks of elephants and like unto large water-jars."
Even those who were born as youths became agitated; you, however, are clearly still a child, so do not seek to depart from that house.
That which arises from portents, for example:
"The earth suddenly crumbles away with immense force, and alas, terrible meteors roar down from above!"
"My child, having been defiled by a serpent, is now wandering along the bank of the Yamunā; what should I do in this situation?"
For example: "Move aside, move aside with haste, O elephant, as beautiful as a rain-cloud, from before me! (Gājo)
O Lord, by the mere sight of your tender gaze, the fickle hearts of the city women tremble.
By means of an elephant, another being such as a beast or the like is characterized as "wicked."
Or as it is said:
"Scattering the horses of the fierce-rayed sun with the dancing of the tips of his mane,
he swiftly puts to flight those who cause blindness to the beautiful-eyed wives of the lord of gods, by means of the dust raised from the cow-pens."

"Let the enemy of the gods, blinded by pride and with his form humbled, draw near before me; while my arm remains ever vigilant here against the most formidable foes, O Mother, why are you so distressed? (RBhṛs 2.4.75)
O noble one, as it says in the *Lalitamādhava* (2.29): "Where is that base Yakṣa, whose arms are as thick as palm trees, whose body is like a mountain slope, and whose chest is like a mountain ridge;
and where is this child, lovely as the god of love, as tender as a young sprout of the dark *tamāla* tree?"
There is no other living being here so skilled at cooperation; alas, O Mistress of the Cow-pen, we do not know what kind of ripening of your asceticism unfolds today!
Or as it says in that very same place (5.30): "A horse, a horse; a chariot here, a chariot; an elephant, my quiver, a quiver;
and a bow, O sir, a bow; a sword, a sword!"
"What fear? What fear? Here I am! Alas, hurry, hurry!
The king’s daughter has indeed been carried off by that lustful cowherd!"
Even if this appearance of agitation is dependent upon another,
it is nevertheless shown here for the purpose of awakening one to the excellence of the hero.
Now, (11) *unmāda* (madness):
*Unmāda* is a whirling of the heart, arising from intense bliss, calamity, separation [from a beloved], and so forth. (RBhṛs 2.4.79)
In this state, there is loud laughter, dancing, singing, and futile movements;
as well as incoherent speech, running, crying out, and contrary actions.
In that regard, due to mature bliss,
as it says in the *Karṇāmṛta* (2.25):
"May Rādhā, whose mind is bestowed by Acyuta, purify the world."
While she was churning curds in a vessel emptied of milk,
her bee-like eyes flickered toward her cluster-like breasts;
even the Lord, his heart captivated, milked the white [milk].
In times of calamity— for example, as it is said: "Sorcerers bow with palms joined even to beasts," and "Physicians go so far as to treat even trees"— one asks for an antidote to poison.
Alas, alas! When Hari entered the lake that was terrifying with serpents, the wife of the King of Vraja fell repeatedly into a state of bewildered confusion.
Due to separation, as it is said in the *Śrī-daśama* (10.30.4):
"Singing loudly of Him alone, they wandered from forest to forest like madwomen, moving together in a group."
They questioned the trees regarding the Person who exists within and without all beings, like the sky.
Although this insanity is mentioned separately even though it is included among the diseases,
it produces a supreme variety of manifestations in cases such as deception and the like.
When the Great State has ascended and reached the condition of delusion,
having attained another stage, it is called Divine Madness.
Now, (12) epilepsy (*apasmāra*):

Epilepsy is a derangement of the mind arising from the imbalance of the bodily constituents (*dhātu*) caused by suffering and other factors; it consists here of falling down, running about, convulsions, and whirling sensations.
Trembling, the flowing of foam, the throwing out of arms, crying out, and so forth.
For example:
"At every step he foams, he hurls his wave-like arms,
he reels, he rolls, he groans, and he sinks."
O ornament of the Vṛṣṇis, today in your absence, your mother— the queen of the king of Vraja— has long been like the shore of the ocean.
Or as it is said:
"Alas! Having heard that you have slain Kaṃsa, the demon and ornament of the Yadu clan, his dearest friend has reached a certain terrible end."
With the edges of his mouth kissed by clusters of saliva and foam, his arms waving,
he does not rest as he whirls in a circle upon the shore of the ocean.
In this context, even this particular type of disease is described as being like madness,
because it produces a supreme aesthetic wonder (*camatkṛti*) in the appearance of the terrifying (*bhayānaka*).

Now, (13) disease: those ailments such as fever and the like, which arise from the aggravation of the humors (*doṣa*), separation [from loved ones], and so forth— here, the state produced by these is designated as "disease" (*vyādhi*).
In this state, there is paralysis, as well as drooping of the limbs, labored breathing, feverish heat, exhaustion, and so forth.
For example:
"Having experienced suffering due to your long separation, my limbs now possess a great numbness as they are being inflamed."
The entire household of the cow-pen wallows upon the surface of the earth, its nostrils struck by the gusts of wind from their panting breaths.
Now, (14) delusion (*moha*):
Delusion is a state of mental bewilderment arising from joy, separation, fear, or despondency; in that state, there occurs the falling of the body to the ground.
There is the state of having empty senses, as well as wandering about and a nature consisting of lack of movement.
In that regard, out of joy,
as it is said in the Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam (10.12.44):
"Thus questioned, he, the son of Badarāyaṇa..."
With all his senses drawn away by the remembrance of Him,
he slowly regained his outward vision with great difficulty and replied to that most excellent of devotees.
Or as it is said:
"With their modes of breathing suspended, the movement of their eyelashes stilled,
all their senses rendered motionless, and the fluctuations of consciousness withdrawn;"
Having beheld the lotus-eyed one in secret within the land of the Kurus,
the lotus-eyed women of Vraja attained the splendor of golden statues.
Due to separation, as in the *Haṃsadūta* (4): "Once, in order to dispel the fire of grief within her heart, she, with her companions, reached the banks of the Yamunā with an agitated mind."
Then, after a long time, her mind— having grown weary of dwelling in its familiar hut— clearly extended toward that state which is the dear friend of deep sleep.
Out of fear, as for example:
"The one whose banner is the best of monkeys, beholding Mukunda who had manifested his universal form..."
The one of unimpaired intellect did not perceive that the Gāṇḍīva bow was slipping from his lotus-like hand before him.
From despondency, as described in the *Śrī-daśama* (10.11.49):
"Seeing Kṛṣṇa seized by the great crane, Rāma and the other boys became unconscious, like the senses deprived of the vital breath. (RBhrs 2.4.97)
Elsewhere, there may be delusion regarding everything up to the self;
however, the specific manifestation of Kṛṣṇa is never lost here.
Now, (15) death:
Death is the relinquishing of the vital breaths due to despondency, disease, terror, combat, exhaustion, and so forth; during that state, there is the utterance of indistinct syllables.
The symptoms include discoloration of the limbs, labored breathing, and hiccups, among others.
For example:
"With breaths that do not rise, repeatedly casting their eyes upward and askance,
they manifest a certain new pallor throughout their bodies."
In Mathurā, the virtuous, chanting the names of Hari which are rendered indistinct by waves of heavy hiccups, give up their lives.
Or as it is said:

"With a circle of lowing sounds (*ghutkāra*) emerging from her throat, heavy with the effort of ceasing, and with the flickering glow of fireflies in her eyes momentarily opening and closing in exhaustion;"
The night of doom, Pūtanā, whose dense darkness had swallowed up the life-breath of the sun-like Hari, suddenly met her destruction.
Generally, in this context, death is considered to be the mental state preceding actual death;
however, some say that "death" here is an *anubhāva* (consequent emotion), while others say it refers to the enemy's death for the sake of the hero's valor. (RBhrs 2.4.102)
Now, (16) laziness— whatever lack of inclination toward action exists even when capability is present, arising from satiety, fatigue, and so forth, that is declared to be laziness. RBhrs_2,4.103 //
In this state, there is drooping of the limbs, yawning, aversion to activity, rubbing of the eyes,
a fondness for a single bed or seat, as well as drowsiness, sleep, and so forth.
In that regard, concerning satisfaction, as it is said:
"O Lord of the Gopas, our satisfaction during the festival of Govardhana was not such as we have now, even when receiving your blessings, as there is a sovereign power [in this]. (RBhrs 2.4.105)
From exhaustion, as for example:
"Having performed a wrestling match for my pleasure, Subala’s body became utterly devoid of strength."
Stretching his own limbs all around,
he suddenly challenged him to the combat.
Now, (17) insensibility (*jāḍya*):
Insensibility is a lack of comprehension [arising] from hearing about or seeing what is desired or undesired, as well as from separation and so forth;
and through that delusion, there is also a state other than the previous one.
In this context, [the signs] include not blinking, silence, forgetfulness, and so forth.
In this regard, by the hearing of what is desired, as it is said in the Śrī Daśama-skandha (10.21.13):
"And the cows [were captivated] by the flute-song issuing from Kṛṣṇa’s mouth..."
Drinking the nectar with their ears pricked up,
the young calves stood with mouthfuls of milk from their mothers' flowing udders, touching Govinda within themselves with their eyes filled with tears.
By hearing what is undesirable, as for example: "Having perceived that his lineage had been overturned and that the arrow had been fixed within the words of Keśava..."
Lakṣmaṇā, her mind fixed and her eyes unblinkingly intent, remained silent for a moment.
By beholding the beloved,
as it is said in the *Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam* (10.71.40):
"Having respectfully brought Govinda, the Lord of the gods of gods, into his home..."
Stricken by negligence, the king did not recognize his duty regarding the worship.
By the sight of the undesirable,
as it is said in that very same place (10.39.36):
"As long as the banner is visible, and as long as the dust of the chariot [is seen]..."
With their selves set forth, they are perceived like paintings.
By reason of separation, as follows:
"In separation from Mukunda, your friends, distressed and long abandoned by their ornaments, sat down upon the ground and remained there."
With garments soiled by slipping and the beauty of their limbs mottled and coarse,
they shine like idols of the gods in the houses of wicked devalakas and brahmins.
Now, (18) *vrīḍā* (shame): *Vrīḍā* is a lack of boldness caused by the neglect of one's own praise due to the occasion of a new union and so forth; in that state, there is silence and reflection.
Veiling the face, drawing lines on the ground, looking downward, and so forth.
In that regard, through a new union,
as it says in the *Padyāvalī* (198): "O lotus-eyed one, you yourself [acted] toward Govinda..."
O friend, blinded by love, offer your excellent body; do not act with such miserliness in granting even a slight glance.
When the elephant has been sold, what dispute can there be over the goad?
By way of improper conduct, for example:
"O Lord of Śacī, do not turn your face downward here, nor make your head hang down out of shame."
If you do not take the wish-fulfilling tree nor Śacī,
how will you look her in the face?
By means of this hymn—as it was said:
"The head of Uddhava, which had been bowed down while Śauri was being praised by him with the weight of his manifold excellent qualities, then shone forth. (RBhrs 2.4.116)
Out of contempt, as in the *Harivaṃśa* (2.67.19) [in the critical edition,
Appendix 29], there is the speech of Satyādevī:
How shall I, who was once beloved, look upon that Mount Raivataka again— so variegated with spring blossoms— having now become one who is no longer loved?
Now, (19) *avahitthā*:
concealment of one's outward appearance through some internal state of being. *RBhṛs* 2.4.118.

In this context, the concealment of one's limbs and other signs that might lead to being inferred by others, as well as looking elsewhere, futile movements, distortions of speech, and so forth, are the [concealing] actions. (RBhṛs 2.4.119)
And so it has been said:
"The emotional state called *avahittha* is said to be for the purpose of concealing one's inner experience. (RBhṛs 2.4.120)
In that regard, as for guile (*jaihmya*),
it is as described in the *Śrī-daśama* (10.32.15): "Having honored him, who kindles the god of love..."
With playful glances and the movement of their eyebrows,
and by the touch of their hands and feet placed upon his lap,
they praised him and spoke while being slightly provoked to anger.
Out of courtesy, as when the Pārijāta tree was led away from the precincts of Sātrājitī’s residence by Madhusūdana of exalted splendor;
Within the vast expanse of the Vidarbha land, it is said that no one perceived any jealousy on her part toward him because of his excellent character.
Out of modesty, as described in the first [chapter] (1.11.33)—
those women of inexhaustible nature embraced their husband with their inner selves through glances born of themselves.
O best of the Bhṛgus, though the tears had ceased to flow from their eyes due to shame, they flowed again out of their distress.
Due to guile and modesty, for example:
"O messenger, what woman of good family would lust after that serpent of a cowherd?
For when he is remembered, my body breaks out in horripilation from fear. (RBhṛ 2.4.124)
Through her goodness—for example:
"Though her love for Kṛṣṇa was mature, it remained hidden within the depths of the caverns of her mind by the perfection of its profundity, and thus it was inconceivable to others. (RBhrs 2.4.125)
With reverence, as for example:
while Govinda was clearly engaging in playful jesting here with his friends, headed by Subala, their faces beaming with smiles.
Then the bird, his face bent down and charming with joy, carefully suppressed his smile with effort.
"There may be a cause, something to be concealed, and one who conceals;
thus, the employment of these three factors is observed here. (RBhṛS 2.4.127)
In this context, the state of being a cause, the state of being a concealer,
and the state of being that which is concealed may occur for almost all entities, both individually and collectively.
Now, (20) memory:
that cognition of an object previously experienced, whether through the sight of a similar thing or by means of firm repetition and so forth, is proclaimed to be memory.
In this case, there may be shaking of the head, as well as the knitting of the eyebrows and so forth.
In that regard, "perception of similarity" (*sadṛśekṣaṇā*) is as follows:
"Beholding the dark cloud, the lotus-eyed one, repeatedly remembering you, O Mukunda, and repeatedly remembering [the deeds of] Smara, experienced [a state of longing]. (RBhṛs 2.4.130)
Through firm practice, as follows:
"Even though I am not currently performing the rite of formal dedication, due to negligence, the pair of lotus-feet of Hari flashes forth in my heart at some time or other. (RBhrs 2.4.131)
Now, (21) *vitarka*—from deliberation (*vimarṣa*) and from doubt (*saṃśaya*), *vitarka* is called *ūha* (inquiry).
This is characterized by the knitting of the eyebrows, the movement of the head, the fingers, and so forth. (RBhṛs 2.4.132)
In that regard, [the emotion arises] from deliberation (*vimarṣa*),
as in the *Vidagdhamādhava* (2.27):
"You do not realize that the entire crest of hair has fallen from your head..."
O young elephant of the playful groves of Vṛndāvana, that garland which you previously placed around your neck has now been lifted up;
O best of bees to Rādhā’s eyes, this is clearly the manifestation of your prowess.
From doubt, for example: "Is this a *tāpiñcha* tree? No, for its splendor is not so stainless; is it a cloud? No, for here there is no spotless moon."
O moon-faced one, Mukunda is surely sporting here on the summit of the mountain, his sweet sound of the flute dispelling the world's delusion.
Others have declared that this reasoning (tarka) ends precisely with the final determination (vinirṇaya).
Now, (22) reflection—*cintā*:
reflection is defined as the failure to obtain what is desired and the acquisition of what is undesired;
it is manifested here by sighing, downcast eyes, drawing on the ground, change of complexion, and sleepiness.
And there are also lamentation, feverish distress, emaciation, tears, wretchedness, and so forth.
In that regard, due to the non-attainment of what is desired,
as it is said in the *Śrī-daśama* (10.29.29):
"Having covered their faces, they wept, drying [their tears] with the breath of their sighing."

Scratching their bimba-like lips with their feet and wiping the saffron from their breasts with the ends of their robes— though they held no pens— they stood silent, burdened by a great weight of sorrow.
Or as it is said:
"O Destroyer of Sins, she who is free from fault, having passed the evening in restlessness and becoming emaciated, finally sat down after a long time on the threshold with great difficulty."
With her face trembling and reeling within from anxiety for you,
alas, O lover of play, has your mother today forgotten the home?
Through the attainment of the undesired, as for example:
"O housewife, do not wither your lotus-face with a flood of hot tears born from anxious thoughts within your deep forest-like heart."
Finding the king’s city together with the son of Gāndinī, I myself shall swiftly turn back your son.
Now, (23) *mati*—the determination of the meaning arising from the investigation of the scriptures and so forth is *mati*. (RBhṛs 2.4.140)
In this context, there is the performance of what is to be done, the cutting away of doubt and error,
instruction for disciples, as well as reasoning, refutation, and so forth.
As it is said in the Vaiśākha-māhātmya of the Padma-purāṇa:
"For the sake of deluding the world of moving and non-moving beings, let various ancient scriptures proclaim, until the end of the kalpa, this or that particular deity as the supreme one."

In our established doctrine (siddhānta), however, it is determined that the Lord Viṣṇu alone is the one [reality] when all the operations of the scriptures have been subjected to analytical investigation.
Or as it is said in the Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam (10.60.39):
"You, whose majesty is proclaimed by sages who have laid aside the rod of punishment, and who are the Self and the giver of the Self to the worlds— you have been chosen by me."
Having abandoned the lords of the gods and the dwellers of the lotus-born [Brahmā], whose blessings were destroyed by the force of Time unleashed by your eyebrows, how could there be any others?

Now, (24) fortitude—fortitude arises from fullness, knowledge, the absence of suffering, and the attainment of the highest; it consists in not performing such acts as grieving for objects that have not been attained, those that have passed away, or those that have been lost. RBhrs_2,4.144 //
In this regard, by means of knowledge,
as Bhartṛhari says in the *Vairāgya-śataka* (verse 55):
Let us eat alms; let us wear garments made of rags; let us sleep upon the surface of the earth—what need have we for lords?
By the absence of suffering, as it is said:
"The cow-pen shines as a house for the play of Lakṣmī,
and cows run about in numbers beyond the highest parārdha."
My son, whose deeds are divine, plays thus;
I have found satisfaction in the happiness of a householder's life.
Through the attainment of the supreme, as it is said:
"Even for one who stands upon the shore of the nectar-ocean of Hari’s divine play, my mind does not regard even the four aims of human life as being worth more than a blade of grass. (RBhrs 2.4.147)
Now, (25) *harṣa* (joy):
"Joy is the clarity of the mind arising from the attainment of the sight of the beloved and so forth;
in this context, it is characterized by horripilation, perspiration, tears, and the blooming of the face."
Agitation, insanity, and dullness, as well as delusion and the like, [arise].
In that regard, by the sight of the beloved, as it is said in the Śrī Viṣṇu Purāṇa (5.17.25):
"Seeing those two, that high-minded one’s lotus-face blossomed."
O Sage, at that moment, Akrūra’s entire body was covered with horripilation.
By the attainment of what is desired,
as it is said in the *Śrī-daśama* (10.33.12): "There, [she smelled] the arm of Kṛṣṇa resting upon one shoulder, which possessed the fragrance of a blue lotus."
Having smelled the sandalwood paste applied [to him], his hair stood on end and he kissed it.
Now, (26) longing—longing is an inability to endure time, caused by the desire to see or obtain what is desired and so forth;
it produces dryness of the mouth, haste, anxiety, sighing, restlessness, and the like. (RBhṛS 2.4.151)

In that regard, longing through the desire to behold the beloved is as described in the *Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam* (10.71.34): "Having heard that the vessel for the drinking of the eyes of men had arrived..."
With their hair and silk garments loosened by eagerness,
the young women immediately abandoned their household chores and their husbands, and went out onto the royal road to see the king’s bedchamber.

Or as it is said in the *Śrī-rādhikāṣṭaka* (14.7) within the *Stavāvalī*: "Having approached from nearby in the forest bower Hari— who had made his own dwelling manifest through the resonant sounds of his affectionate flute and whose gait was swift— the smiling-eyed one [gazed upon him]."
When will Rādhikā, her face cast down as she spreads an itch within the hollows of my ears, bathe me in her own service?
Out of a longing to attain what is desired, for example:
while her circle of friends prolongs the conversation before the Destroyer of Sins (Śiva) by means of playful jesting, [she remains silent].
Under the pretext of gathering flower clusters,
she proceeded swiftly with quick steps into the thicket.
Now, (27) *augrya*—it is ferocity (*ugratā*), a state of violence arising from offenses, harsh speech, and so forth;
it consists of acts such as killing, binding, shaking the head, threatening, and striking. (RBhṛs 2.4.155)

In that regard, regarding offense, for example: "While my lord— whose fame spreads from the loosening of the womb of the serpent-queen— is manifesting himself, even Kāliya commits an offense against me."
Alas, I would offer him into the fire-god Agni with the exclamation *vauṣaṭ* in my stomach;
yet, I fear the wrath of the slayer of demons.

Regarding the ill-spoken, as in the words of Sahadeva: "He who is unable to endure the foremost worship of the preeminent among the wise [Indra]— that enemy of the Danujas, whose fame is well-established— "
With my left foot, its brilliance fierce with the harsh punishment of Yama, I shall place it upon his broad head.
Or as Baladeva said: "Indeed,

those wicked ones, the lowest of the Kuru lineage, who were once intent on the royal throne abandoned after being enjoyed by hundreds of thousands of kings, now [seek] their Lord within millions of cosmic eggs."
Alas! What a mockery this is, O Śiva! Today, as we listen, they are forcibly casting sidelong glances here at Acyuta, who is worthy of being worshipped by all.
Now, (28) indignation—indignation is the inability to endure insults, humiliation, and the like. (RBhṛS 2.4.159)
In that state, there is perspiration, trembling of the head, change of complexion, brooding,
searching for means [of escape], lamentation, aversion, beating, and so forth.
In that regard, [an example] of insult (*adhikṣepa*) is found in the *Vidagdhamādhava* (2.53):
"The foremost of all the beauties of the entire earth, having been thoroughly washed away..."
"My virtuous bride, newly wedded, dwells by my side; look!
She is dancing within the courtyard, casting sidelong glances from the corners of her eyes.
You may wander here without fear; how could there be any agitation for me?"
From insult, as in the words of Padmā:
"O thief in the *kadamba* grove, depart quickly! What is the use of your flatteries? For there can be no greater humiliation for a person such as I."
Alas, in the assembly of those with the eyes of forest deer, even the excellent Candrāvalī was clearly defiled by you through that unworthy woman named Tārā.
By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), deception is also included,
as in Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam 10.31.16: "Husbands, sons, descendants, brothers-in-law, and kinsmen..."
Having utterly transgressed [all bounds], those women have come to you, O Acyuta; who, knowing your ways, would abandon those women— deluded by your song— at night, O gambler?
Now, (29) *asūyā* (envy): Envy is hatred toward the rise of another due to their good fortune, virtues, and so forth.
In this regard, its manifestations include jealousy, disrespect, and derision, as well as the attribution of faults even where virtues exist.
Turning away, looking askance, the knitting of the eyebrows, and so forth; these are the signs of anger.
In that regard, [an example] of [jealousy] caused by another's good fortune is as follows, from the *Padyāvalī* (verse 302):
{*Attributed to Dāmodara in the *Padyāvalī*. Also found in *Amaruśataka* 55;}.
—of Keśaṭa;
SāhD 3.105 (as an example of *mada*); Daśa 2.22.}—
"Do not harbor such pride, thinking, 'The fresh cluster of blossoms written by Kṛṣṇa’s own hand shines upon the surface of my cheek.
O friend, is not even another woman a worthy recipient for such things?"
If there is no enemy, then internal trembling is the obstacle.
Or as it is said in the *Śrī-daśama* (10.30.30):
"These high words of hers cause us great agitation,
for she alone, having drawn away the cowherd girls, enjoys the lip of Acyuta in secret."
By way of quality, for example:
"If the powerful factions of Balarāma have conquered us—the factions of Kṛṣṇa who have themselves suffered defeat—then who on earth are weak? (RBhṛs 2.4.167)
Furthermore, regarding restlessness (*cāpalya*):
Restlessness is the lightness of the mind caused by passion, hatred, and so forth; therein lie lack of discernment, harshness, acting according to one's own whims, and the like. (RBhṛs 2.4.168)
In that regard, concerning passion (*rāga*), as it is said in the *Śrī-daśama* (10.52.41):
"Tomorrow, at your marriage to the unconquered one (*ajita*), you shall go to Vidarbha..."
Having approached in secret and surrounded by the commanders of the armies,
and having forcibly crushed the forces of the lords of Cedi and Magadha,
marry me— who have valor as my dowry— by the Rākṣasa rite.
Out of hatred, for example:
"May the flute of Kālindī carry away the ocean, which causes the waist-knots of fair-browed women to slip even in the presence of their elders. (RBhrs 2.4.170)
Now, (31) sleep—sleep is the closing of the mind due to anxiety, laziness, natural fatigue, and so forth.
In that state, there occur stretching of the limbs, yawning, dullness, labored breathing, and the closing of the eyes. (RBhṛs 2.4.171)
In that regard, by means of reflection, as it is said:
"While the sun was turning red, the wife of Nanda, not hearing the sound of the flute and with her heart overcome by anxiety, fell asleep. (RBhrs 2.4.172)
Due to exhaustion, as it were—
this slender-bodied mistress of Vraja, her limbs utterly spent by the labors of binding Dāmodara, now appears with her head slightly reeling and her body trembling. (RBhrs 2.4.173)
By nature, as it is said:
"O Remover of Evil, with all anxieties dispelled by Your power, we have abandoned the constraints of home, property, and doorways."
Behold, O cowherds, how they lie here comfortably during the night, adorning their respective courtyards with limbs that remain motionless.
From exhaustion— just as Viśākhā, her limbs cast upon Hari’s chest at the end of lovemaking, her body variegated by the transferred bodily humors, today fell into a deep sleep. (RBhrs 2.4.175)
When the heart is closed by some indeterminate, undifferentiated manifestation of Him alone, that state which stands before one is called "sleep" (nidrā) among devotees. (RBhṛs 2.4.176)
Now, (32) *supti* (sleep):

*Supti* is characterized by sleep (*nidrā-vibhāva*); its essence consists in the experience of various objects, and it brings about the cessation of the senses, the slowing of breath, the closing of the eyes, and so forth. (RBhṛs 2.4.177)
For instance:
"O lotus-eyed one, let this youthful playfulness and the excessive pride of the lord of serpents, which have been manifested at will, be swiftly shaken off."
Thus, with the words of his dream-tales, the wielder of the plow (Balarāma) long caused the assembly of the Yadus to marvel;
then, with a sigh that made his belly heave with rising waves, he fell asleep.
Now, (33) awakening: Awakening is the destruction and the emergence from ignorance, delusion, sleep, and so forth; it is the state of being fully awakened. (RBhṛs 2.4.179)
In that regard, through the destruction of ignorance—

the awakening resulting from the destruction of ignorance is preceded by the dawning of knowledge and effects the cessation of all afflictions as well as the realization of one's true nature. (RBhṛs 2.4.180)
For example:
"Having found the lamp of knowledge and immediately realized one's own true nature, which consists of the realization of truth,"
I seek that supreme Brahman, which is free from all obstacles, embodied, and whose form is intense bliss.
Through the destruction of delusion—

upon the waning of delusion, the awakening of consciousness regarding Hari brings about the opening of the eyes, horripilation, rising from one's seat, and so forth, by means of [perceiving] His sounds, scents, touches, and tastes. (RBhrs 2.4.182)
In that regard, by way of sound, for example:
"At the first sight of him, her sensory functions became swallowed up by a succession of joys that had taken root."
When the name "Aghabhid" was heard uttered in a sweet voice, her eyes closed here.

By its fragrance— just as [the elephant] Śabalāṅgī, whose limbs had slackened from exhaustion in the forest region after a long time spent freeing others from calamity, now lay with her movement of breath stilled; |||
See, as the fragrance of the forest garland spreads, Rādhā,
her body covered in horripilation, has risen from a heap of dust.
By touch, for example:
"Whose is this victorious, sweet, and smooth touch of a hand, which belongs to her who, having seen the forest on the banks of the Yamunā, was being shattered [by grief]?"
Having forcefully shaken off the pervasive delusion consisting of destruction,
O friend, it quickly causes within her a blossoming of blissful ecstasy.
By way of rasa, for example:
"O younger brother of Balarāma, when you had vanished during the rāsa-sport,
my friend’s slender body became limp and she fell unconscious."
Having received the betel-chewed from you, O lotus-eyed one,
she stood radiant with horripilation as it was placed within the cavity of my mouth.
Regarding the destruction of sleep: awakening occurs through the exhaustion of sleep, through the completion of dreams, sleep, or sounds, and so forth;
therein [occur] rubbing the eyes, leaving the bed, stretching the limbs, and other such actions. (RBhṛS 2.4.187)
In that regard, by way of a dream, as follows:
"Let this beauty of your laughter cease; let go of this flickering glance before I clearly declare your fickleness to my mother."
Thus she prattled in her dream for a moment; then, having suddenly awakened and seeing the Guru before her, Gaurī repeatedly lowered her face like a blossoming lotus.
Due to the fulfillment of her sleep—for instance: "The messenger arrived at her abode, and Rādhikā woke up;
for the exertion of the meritorious quickly bears fruit. (RBhrs 2.4.189)
With its sound,
it shone forth like a rain-cloud from the flute, driving away from afar the female swans of sleep belonging to the fair-browed cowherd girls, and causing the deer to frolic.
Thus, thirty-three transitory emotions (vyabhicāribhāvas) have been described;
they should be depicted as appropriate for characters who are superior, middling, or inferior.
Miserliness, agitation, hypocrisy, envy, discernment, as well as resolution, impotence, forbearance, curiosity, longing, and even modesty; 2,4.192.
Doubt, audacity, and other such states that may exist elsewhere are included within those already mentioned; therefore, they have not been shown separately.
For instance: envy is indeed included within malice, and agitation within fear;
likewise, hypocrisy is included within dissimulation, and both jealousy and resentment are considered forms of intolerance.
Discernment and resolution—these two [are found in discernment]; while dejection and weakness [are found in delusion], and patience and fortitude [in courage].
Longing is included within curiosity and yearning; modesty likewise within shame; doubt within reasoning; and audacity within fickleness.
Among these transitory mental states (sañcāribhāvas), some may indeed function as both the determinants (vibhāva) and the consequents (anubhāva) for one another.
But in the case of world-weariness (*nirveda*), just as envy (*īrṣyā*) may serve as its determinants (*vibhāva*),
so too is malice (*asūyā*) clearly stated to be its consequents (*anubhāva*).

In this context, anxiety is said to be the ensuant (anubhāva) with respect to longing, while sleep is its determinant cause (vibhāva); in this same manner, these other [emotions] are also to be understood.
And regarding these sattvic states and the expansion of various activities,
the relationship between cause and effect should generally be understood from worldly experience.
It is held that blame (*nindā*) serves as a *vibhāva* for both discoloration (*vaivarṇya*) and indignation (*amarṣa*);
furthermore, its status as an *anubhāva* for envy (*asūyā*) has already been stated.
The state of being a *vibhāva* for striking consists in fainting and paralysis;
its state of being an *anubhāva* is with respect to ferocity. In this same way, other [emotions] are also to be understood.
For those wandering beings who are devoid of awakening and who overcome fear, sleep, fatigue, indolence, and intoxication,
there may arise in this world the state of being an attendant emotion (*anubhāva*) of love.
There is no direct connection between direct sexual pleasure (*sākṣād-rati*) and the six [emotions] beginning with fear;
however, there may be an indirect connection for the sake of conforming to the playful mood (*līlā*).

In certain cases, there is the state of being a determinant emotion (*vibhāva*) for discursive thought, intelligence, world-weariness, fortitude, mindfulness, joy, awakening, differentiation, dejection, and sleep, as well as for passion.
Thus it is said that those who migrate are of two kinds: dependent and independent.
Among those, the dependent [powers]—
though dependent powers are said to be twofold according to their being superior or inferior— are described as such.
In that regard,
the bridegroom— whether direct or indirect— is also declared to be of these two kinds.
In that context, "directly" (sākṣāt) means nourishing the primary [form of] delight itself; thus it is designated as "direct."
For example:
"The hair on his body and his slender form perform a dance for me upon hearing his name."
Alas, for one who does not behold that region of Mathurā, what is the use, indeed, of this pair of eyes?
Now, the "separated" (vyavahita):
that which nourishes a secondary passion is considered "separated."
For example:
"Fie upon my two arms, which resemble Bhīma’s iron mace; fie upon them, for though they are wicked enough to hurl Mādhava, they do not crush the King of Cedi. (RBhrs 2.4.211)
This state of despondency arises from being subject to anger; thus, it is an obstacle to sexual pleasure.
Now, regarding the *avara*:
that which attains the status of a subordinate member (*aṅga*) for both types of aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) is considered the *avara*.
For example:
"Licking the worlds with his flaming mouths, [the Lord] has the heads of his victims split open by his fangs."
Beholding Kṛṣṇa who had assumed the universal form,
Jiṣṇu did not remember his own self, being utterly overwhelmed.
Having concealed innate bliss through the influence of terrible rites and the like, fear manifested as a difficult-to-overcome state; from that subjection to fear, this delusion arose.
Now, regarding those who are independent: even while always in a state of dependence, there is in some cases independence for these [powers],
just as for a king’s servant engaged in the act of collecting taxes.

Those who know the internal states have proclaimed three types of independent [sexual union]: the one devoid of passion (*rati-śūnya*), the one characterized by the touch of passion (*raty-anusparśana*), and the one permeated by the scent of passion (*rati-gandhi*).
In that regard, one who is devoid of passion—
among people who are devoid of passion— he too shall become devoid of passion.
As it is said in the Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam (10.23.39):
"Fie on our birth, fie on our triple knowledge, fie on our vows, fie on our great learning,
fie on our lineage, and fie on our ritual initiations, since we are turned away from Adhokṣaja!"
Here, *nirveda* (dispassion) is independent.
Among these, it is that which touches upon *rati* (pleasure)— that which, though naturally devoid even of a trace of pleasure, [arises] by way of association.
Afterwards, he should touch the pleasure; this is considered the "touching of pleasure."
For example:
"Distressed by the most terrible and piercing clanging sounds, and rendered deafened, the cowherd girl cried out, 'Alas, Kṛṣṇa! Save me! Save me! (RBhrs 2.4.221).
In this context, there is fear.
Now, as for that which is "scented with passion" (rati-gandhi): it is that which, even in a state of autonomy, manifests the scent of that [passion], being thus scented with passion.
For example:
"I recognize this yellow garment worn upon your body;
O grandson, do not trouble yourself to conceal it."
Thus addressed by the noble lady,
Rādhā, with her head bowed and her face veiled, immediately became silent.

In this context, there is shame; furthermore, their semblance arises from occurring in an inappropriate place (*asthāna*). Inappropriateness (*anaucitya*) and being out of place (*asthānatva*) are said to be of two kinds. (RBhṛS 2.4.224)
In this context, "opposition" (prātikūlya) means that their occurrence in the presence of the contrary factors is what is termed opposition.
For instance:
"Alas! Even a cowherd, though untrained in combat, slays that horse-demon who is no different from my own life."
For me, who have defeated the Lord of the Gods in play and slain King Kaṃsa, this miserable life is quite enough.
Here, there is a semblance of despondency;
or as for example:
"That water-dwelling serpent Kāliya..."
Even a cow-pen is like a mountain, and a clod of earth is its sibling;
what wonder is there in that action among people, O fool, by which one is called a "Lord of the World"?
Here, [there is] the censure of envy.
Now, regarding impropriety (*anaucitya*):
"Untruthfulness and unfitness constitute the two-fold nature of impropriety."
The first [type of killing] occurs regarding that which is inanimate, and the last [type] regarding animals and so forth.
In that regard, concerning that which is not a living being, for example:
"Alas, shame on my birth, for whose shadow was never once sought after by Kṛṣṇa!"
O Kadamba tree, do not be distressed; Hari, while trampling upon the serpent Kāliya, will bring you to the fulfillment of your purpose.
Here is an example of world-weariness (*nirveda*) regarding the animal realm:
"What other bird could today ascend the side of me, who am fit for sacrifice?"
Even abandoning the wings of Tārkṣya, Hari resorts to his wing.
In this regard, pride is addressed:
even while the Kadamba and other trees always carry the sweetness of knowledge and realization, they are said to possess only the semblance of ordinary perception.
The origination, conjunction, agitation, and pacification of entities—these are their four stages; among them, "origination" (utpatti) here refers to "coming into being" (sambhava).
For example:
Having observed that something in the orb of the fierce-rayed sun was turning red, Yaśodā—
Not far away, she sat in a bodice drenched by the flowing stream, [like] the very essence of the sound of the flute.
Herein lies the arising of joy;
or as it is said:
"Even though she was bent by the weight of her agitation as she met you in secret,"
"O friend, look! Your girdle shines at dawn.
May Rādhikā, who thus reveals her secret while casting a sidelong glance with knitted brows, purify you.
Herein arises the origin of *asūyā* (envy).
Now, regarding *sandhi* (junction):
"The junction (*sandhi*) of two states, whether similar or different, is their union (*yuti*). (RBhṛs 2.4.235)
In that regard, the conjunction of similar [vowels] is as follows:
"The conjunction of two similar [vowels] there is considered to arise from different causes. (RBhṛs 2.4.236)
For example:
"Having observed at night a Rākṣasī with her limbs fallen [upon him] at the end of the night, the housewife of the Lord of Gokula..."
And alas, she remained for a moment with her body motionless upon his breast, where he was laughing.
In this case, there is a conjunction of two inertnesses produced by the observation of the undesirable and the desirable;
or else, when they are distinct— that is,
when two [inertnesses] have arisen from a single cause that is itself distinct.

Now, regarding those arising from a single cause: for example— "This child, whose restlessness is difficult to restrain, running here and there within and without the cow-pen, though free from fear of anything, delights my heart and yet pains it. (RBhrs 2.4.239)
In that regard, concerning joy and apprehension:
when these two arise from different causes, for example—
Devakī, beholding [him] sporting...
Upon hearing [the news], his eyes blossomed wide as he beheld before him a powerful circle of wrestlers;
he perceived both the cold and the hot water as if it were fire.
In this case, there is a conjunction of joy and sorrow;
for even many states of being, arising from a single cause as well as from multiple causes, are clearly observed to be in conjunction. (RBhṛs 2.4.241)
Among those born from a single cause, for example:
"On the bank of the Yamunā, when Mukunda forcibly seized her as she was smiling within, with her pupils trembling and radiant with a shimmering digit..."

Triumphant is this jewel of the lineage of Vṛṣabhānu, upon whom she casts her gaze— a sight whose beauty lies in its slightly reddish, curved outer corners, expressing a disdain for all other manifestations.
Herein occurs the conjunction of joy, longing, pride, indignation,
and envy arising from various causes, as follows:
"Having seen her mother wearing a golden necklace, Rādhā..."

On the ground nearby, she who was previously possessed of logic now beheld the smiling lotus-like face of Hari; yet even as her Lord sat there in that splendor, she remained at a slight distance with her face bowed and her countenance withered from quivering.

In this case, there is a combination (*saṃdhi*) of shame, indignation, joy, and despondency. Now, as for variegation (*śābalya*): "Variegation, however, is the mutual intermingling of emotional states. (RBhṛ 2.4.244)
For instance:
"What indeed can that child do, though he is capable? Alas! He has burned my friends' factions;
therefore, I shall quickly take refuge in him alone—though these heroes might not do so."

"Ah! The divine assembly of wrestlers is sporting; he who lifted the best of mountains with his trunk—should I not go this very day to the land of Vraja and cause a slaughter? Alas! Then my mind trembles."
Here, there is a commingling (*śabalatva*) of pride, despondency, dejection, mental confusion, memory, apprehension, indignation, and fear.
Or, for example:
"Fie! Let my eyes be long; yet let Mathurā be [far away], since she is not seen by them."
This knowledge of mine has made kings my servants, yet time devours everything;
Lakṣmī’s playhouse is my home, alas, while my body constantly wastes away even within that very house.
I should worship Hari in my heart, for the forest of Vṛndāvana draws me away.
Here, there is a commingling (*śabalatva*) of despondency, pride, apprehension, fortitude, dejection, intelligence, and eagerness.
Now, as for tranquility (*śānti*): the dissolution of an excessively heightened state of being is called tranquility. (RBhṛS 2.4.247)
For example:
"With faces distressed and luster withered,
they searched for that remover of evil in the thicket."
Upon hearing the soft-toned flute on the mountain,
the children of Vraja became radiant with horripilation.
In this regard, there is a consolation for despondency:
"In my speech, there is no particular variety of word, meaning, or aesthetic flavor; I have merely stated this as an example of emotion (bhāva) in whatever way possible. (RBhṛS 2.4.249)
These thirty-three and the eight which will be mentioned as the stable emotions—
these forty-one are traditionally known as the primary emotional states (mukhya-bhāva).
The fluctuations of the mind are said to be produced by the manifestation of mental states that cause transformations in the group consisting of the body and the senses.
In some cases a state is innate, and in some cases it is adventitious;
that state which is innate exists pervasively both internally and externally.
Just as a dye in substances such as madder is seen to be composed of that very substance,
so too here, through mere designation, the state of being an excitant belongs to that which is devoid of intrinsic nature.
The delight that follows from this very innate state,
though uniform in nature, appears manifold within devotion.
But that which is an adventitious state, such as redness in a cloth and so forth,
is precisely what is placed and also illuminated by those various determinants (vibhāvas).
Due to the distinction of the process of contemplative dissolution (*vibhāvanā*) and so forth, as well as through the differences among devotees,
a distinctiveness generally arises in all states of being.
Due to the diversity of various devotees, the mind is indeed manifold; for according to the mind, there arises a gradation in the intensity of their spiritual dispositions.
When the mind is most weighty, profound, vast, harsh,
and so forth, these [qualities], though correctly manifested, are not clearly perceived by people.
When the mind is light, expanded, subtle, tender, and so forth, these [objects], though only slightly opened, are perceived as prominent externally.
The heaviest [element] has the appearance of a lump of gold, and the lightest is like a bundle of cotton;
in this pair of minds, the nature of existence should be understood as being like the wind.
The mind is deep like the ocean, yet superficial like a pond;
regarding these two states of mind, the existence [of an object] is like the peak of a great mountain.
The greatest [state] would have the radiance of a city, while the smallest is like a hut;
here, in this pair of minds, there is a comparison of existence to a lamp or an elephant.
The harsh [substance] is said to be threefold: diamond, gold, and lac.
Regarding these three types of mind, the state of being should be known as being like fire.
The diamond is extremely hard and possesses no softness whatsoever;
such is the mind of ascetics and others that it is observed to be.
Gold melts under the extremely intense heat of the fire of contemplation,
whereas lac reaches a state of liquefaction from even a slight amount of heat on all sides.
The *komala* [type] is said to be of three kinds: *madana*, *navanītaka*, and *amṛta*; in this context, the state [of arousal] generally resembles the heat of the sun.
Just as a pair of metals would melt here today by heat according to their nature, so too, that which has become liquefied by its very essence would always be nectar;
indeed, the mind of those most excellent among the beloved of Govinda is truly nectar.
The mind may become endowed even with two or three of these qualities, such as the preeminence and other virtues of the particularity of devotion to Kṛṣṇa.
But when the state of extreme greatness has indeed fully arrived,
it thoroughly and completely agitates this mind in every possible way.
As it is said in the *Dānakelikaumudī* (4):
"Though profound, yet never weary; though its further shore is exceedingly difficult to reach, yet it maintains an unassailable boundary; and though it is the abode of Hari..."
When a complete hymn of praise for the virtuous arises with love, it is not able to restrain the expansive transformation, just as the ocean cannot contain the moonlight.

Thus ends the fourth wave, concerning the transitory moods (*vyabhicārin*), within the general exposition of the aesthetic flavor of devotion (*bhakti-rasa*) in the southern division of the *Śrī-Śrī-Bhakti-Rasāmṛta-Sindhu*.
(2.5) Now begins the fifth wave, concerning the permanent moods (*sthāyī-bhāva*).
He who brings both compatible and incompatible states under his control shines like a great king; he is called the stable state (sthāyībhāva).
In this context, that which is declared to be the permanent emotion (sthāyī-bhāva) is love directed toward Śrī Kṛṣṇa;
it is proclaimed by those who know the aesthetic flavors (rasa-jña) to be of two kinds: primary and secondary.
In that regard, the primary [form] is as follows: "Rati, whose nature is a particularity of pure sattva, is proclaimed as the primary.
This primary [rati] is also said to be of two kinds: for one's own sake and for the sake of another.
In that regard, self-interest (*svārthā*):

"That passion which nourishes only oneself through clear states that are not contradictory, while suffering and exhaustion arise from those that are contradictory, is called self-interested passion. (RBhṛS 2.5.4)
Now, as for that which is for the sake of another (*parārthā*):

"That pleasure which, contracting both the non-contradictory and the contradictory [states], spontaneously favors the internal state (*bhāva*), is declared to be for the sake of another. (RBhṛs 2.5.5)
Pure joy, as well as friendship, affection, and endearment—this [joy] is primarily for the sake of both oneself and others; furthermore, it becomes fivefold.
This delight attains its excellence through the excellence of the recipient,
just as the sun, appearing as a reflection, does so in objects such as crystal.
In that regard, the first [state] is threefold: the pure (*śuddhā*), the common (*sāmānyā*), and likewise the clear (*svacchā*) and the peaceful (*śānti*);
this [first state] produces trembling of the limbs, the closing and opening of the eyes, and so forth.
Among those, the common [love] is that which has not attained any particular excellence and is shared by ordinary people;
that love for Kṛṣṇa is considered common by the girls.
For example:
"O friend, tell me, as this sweet sun rises here in the streets of Mathurā before me, why does this softness of mind and passion arise within me? (RBhrs 2.5.10)
Or as it is said:
"Behold this girl, barely three years old,
who, seeing Kṛṣṇa before her, runs toward him while uttering the sound 'huṃ'."
Now, the "pure" (svacchā) [form of love] is considered to be that which,
through various means and through the engagement in manifold types of devotion,
attains a state of diversity among practitioners. (RBhṛs 2.5.12)
Whatever kind of attachment a devotee may have at any given time, the [deity] assumes that very form like a crystal; for this reason, she is celebrated as being "transparent" (svacchā).
For example:
in one place praising him as "the Lord," in another laughing at him as "a friend," in another bowing down to him as "a son," and in another rejoicing in him as "a beloved."
In some cases, contemplating in his mind that "this supreme one is the Self," this noble twice-born man became a man of various livelihoods through various forms of service.
For those whose intellects have not been refined, there is a fixation on various states within the ocean of pleasure;
however, for the most part, the delight of the noble ones who are utterly pure is transparently clear.
Now, regarding tranquility: the state of being free from conceptual construction in the mind is designated as *śama*.

And thus it has been said: "Since the state of abiding in one's own bliss arises from abandoning the orientation toward sense objects, that is here called the inherent nature of the self; this is tranquility. (RBhṛs 2.5.17)
Generally, for those whose primary quality is tranquility and who are devoid of even a trace of possessiveness,
a peaceful devotion toward Kṛṣṇa is considered to have arisen through the realization of His identity with the Supreme Self.
For example: When the great festival of Hari’s pastimes was drunk in by the lute of the divine sage, even Sanaka, though an experiencer of Brahman, experienced a tremor in his body. (RBhrs 2.5.19)
Or as it is said:
"By serving the Beloved of Hari, one indeed disregards the experience of all other categories on every side."
My mind desires to behold the Supreme Brahman, which is more intensely beautiful than even a solid mass of loveliness and is the most cherished object of my own self.
However, because this [state] lacks contact with the pleasures to be described below—which are the basis for attachment and so forth—it is called "pure" (śuddhā). (RBhṛS 2.5.21)
Now, the threefold division of *bheda* (distinction) within *rati* is described as beginning with *prīti* (affection);
it arises from intense compatibility and is always characterized by a sense of "mine-ness."

Among the three types of devotees of Kṛṣṇa—those to be favored, those who are friends, and those worthy of worship—there are respectively these three kinds of affection: friendship, and parental fondness (vatsalatā).

In this context, this threefold passion (rati) is of two kinds: the simple and the complex, consisting of the blossoming of the eyes and so forth, yawning, rolling [of the eyes], and other such signs.
In that regard, "exclusive" (kevalā) means being devoid of even the scent of another rasa;
it occurs when [the rasa] is directed toward a companion such as Śrīdāma or toward one following Kṛṣṇa, such as Rasāla.
And in the Guru, Vrajanātha, and the others, this [state] manifests in due order.
In that context, *saṅkulā* (the mixed) refers to the conjunction of two or three of these;
it occurs respectively in Udbhava and so forth, Bhīma and so forth, and Mathura and so forth.
Whichever [element] should predominate in a particular [state], that state is designated by that [element].
Now, regarding *prīti*:
"Those who are inferior to oneself are considered by Hari to be objects of grace;
the devotion toward them, characterized by their being worthy of worship, is called *prīti*. (RBhṛs 2.5.27)
For that [meditation] causes detachment from one thing while withdrawing attachment to another.
As it is said in the *Mukunda-mālā* (8):
"O Destroyer of Naraka, let my dwelling be as I desire— whether in heaven, on earth, or even in hell."
I think of your feet, which have surpassed the autumnal lotuses, even at the moment of death.
Now, regarding friendship: those who are equal to Mukunda are considered friends by the virtuous.
Because of this equality, their love, which takes the form of confidence, is here called friendship.
This lack of restraint consists in performing jests, laughter, and the like.
For example:
"My mind, torn asunder by the separation of even a moment, [longs for you] who have come with the desire to behold me in the flowering forest."
Touching one another, their splendor enhanced by the bristling of their hair,
they took delight today from afar in a spirit of "I first, I first."
Or as it is said:
"O Dāmodara, you have been rendered utterly destitute of pride here by the playful movements of Śrīdāma’s arms."
But by you, even that very act of speaking was immediately performed,
offering three handfuls of blazing palms to the Goddess for the sake of modesty.
Now, regarding parental affection (vātsalya):
those who are the gurus of this Hari are renowned as "the venerable ones" (pūjyāḥ);
the love for them that consists of grace is called parental affection.
This [is the practice] performed by those capable of fondling, such as the kissing of the chin and so forth.
For example:
"That which was swallowed by the hosts of Kaṃsa’s servants— who were engaged in hostilities without any ulterior motive— even from mountains that were towering high."
Alas, what shall I do? To protect the cattle there in the thicket, my tender young son goes forth incessantly.
Or as it is said:
"Her mind moist with compassion, the woman with flowing breasts placed her son upon the tip of her chin with her fingers."
From the impure storehouse-consciousness (ālayavijñāna),
the wife of the King of Vraja brought forth that which abides in the state of the manifest (pravṛttivijñāna).
The primary cause of the mutual enjoyment between Hari and the deer-eyed woman is that love known as *priyatā*,
which is also termed *madhurā*.
In this state, there are side-long glances, the knitting of eyebrows, endearing speech, smiles, and so forth.
As it is said in the *Govindavilāsa*:
"Victorious is that indescribable sprout of hope, born of secret glances, belonging to Rādhā and the Enemy of Mura, whose minds have long been filled with longing. (RBhrs_2,5.37)
Thus, in this [state], although it consists of the ever-increasing splendor of specific aesthetic relish (*svāda*),
for some person, due to latent predisposition (*vāsanā*), a certain indescribable delight appears as something to be savored.

Now, as for the secondary (gauṇī) [love]: that particular state of being born from the excellence of the determinants (vibhāva), which is sustained by love itself while it is contracting, is called secondary love (gauṇī rati). (RBhrs 2.5.39)
Laughter, wonder, enthusiasm, sorrow, anger, fear, and likewise disgust— this specific category of mental states (bhāva) is said to be sevenfold.

Moreover, the state of being a *vibhāva* (excitant cause) for the first six [rasas] may belong to Kṛṣṇa; however, the state of being a *vibhāva* for the body and so forth belongs to the seventh rasa, namely *rati* (erotic love), by virtue of its power.

Although laughter and the other [emotions] here are distinct, the term "rati" (joy) is applied because of their connection with the joy that aims at the welfare of others, due to its specific nature as pure sattva.
That pleasure which is preceded by laughter is called the pleasure of laughter (*hāsa-rati*);
in this same way, the six types of pleasure, beginning with the pleasure of wonder (*vismaya-rati*) and so forth, are to be understood.
For some time, in a certain devotee, these [emotions] such as laughter attain the status of a permanent sentiment (sthāyibhāva) through the influence of Rati’s charming pastimes and so forth.
Therefore, these seven occasional [powers], whose supports are not fixed,
dissolve even when they are innate, being overwhelmed by that which is more powerful.
There is a certain unswerving *rati*, which by its own nature is self-supported within all devotees as a permanent, abiding emotion (*sthāyībhāva*);
without this, all other emotions would be devoid of meaning. (RBhrs 2.5.46)
Even though anger and other such emotions always attain the status of stable dispositions (sthāyibhāva) within their respective opposites and so forth,
because they are devoid of delight (rati), they do not possess the fitness to be aesthetic flavors (rasa).

Even when touched by all the transitory states (sañcārins), such as despondency (nirveda) and others, which are themselves not contradictory [to one another], they dissolve; therefore, they do not deserve the status of a permanent emotion (sthāyin).

Therefore, the permanence of mental states such as pride and the like is not tenable; even though some maintain that they are permanent, those who know the truth regard this as lacking authoritative proof.
These seven, beginning with laughter (hāsa), have been brought to full maturity by their respective causes;
attaining the status of stable emotions (sthāyibhāva) among the devotees, they extend their aesthetic relish (ruci).
And so it has been said:
"The capacity to instill a latent impression (saṃskāra) is held to belong to only eight states;
other states, whose impressions are obscured by those [eight], are not suitable to be permanent (sthāyin). (RBhrs 2.5.51)
Among these, the rasa of laughter (*hāsa-rati*) is as follows:
Laughter is an expansion of the mind caused by distortions of speech, dress, movement, and so forth;
it produces such effects as the widening of the eyes, a beautiful expression, and the quivering of the cheeks. (RBhrs 2.5.52)
This laughter, arising from activities related to Kṛṣṇa, wherein one’s own self is spontaneously shrinking away and being reciprocally favored [by Him], becomes *hāsa-rati*.
For example:
"O fair-faced one, I swear by you that I did not even cast a glance at the curd; yet your friend, unrestrained, smells my mouth!"
"Rule over her; she has been deceived in vain," as Acyuta spoke thus, the female messenger became unable to suppress her laughter.
Now, regarding *vismaya-rati* (the sentiment of wonder): Wonder arises from the perception of supermundane objects and the like; it is an expansion of the mind.
In this state, there may be the dilation of the eyes, eloquent speech, horripilation, and so forth.
Accomplished in the manner previously described, he shall become one whose delight is wonder.
For example:
"Even among the cowherds and cowherd boys, there is one clad in yellow garments,
marked with the shining Śrīvatsa, whose splendor is sustained by his four broad arms."
Having begun his hymn of praise, he—sufficiently accompanied by the rituals of the Ajāṇḍālis—carries the effulgence of the Supreme Brahman; alas, what is this? What indeed is this?
Now, enthusiasm (utsāha): "Enthusiasm is declared to be a firm and swift attachment of the mind toward virtuous activities such as battle, which yield praiseworthy fruits. (RBhrs 2.5.57)
In that regard, disregard for time, as well as fortitude, renunciation, effort, and so forth, are required;
when perfected by the previously mentioned method, that enthusiasm becomes delight (rati).
For example:
"On the bank of the Kālindī, where the sky is made resonant here by the sounds of the leaf-flute and the bamboo flute..."
Thundering with the desire to fight Aghadamana,
Śrīdāmā bound his formidable girdle.
Now, regarding sorrow and attachment:
Sorrow is defined as a heavy burden of mental affliction arising from separation from the beloved and other such causes;
it produces lamentation, falling down, sighing, parchedness of the mouth, dizziness, and so forth.
Having accomplished this by the very method previously described, one should become joyful and free from sorrow.
As it is said in the Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam (10.7.25):
"Hearing that crying there, the gopīs,
their minds deeply distressed and their faces filled with tears,"
They wept, unable to find the son of Nanda, now that the wind had ceased its force of raining dust.
Or as it is said:
"Beholding her son, who was dearer than thousands of lives, held fast by the king of serpents..."
The heart does not split in two; fie on this hardness of the mortal body!
Now, regarding *krodha-rati* (delight in anger):
Anger is defined as the inflaming of the mind due to hostility and the like;
it produces transformations such as harshness, the knitting of eyebrows, and the reddening of the eyes. (RBhṛS 2.5.63)
Thus, as previously stated, the wise know that the passion of wrath (krodha-rati) is established;
it is proclaimed to be twofold by virtue of its nature as being either directed toward Kṛṣṇa or toward His enemies.
Now, the dark-colored manifestations (kṛṣṇa-vibhāva), as follows:
Having recognized the pearl necklace of Rādhikā, possessing a luster, upon the boundary of Hari’s neck;
After a long time, the matted-haired ascetic beheld him with a gaze made even more terrifying by the contraction of his formidable eyebrows.
The manifestations of its enemies are as follows: now, as Hari advanced against the fierce forest-fire that was Kaṃsa’s brother, wielding sharp weapons—
From the impetuosity [of his movement], a cloud-like line of knitted brows appeared upon the forehead of the enemy of Pralamba.

Now, regarding fear and passion: Fear is an extreme agitation of the mind caused by threats, terrible glances, and so forth; it produces self-concealment, a parching of the heart, flight, wandering, and other such effects. (RBhṛs 2.5.67)
The wise know this perfected state to be both fear and pleasure, as before;
the learned have declared that this too is of two kinds, like the pleasure of wrath.
Among those, the excitants (vibhāvas) related to Kṛṣṇa are as follows:
The son of Gāndinī was entreated for the Syamantaka jewel by Śauri in the assembly with flattering words.
This fool, whose mind was obscured by his clothes, went to exhaustion with his lips parched while searching for that jewel.
Arising from a wicked stimulus (vibhāva), for example:
"Alas! Alas! While the demon Vṛṣāsura, resembling a rain-cloud, was uttering terrifying cries at the gate of Gokula—"
The Queen of Vraja, her body trembling with the intensity of her effort to protect her son, became motionless.
Now, regarding disgust-attachment (*jugupsā-rati*): Disgust is the closing of the mind resulting from the experience of the unpleasant;
in that state, there are actions such as spitting, contorting the face, and reviling.
Born from the grace of passion, that which is considered "disgust-passion" (jugupsā-rati) is [the result].
For example:
"From the moment my mind became intent on sporting in the lotus-feet of Kṛṣṇa, which are the abode of ever-fresh aesthetic rasa..."
Alas, until that time, when the union with a woman is remembered,
there occurs a distortion of the face and copious spitting.
Because they consist of delight (*rati*), there is first only one [permanent emotion]; likewise, there are seven beginning with mirth (*hāsa*).
Thus, there are eight permanent emotions (*sthāyibhāva*) as long as they have not yet reached the state of aesthetic flavor (*rasa*).
If these thirty-three were independent, they would be inconsistent;
however, here there are eight *sāttvika* ones, and these states (*bhāva*) are said to be innumerable.
Although these [beings] born of the lineage of Kṛṣṇa consist of mature bliss that transcends the qualities (guṇas),
they appear as if composed of the pleasure and pain produced by the three qualities.
Therein, qualities such as modesty, the aspiration for awakening, and enthusiasm flash forth like those of the *sattva* nature;
likewise, pride, exhilaration, sleep, and laughter appear like those of the *rajas* nature;
and despondency, wretchedness, delusion, and grief appear like those of the *tamas* nature. (RBhrs 2.5.76)
In this world, cold sensations are generally composed of pleasure, while hot sensations are composed of pain;
yet this supreme passion (rati), though intensely blissful, is considered to be hot.
When nourished by powerful cold dispositions, it indeed becomes cool;
but when delighted by hot ones, it appears excessively hot, as if causing torment.

When that love (rati) is brought to the state of an aesthetic flavor (rasa) among the devotees by means of those [objects]— such as Kṛṣṇa and others— which are heard, perceived, or remembered in their two-fold manner as excitants (vibhāva) and so forth, it becomes rasa.
Just as substances such as curd, through a particular method of combination with sugar, black pepper, and so forth, become the flavor known as *rasālā*.
Therefore, in this regard, devotees experience a certain extraordinary wonder of mature bliss, arising from the direct perception of Kṛṣṇa and others in every way.

Although he consists of the state of oneness with the excitants (vibhāva) and other factors such as Rati, he also manifests through the differentiation of those respective [factors], being made known by their specific characteristics.
And as it has been said:
"The excitants (vibhāvas) and so forth, being first perceived individually, attain the state of Rasa when combined, reaching a state of indivisibility. (RBhrs 2.5.83)

Just as in a refreshing drink (*prapānaka*) made from a mixture of black pepper, sugar, and other ingredients, a certain flavor emerges somewhere within; so too does it occur in aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) through the various determinants (*vibhāva*) and other factors.
Those such as Kṛṣṇa and the beloved of Kṛṣṇa who have become the causes are the *raty-ālambanas*;
