those such as paralysis (*stambha*) which have become the *kārakas* (instrumental factors), and those such as despondency (*nirveda*) which are the assistants (*sahāyakas*). 2,5.85.
Having abandoned here their status as being denotable by terms such as "cause" and "effect," they acquire the designation of "determinants" (vibhāva) and so forth upon the arousal of rasa.

The wise have stated that the *vibhāvakas* (excitants) are so called because they cause [the spectator] to experience a specific capacity for the particular relish of this or that [emotion]. (RBhrs 2.5.87)

And those which cause that [rasa] to be experienced within, being filled with its savor, are called the *anubhāvas*—such as side-long glances and so forth—along with the *sāttvika* [emotions]. (RBhṛS 2.5.88)
Those states such as despondency (nirveda) and the like, which cause a variety [of emotions] to circulate and lead it to such a condition, are considered transitory (sañcārin).
Regarding the existence of these [qualities] in the poetry and drama of the Blessed One,
some who are partial to his side say that service [to him] is the supreme cause.
However, in that case, the supreme cause would be the power of this *rati*, which possesses the wonderful wealth of sweetness born from difficult reasoning.
This state, whose essence is the play of great power and which possesses an inconceivable nature, is appropriately termed "Rati"; for it cannot be subverted by logical reasoning.
Indeed, this statement from the *Mahābhārata* and other texts has been cited even by the ancients.
As it is said in the Udyoga-parvan (Mahābhārata 6.6.11):
"Those entities which are indeed inconceivable, one should not attempt to apply reasoning to them;
and that which is beyond the primary elements (prakṛti) is the characteristic of the inconceivable."
Bringing forth the states of dissolution and so on, beautiful passion clearly causes herself to flourish by means of these very factors, such as Kṛṣṇa and the others, who have likewise become such.
Just as the ocean, by filling the clouds with its own waters, becomes a repository of jewels through those very waters when they have been rained down; so too is it with these [virtues].
When the sprout of passion has arisen in a certain devotee of Hari, it serves as the cause for the factors such as the determinants (*vibhāva*) and so forth in poetry and drama. (RBhrs 2.5.96)
The virtuous may experience a savoring of rasa even upon merely hearing a little of Hari;
this is the power of *rati* itself, which serves as the cause for their acting in such a way.
Love extends toward Kṛṣṇa and others as the locus of sweetness and other qualities;
being experienced in that way, they cause love to expand.
Therefore, in this case, the mutual and constant assistance of that quartet— consisting of the determinants (vibhāva) and so forth— is clearly evident even for the erotic sentiment (rati).
However, even the power of this [rasa] falters when there is a lack of propriety;
and this lack of propriety is said to arise from the inappropriateness of the determinants (vibhāva) and the other factors.
This state of aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) is, by its very nature, transcendent and extremely difficult to fathom,
wherein these mental states (*bhāva*) shine forth perfectly through their universalization.

Indeed, that which is the determination of the restriction regarding the relationship between these [entities] themselves and others was called "universality" (sādhāraṇya) of entities by the ancient masters.
Thus it has been said by the venerable Bharata:
"There exists a certain power in the excitants (*vibhāva*) and so forth for the purpose of making them universal;
by means of this, the cognizer perceives himself as non-different from that [aesthetic emotion]. (RBhrs 2.5.103)
Even though suffering and the like flash forth, when they occasionally appear within the heart as one's own,
they produce nothing but the savoring of the wonder of mature bliss.
Even when these [states] such as pleasure appear by depending on something else,
they accumulate a mass of supreme bliss within the heart.
If even a slight degree of the true state (*sad-bhāva*) arises from the determinants (*vibhāva*) and so forth,
then fullness is immediately attained through the implication of the fourfold [set].
Furthermore:
"Since aesthetic delight (rati) resides in the characters being represented due to reasons such as their worldly nature,
it cannot be rasa"— this is exactly what the experts in drama have said, and that is indeed correct.
But this transcendental love for Kṛṣṇa is the most wonderful of all wonders;
O beloved of Hari, it indeed attains the status of a specific aesthetic relish (rasa) within yoga.
But in separation, although it manifests as a transformation of wondrous bliss,
this powerful [state] spreads the appearance of an intense burden of suffering.
Even there, the passion (rati) directed toward the son of the cowherd lord is held to be the ultimate limit of the wonder of intense bliss.
By its own splendor, it is as if the Agastya star drinks up even the ocean of bliss from the direct realization of the sweetness of Rēmaśa, which is like a mere drop within that flood of happiness.
Furthermore:
"Because of its identity with supreme bliss, this aesthetic flavor (rasa), consisting of erotic love and the rest, is established in reality as self-luminous and indivisible. (RBhṛs 2.5.112)
Based on the two-fold division previously mentioned according to whether the rasa of delight (rati) is primary or secondary,
this aesthetic flavor of devotion (bhakti-rasa) likewise becomes twofold, being either primary or secondary.
Because *rati* is essentially one, even though it is fivefold, it is declared here as the primary [rasa] in one way;
likewise, the secondary [rasas] are sevenfold here. Thus, the *bhakti-rasa* is eightfold.
Among those, the primary [types] are as follows:

"The primary [hero], however, is fivefold: the tranquil (śānta), the pleased (prīta), the beloved (preyān), the affectionate (vatsala), and the sweet (madhura); these should be known as unsurpassed in their respective order. (RBhṛs 2.5.115)
Now, the secondary [rasas]:
the comic, the marvelous, as well as the heroic, the pathetic, the furious, the terrifying, and the loathsome; thus the secondary is sevenfold.
Thus, the rasa of devotion is said to be twelvefold based on its divisions into two;
however, in reality, it is observed as only fivefold in the Purāṇas and other such texts.
White, variegated, ruddy, crimson, dark-brown, pale-yellow and tawny, fair-complexioned, smoky-grey, as well as red, black, and blue— these [colors] follow in sequence.
Kapila, Mādhava, Upendra, Nṛsiṃha, Nandanandana, Bala, Kūrma, as well as Kalkī, Rāghava, Bhārgava, Kirī,
and Mīna— these are declared to be the twelve deities in their respective order.
The tasting of the flavor of all devotion is proclaimed to be fivefold, through fulfillment, transformation, expansion, dispersal, and agitation.

Fulfillment (*pūrti*) occurs in the *śānta* rasa; expansion (*vikāśa*) occurs in all five rasas beginning with *prīta*; extension (*vistāra*) occurs in the *vīra* and *adbhuta*; distraction (*vikṣepa*) is declared by the wise to occur in the *karuṇa* and *ugra*; and agitation (*kṣobha*) occurs in the *bhayānaka* and *bībhatsa*.
Even though these are of the nature of unbroken bliss, within the aesthetic flavors (rasas), there exists here and there a certain unsurpassed and profound excellence of savor.

Although the sentiments such as *karuṇa* (compassion) and others are perceived instantly as if they were painful by the ignorant and the vulgar, they are considered by the wise to consist of mature bliss.
It is an established principle that for those who have been led to a state beyond the worldly through the play of passion and by means of sublime speech, bliss shall manifest from them very clearly.
And likewise, regarding drama and so forth:
"Even when a rasa such as the pathetic (karuṇa) arises, that supreme bliss which is produced is experienced by those of pure mind; therein, experience alone is the sole authority. (RBhrs 2.5.125)
Because the aesthetic flavor (rasa) known as compassion is established everywhere [in these works],
otherwise the Rāmāyaṇa and similar texts would result in nothing but causes of suffering.
If that were so, how could Hanumān, who is an ocean of surging waves of love for Rāma’s lotus feet, constantly listen to the Rāmāyaṇa out of affection?
Moreover:
A friend’s love for Kṛṣṇa may be either transitory (sañcārī) or common (samāna);
if it is being nourished, it becomes an elevated love characterized by the effulgence of emotion (bhāvollāsa).
Those whose inferior dispassion has been consumed by fire, who possess dry knowledge and are mere rationalists—
especially the Mīmāṃsakas— are turned away from the savor of devotion.
Thus, this nectar of devotion to Kṛṣṇa must always be protected from the aging Mīmāṃsaka, just as a great treasure is guarded from a thief. RBhrs_2,5.130 //
In every way, this nectar of the Blessed One is difficult for those who lack devotion to grasp; it is relished only by devotees who regard his lotus feet as their all-in-all.
That which, having transcended the path of meditative cultivation, becomes a source of wonder and is intensely relished within a heart radiant with being— that is considered *rasa*.
That state which is cultivated in the mind by a wise person of undistracted intellect through intense mental impressions during the stage of meditative cultivation is called *bhāva*.
Though bearing the beauty of the form of Gopāla, may he who expands the state of Raghunātha be pleased— the eternal Self in the southern region of the ocean of nectar.

Thus ends the fifth wave, on the Stable Emotions (*sthāyī-bhāva*), within the General Description of the Sentiments of Devotion (*bhakti-rasa*) in the Southern Division of the *Śrī-Śrī-Bhakti-Rasāmṛta-Sindhu*.
Thus [ends] the *Śrī-Śrī-Bhakti-Rasāmṛta-Sindhu*.
The Southern Section, titled "An Exposition of the General Sentiment of Devotion to the Blessed Lord," is completed.
(3) [Now begins] the Exposition of the Principal Sentiment of Devotion.
The Western Section (3.1):
The First Wave, titled "The Sentiment of Peaceful Devotion" (śānti-bhakti-rasa).
May that Supreme Person (Puruṣottama), who bears the weight of a charming form, whose vast love is offered to the devotees, and who is my eternal embodiment, grant me satisfaction.
In this third part, named "The West," of the ocean of the nectar of rasa,
the primary rasa of devotion (bhakti-rasa) is declared to be fivefold, beginning with the peaceful (śānta).
Therefore, five types of waves are proclaimed here according to their fivefold nature;
now, these five flavors (rasas), beginning with the peaceful (śānta), are characterized in sequence.
Among these, the flavor of peaceful devotion (śānta-bhakti-rasa) is defined as follows:

"The stable emotion (sthāyī-bhāva) of peace, which has become an object of savoring for those who have attained tranquility through the excitants (vibhāva) and other factors to be described hereafter, is known by the wise as the flavor of peaceful devotion. (RBhrs 3.1.4)
Generally, for yogins in this state, happiness will be of the same nature as their own happiness;
however, that happiness is not a dense mass of self-centered bliss, but rather the bliss of the Lord, which is indeed dense.

Even in that case, only the experience of the Lord’s own nature is considered the primary cause for [the attainment of] mental mastery, divine play, and so forth; it is not regarded as such in the same way as [the experience of] being a servant and the like.
In that regard, the objects of focus—
the four-armed and the peaceful forms— are considered the objects of focus in this [practice].
Therein, the four-armed one—
dark-hued and beautiful with four arms— shines forth as this mass of bliss, a wave upon the ocean of the self of all.
When he has entered the path of the eyes, even the mind of the Paramahaṃsa sage emerges from its state of withdrawal.
His body is dense with truth, consciousness, and bliss; he is the crest-jewel of those who delight in the Self;
he is the Supreme Self, the Supreme Brahman—tranquil, self-controlled, pure, and self-restrained.
Hari, who has eternally attained His own true nature, who bestows the state where all enemies are destroyed,
and who possesses such qualities as omnipresence— He is the object of focus (ālambana) in this [practice].
Now, the peaceful ones (*śāntāḥ*):
they are the peaceful ones who, through the compassion of Kṛṣṇa and His devotees, have attained delight;
they are ascetics who find joy in the Self and whose faith is bound to His path. (RBhrs 3.1.11)
Now, regarding those who delight in the Self:
"Those who delight in the Self are considered to be headed by Sanaka, Sananda, and others.
For the sake of prominence, the form and devotion of Sanaka and the rest are described. (RBhrs 3.1.12)
Regarding their appearance there:
"Those four boys, appearing like children of five or six years, radiant with splendor, fair-limbed, and clothed in wind-garments, are generally companions. (RBhṛs 3.1.13)

And therein lies devotion: when all qualities have been stripped away and, through the instruments of the senses, one has turned inward toward some ineffable reality, bliss itself shines forth spontaneously.
O Mukunda, this direct realization of yours— wondrous, consisting of the dense mass of blissful consciousness, and possessing the dark-blue luster of a fresh tamāla tree— had not yet occurred.
Now, as for the ascetics (tāpasa):
those who have attained disciplined detachment because devotion is indeed unimpeded by liberation itself,
and who do not abandon the desire for liberation— they are the ascetics.
For example:
"When, dwelling in the hollows of mountain caves within the embrace of broad trees,
wearing only a loincloth, and taking delight in a diet of fruits and roots..."
Meditating again and again in my heart upon that light called Mukunda, which is consciousness and bliss, I shall pass these nights as if they were a single moment.
The ascetics, through the very expansion of their compassion for those whose souls are devoted [to the Lord],
have taken refuge in a fraction of the moon of the state called "peace" within the sky of the heart.
Now, the excitants (uddīpanas):
hearing the great Upaniṣads, resorting to secluded places, a particular internal mental state, the manifestation of this [state], and the discernment of reality. (RBhrs 3.1.18)
The predominance of the power of knowledge (*vidyā-śakti*), the manifestation of universal forms,
association with those who possess knowledge and devotees, and likewise the *brahmasattra* and other such rites—
these are declared by the wise to be the uncommon excitants (*uddīpana*) among these [five types of love]. (RBhrs 3.1.19)
In this regard, there is the Mahopaniṣad Śruti, as follows:
"The lotus-born [Brahmā] and others, free from affliction, having entered the assembly,
being learned in what has been heard, perform the recitation of the Vedas, which are the heads of the Śrutis."
The lords of yogis, their hair standing on end with thrill, have newly attained that lofty stage for the sake of union with the Supreme.
The fragrance of the tulasī from the lotus feet [of the Lord], the sound of the conch of the enemy of Mura,
the sacred mountain, the auspicious forest, the field of the perfected ones (siddhakṣetra), and the celestial river.
The perishability of objects and the like, and the all-devouring nature of time—
these and others are indeed the common excitants (uddīpana) for those [rasas] based upon them.
Now, regarding the fragrance of the *tulasī* from His lotus feet,
as it is said in the Third Canto (3.15.43):
"Of that lotus-eyed one, from the lotus of His feet..."
The breeze, carrying the nectar of tulasī mixed with its filaments,
entered through their own pores and stirred both the minds and bodies of those who were devoted to the Imperishable.
Now, the physical manifestations:
fixing the gaze upon the tip of the nose, the conduct of an ascetic (avadhūta), moving with a gaze fixed at the distance of a yoke, and displaying the gesture of knowledge (jñāna-mudrā).
One feels no hatred even toward an enemy of Hari, nor excessive attachment even toward those who are dear;
likewise, there is a high regard for perfection as well as for liberation while living.
Indifference, absence of possessiveness, absence of egoism, discourse on [these matters], and silence— these and similar practices are cooling and unique [to this path].
In that regard, the state of having the eyes fixed on the tip of the nose is as follows:
"With his gaze fixed on the tip of his nose, this sage shines before us, his veins visible due to the restraint of his breath."
Surely Hari plunges into the undisturbed slope of his mountain-cave-like mind.
Yawning, stretching the limbs, instruction in devotion, bowing to Hari, hymns of praise, and so forth— these are the common activities performed by servants and others when they are weary.
In that regard, yawning is as follows:
"O Lord of Yogis, the jewel of the sky of being surely rises for you in the sky of the heart."
This is because your lotus-face is assuming a yawn.
Now, the *sāttvika* [emotions]—
trembling of the hair, perspiration, trembling, and so forth— are the *sāttvika* [states], excluding *pralaya*.
Then there is horripilation, as for example: "The sound produced by the Pāñcajanya conch, suddenly piercing his meditative absorption, agitated him from within."
It brought a thrill of horripilation to the person of the yogins dwelling in mountain caves.
In these yogins who are free from conceit regarding their bodies and so forth,
the sattvic [fires] indeed blaze, yet they do not become inflamed.

Now, as for the transitory states (*sañcārin*): here, the transitory states are proclaimed to be despondency, fortitude, joy, intelligence, memory, dejection, eagerness, agitation, deliberation, and so forth. (RBhṛS 3.1.33)
In that regard, there is detachment, as follows:
while this Supreme Self, whose form is a mass of bliss, shines forth in the city of the Vṛṣṇis.
Alas, because I delighted only in myself, this long period of time has passed in vain.
Now, regarding the stable emotion (sthāyin):
here, the stable emotion is the delight of tranquility (śānti-rati); it is both even and intense, and thus twofold.
Among these, the first is as follows:
"When I was effortlessly attained by the yogi in that state called asamprajñāta-samādhi, his body began to tremble. (RBhrs 3.1.36)
It is dense, as follows:
that which has manifested from the destruction of all ignorance within the non-conceptual samādhi.
When the Lord of the Yādavas was born visibly, that bliss which I found attained a state of intensity ten millionfold.
This tranquility is twofold, distinguished by its indirect and direct realization.
Now, as for the indirect method (*parokṣya*), it is as follows: "O Lord of Sages, will this great austerity, this ancient practice of the supreme yoga consisting of the eight limbs, attain fruition?"
Tell me, what indeed will that Supreme Brahman, who bears the luster of a fresh rain-cloud in human form, create next to cause wonder to my eyes?
Or as it is said:
"When, during an eclipse of the fierce-rayed sun, there was a certain thick radiance upon the eyes on the road in the field of Kuru..."

Realization— for instance: "Alas, from the joy of direct realization, [the world] becomes exceedingly tender by virtue of being the Supreme Self."
O Blessed One, what further purpose exists even for one who knows Brahman?

As stated by Bilvamaṅgala:

In that regard, the objects of focus are as follows:

There in Vraja—
beautiful as a fresh rain-cloud, holding a flute that puts glittering gold to shame against his lotus-like face with both hands, and clad in silken garments;

Otherwise, he may have two arms, as follows: "This Lord, ever clad in saffron robes,
holding a conch in his pair of hands, has the luster of a cloud."
Like a fresh cloud enveloped by lightning,
it shines, adorned with the orbs of the sun and the moon.
In that regard, he is four-armed,
as described in the *Lalitā-mādhava* (5.15):

With his four arms enriched by two lotuses made radiant by friendship,

Each single pore of his body is the abode of millions of cosmic eggs; he is an ocean of compassion, possessed of inconceivable great power, and served by all supernatural attainments.
The seed of the lineage of incarnations is the quality of the heart that always delights in the Self;

Prosperous, patient by nature, a protector of those who have come for refuge, liberal, truthful in speech, skillful, and the bringer of all that is auspicious.

The sounding of the flute and the horn, the glance preceded by a smile,
the hearing of the excellence of his virtues, the lotus-marked feet, fresh clouds,
and the fragrance of his limbs and so forth, are considered common to all. (RBhṛs 3.2.59)
In this regard, the sound of the flute is as described in the *Vidagdha-mādhava* (1.30):

From the thousand eyes of this Lord of the Gods, tears flowed onto the earth; it is a marvel that even without clouds, by those tears which were now like torrents, the circle of the Vṛndā forest became filled with rain from afar as they gazed upon the Mother of the Gods.

all the *sāttvika* states, beginning with paralysis (*stambha*), are considered to occur in the triad of joy and the others.

wretchedness, anxiety, memory, apprehension, discernment, eagerness, and fickleness.

Disgust [with worldly life], as for example:
"Blessed are those upon whom a thousand rays of your sun shine, O Lord of the Yadus, who always fall at the feet of the Lord of the Yadus."

for she remains far away, not beholding him even for a moment.

"Today my inauspiciousness has perished, and my very existence has become fruitful."
I pay homage to the Blessed One’s lotus feet, which are the object of meditation for yogins.

"When shall I pay homage to that Lord in the form of a cowherd, who is the beloved of the Kadamba groves on the banks of the Yamunā? (RBhrs 3.2.80)

when it has cast off the fear of diminution and is firmly rooted, it is called *prema*.

"Though cursed by the son of Bhṛgu, whose intellect was inflamed with rage, I have sufficiently removed the three worlds by spreading my vast deception."

For example:
"Out of hypocrisy, upon seeing Keśava, your heart melted and you shed a torrent of tears."
O Dāruka, for you who hold such high pride, this state of being like wood is not surprising.
Or as it is said:

"Bringing forward the supreme wife of the treasure-house of jewels, with a flood of tears, he begins the syllables of a hymn of praise tumbling from within his throat, which has become sweet with emotion."

Kissing [the lotuses] with limbs that rivaled the splendor of full-blown kadamba flowers, Uddhava, though stunned upon beholding Acyuta’s surpassing glory, bowed down before the multitude who were themselves bowing in reverence.
Now, as for passion (*rāga*):
that is affection (*sneha*), by which pleasure and even pain become manifest;
it is a fondness here [in this world] for even a mere fragment of connection with that [object], even at the cost of one's life.
For example:
"Even for a guru, there is fear of the serpent Takṣaka; the loss of a vast kingdom is extreme; and the practice of penance is heavy."

"If even a mere fragment of Keśava’s compassion were to fall upon me, then even the submarine fire (bāḍava) would surely become sweet to me like a dish of six flavors (ṣāḍava)."

even though it be a place of perfect accomplishment, it would still be merely a "Kuśa-grass ground" for me.
Generally, in the first two [categories], it is love (prema); this affection (sneha) is found among the attendants;
toward Parīkṣit it would be passion (rāga), and likewise toward Dāruka and Uddhava.
Among the many followers of Vraja, headed by Raktaka and others,

For example:

As it is said in the *Nārasiṃha*:

In that regard, longing is as follows, for example, in the *Śrī-Kṛṣṇakarṇāmṛta* (41):
"These other days are unfortunate..."

the pair of your lotus feet, belonging to you who are an ocean of nectar for the eyes,

O Lord, ocean of compassion, sprinkle me even once with a mere fraction of the kindness of Your sidelong glance, so that I may release my throat from the incessant throes of rising despair.
Or as it is said:

"O Destroyer of Sins, though You are one whose sight cannot be obtained even by Śiva, the Moon-crested Lord, and others, You are easily accessible; whereas I, who perform deceitful deeds, am lower than even an insect."
Thus, even though there is such a great disparity, I pray for your favor; O friend of the wretched, bathe me with the glances from the corners of your eyes.

Disgust [with worldly life], as follows: "Though my dull eyes have clearly resorted to the service of the Vedas and have become praiseworthy by being devoted to the cessation of worldly existence (nirata), may they [nevertheless] be so."
Indeed, there could not exist for those two a station that is the abode of the splendor of sweetness,
even compared to the radiance spreading from the sprout-like nails of your lotus-feet.
The thought, as follows:
"Even for one whose mind is restless with a thirst to behold the lotus-feet of Hari, [the Lord] does not grant [his grace] without first observing [one's] worthiness."
With my face cast down in anxiety, alas, alas! the nights pass for me as I sigh.
And restlessness, as in the *Śrī-Kṛṣṇakarṇāmṛta* (32):
"Know that Your childhood is a wonder to the three worlds; and my restlessness is to be understood by You or by Me."
So what shall I do? With my two eyes, I long to behold that rare, charming lotus-face of the flute-player.
Or as it is said:
"O remover of sin, having cast aside my shame, this female sun of my vision, parched with thirst, has overcome even its fear of the multitude of devotees."
O Lord, disregarding its own boundless size and without considering its own smallness,
it desires to lick Your lotus feet.

Inertness (*jaḍatā*), as described in the seventh [chapter] (7.4.37): "Like a child who has set aside his playthings, because his mind is fixed on that [object], he whose self is seized by the planet Kṛṣṇa does not perceive the world in this way. (RBhrs 3.2.108)
Or as it is said:
"With eyes closed in a wink, how does the lord of birds remain here like a mere statue, his body motionless?"
Ah, it is understood! Alas, this person, addicted to the fresh passion for the flute and its melodies, has cast his gaze upon the dark cloud before him.
Madness, as described in the seventh [chapter] (7.4.40):
"In one place he cries out with longing; in another, he dances without shame; in another, joined with the contemplation of that [state], he indeed acts as if identified with it. (RBhrs 3.2.110)
Or, for example:
in one place he dances without a trace; in another, he renders the impossible possible; in another, he laughs aloud; and in another, he cries out intensely.
In one place he is active, in another he is idle; at times he acts as if afflicted, yet the sage has consumed the wine of Hari’s ever-fresh and bold love.
Delusion is as described in the *Haribhaktisudhodaya*: "In the vision of the Lord, he considers himself unworthy;
thus, fearing that he will not attain Him,"
O twice-born one, with his mind submerged in an overflowing ocean of suffering and streams of tears flowing from his ears, he fell down in a swoon.
Or as it is said:
"Alas! In this most excellent of holy places, where the waters of consciousness have been shaken forth by the rows of heat from the ocean of beholding the feet of Hari—"
O you who possess true sacred sites, surely sprinkle the nectars of the Lord’s names into the hollows of the ears; let the swan of the vital breath then begin its movement.
Now, regarding separation (viyoga):
separation is the severance from the one who has attained union by the Enemy of the Danujas (Viṣṇu).
For example:
When Puruṣottama had gone to the city of Kṣataja to destroy the mass of arms belonging to the son of Bali—
With his intellect shaken by distress, Uddhava’s joy departed; his mind obstructed by the pangs of separation, he became devoid of delight.

In the wise, the ten stages of agitation born of love during separation are proclaimed as: fever in the limbs, emaciation, sleeplessness, emptiness of support, lack of fortitude, dullness, illness, madness, fainting, and death. (RBhrs 3.2.116)
Instability is explained as the mind’s emptiness of its object;
however, the wise have described non-attachment as the lack of steadiness toward everything.
The other eight, beginning with suffering (tāpa), have not been defined here because their meaning is already manifest.
In that regard, *tāpa* (torment) is as follows:
"The lotus, the friend of the sun, torments us;
and the ocean, whose form is hidden by the submarine fire (*vaḍavānala*)."
O Lord of Sages, how is it that the blue lotus, which is a friend to the moon, causes pain to the members of this assembly by reminding them of that Supreme Lord?
Emaciation, as for example:
"Today your servants' arms, which are like iron bars, bear both emaciation and paleness."
Alas, O friend of the Pāṇḍavas, it falls clearly here that the white-winged bird [the swan] is struck down by one who mistakes it for a lotus stalk.
Regarding wakefulness (*jāgaryā*), as it is said:

"Due to the long separation from the enemy of Mura, the nights—whose lover was the moment—became many for her whose body was distressed and whose heart was exhausted; they became like the month of Bahulāśva (Mārgaśīrṣa), full of many nights. (RBhrs 3.2.120)
The emptiness of the objective support (*ālambana-śūnyatā*), as follows: "Indeed, there is no other household for us in these three worlds besides Vijayaratha and his wife."
Wandering about and disregarding that lotus-foot, my mind today finds no stability anywhere.
Lack of fortitude, as for example:
having seen a cluster of peacock feathers, she closes her eyes; seeing a herd of cows, she casts them far away.
O Murāri, today even the red lotus desires a staff, for it has become as red as your lotus feet.
Inertia, for example:
when Padmanābha entered the city of Yudhiṣṭhira, [the world] became exceedingly distressed by the confluence of the fires of exhaustion.
Indeed, it was not merely through sweat and tears that Uddhava’s limbs attained the state of water,
but also because of their lack of activity.
An illness, for example:
"When Murabhid set out from the city of Kuśasthalī to search for the jewel, he delayed."
He was born bearing a new disease;
thus Pavanavyādhi was one whose name was true to its meaning.
For example, [the verse on] insanity: "Alas!
While my own tutelary deity Raivata is away, seeing this new cloud..."
Behold this Uddhava, whose mind is deluded; he cries out, rejoices, and bows down with agitation.
Viśvanātha says that "nauti" means "fainted," as in:
"The condition of those who serve your lotus feet was born from separation."
O best of the Yadus, there was not even a trace of sleep in Vraja as there once was;
now, their lives sustained only by the hope of your merciful breath, they lie perpetually motionless upon the riverbanks.
Death, as for example:
"O subduer of the Danujas, when you have departed from life, she whose heart-lotus destroys darkness [the moon] will suddenly suffer the torments of intense separation."
Indeed, those distressed swans do not wish to make their dwelling all around Vraja, amidst the rows of mud from the lakes of the Dāsas.
Because it is inauspicious, this death does not occur for anyone devoted [to the Lord] anywhere;
because it causes agitation and separation, it is said to have "already occurred. (RBhrs 3.2.128)
Now, as for *yoga*: "That which is union with Kṛṣṇa is proclaimed as *yoga*.
In *yoga* as well, *siddhi* (perfection) is said to be threefold: *tuṣṭi* (contentment) and *sthiti* (steadfastness). (RBhṛs 3.2.129)
In that regard, accomplishment (siddhi) is as follows: the attainment of Hari by one who is longing is designated as accomplishment.
As it is said in the *Śrī-Kṛṣṇakarṇāmṛta* (57):
"A head adorned with the moon as its crest-jewel; a body as beautiful as pillars of emerald;
a face sweet with a wondrous and charming smile; and two eyes, O young girl, tremulous and rolling."
With speech as cool as childhood and a graceful bearing worthy of a rutting elephant,
who is this that slowly, very slowly, enters the streets of Mathurā together?
Or as it is said in the *Śrī-daśama* (10.38.34):
"Leaping swiftly from his chariot, Akrūra, overwhelmed with love,
fell like a staff at the feet of Rāma and Kṛṣṇa."
Contentment— when separation from the enemy of Kaṃsa has occurred, the attainment [of him] is called contentment.
As it was said in the first [chapter] (1.11.10):
"O Lord, how shall we— while you have been long absent— [attain] the drying up of all our suffering by your gracious glance?"
May we live without beholding your enchanting face, which is adorned with a beautiful smile.
Or as it is said:
Seeing Hari before him, Dāruka was unable to join his palms in salutation;
at the gate of Dvārakā, he fell there into a state of stupor.
Stability—
dwelling together with Mukunda— is declared as stability by the wise.
As it is said in the *Haṃsadūta* (verse 50)—
though this appears to be a conflation of verses 50–51— he, whose name inspires fear in the throngs of Ābhīra women, is cruel before [the eyes of others].
Leaning against a jeweled pillar and recounting the tales of the Kuru dynasty,
that disciple of the Guru will surely be intent upon massaging his lotus-feet, supporting the earth of the dice-board with his knees.
Attentiveness in performing service during one's own opportunity,
as well as sitting before him and so forth— these actions are considered appropriate in this yoga.
Some, being averse to the savor of devotion to Kṛṣṇa within this rasa,
have determined that it is merely the state of worldly existence (bhava) and have not declared it to be a state of aesthetic relish (rasa).
Thus, it is not at all incorrect that this aesthetic flavor (rasa) is clearly observed in certain Purāṇas and in the Śrīmad-Bhāgavata.
For it is said in the eleventh [chapter] (11.3.32):
"In some places they weep with thoughts of Acyuta; in some places they laugh, rejoice, and speak like those beyond the world."
They dance, they sing, they practice [meditation] upon the Unborn; having attained the supreme state, they become silent and are fully at peace.
And in the seventh [chapter] (7.7.34):
"Having heard of the incomparable deeds, qualities, and heroic exploits performed by his playful incarnations..."
When, with hair standing on end from excessive joy, with tears and a faltering voice, he sings aloud, cries out, and dances in intense longing; // RBhṛs_3.2.142 //
This general process for those whose disposition is that of a devotee has been described here;
however, due to the particularity of time and other factors, there may occasionally be a transgression of the boundaries.
Now, regarding affection born of reverence:

for those who possess the conceit of being cherished, there may arise toward Kṛṣṇa an affection characterized by supreme reverence; when that is nourished by the determinants (vibhāva) and other factors, it is called "affection born of reverence. (RBhrs 3.2.144)
In this regard, the objects of focus are as follows: here, Hari and his beloved ones become the objects of focus.
In that regard, Hari is as follows:
"This Lord of the Yadus, whose ears were pierced by the elders of the Vṛṣṇis during the recitation of the Itihāsa, has a face radiant with a gentle smile."
Seated in the midst of the Sudharmā assembly hall, he teaches what is beneficial here for us, his own children, by means of his very own manifest activity while sporting.
Hari is the object of focus through such qualities as being the Great Guru, of great fame, of great intelligence, of great strength, the protector, and the caresser.
Now, regarding the *lālyas*: the *lālyas* are indeed those who take pride in being the youngest, sons, and so forth;
they are known as the younger ones, headed by Sāraṇa, Gada, Subhadra, and others.
Pradyumna, Cārudeṣṇa, and others, as well as Sāmba and other young princes.
Their appearance was such that— even compared to the circle of attendants of Murāntaka— their splendor of beauty, their ornaments, their dress, and their virtues were superior.
Endowed with the yellow, blue, and white splendors,
the hosts of Yadu youths took delight in the city.
Their devotion is as follows: they enjoy a feast together with Hari; raising their faces, they eat the chewed betel-leaf being offered to them.
And having smelled their heads and embraced them, the Aśvins, Sāmba, and others— who in former times performed austerities— became [his protectors].
Among those beloved ones, the son of Rukmiṇī is considered the most excellent.
His form— victory to him, the subduer of Śambara, the delicate crown of the Yadu princes' lineage, who,
by his exquisite beauty, produces in people the delusion that he is Janaka himself.
His devotion [is expressed thus]:
"O Prabhavati, behold! In heaven, he is the ocean of compassion for those like me;
he is that supreme guru, the Lord of the Yadus and of Garuḍa."
For, having obtained some measure of indulgence, we have become arrogant and can even defy the Foe of Tripura (Śiva) when he is provoked by great wrath in battle.
For both types of servants who worship with a mind intent solely on propitiating [the Lord],
the primary factor here is indeed the knowledge of sovereignty.
But for those who are to be cherished, [the realization] arises from the very manifestation of their own relationship [to the object] on all sides.
Even for those residing in Vraja, whose minds are devoid of knowledge of supreme sovereignty,
there certainly exists the awareness of the sovereignty inherent in being the son of the Lord of the Cowherds.
Now, as for the excitants (uddīpanas):
the excitants of Hari are affection, smiles, glances, and so forth. (RBhṛs 3.2.156)
For example:
"Beholding his elder brother looking upon him with favor, Gada, his mind filled with agitation, performed a prostration like a staff at his lotus feet. (RBhṛ 3.2.157)
Now, as for the indicative signs (anubhāvas):
the indicative signs [of devotion] toward him are sitting on a low seat in his presence,
following the path of the guru, and taking up the burden of his responsibilities.
The Śītā [mudrās], beginning with Svairācārā and Vimokṣā, are proclaimed for those who are to be cherished.
In that regard, there is the act of sitting on a low seat, as follows:
"While being quickly approached by the lords of the gods in the assembly of the Yadus,
his limbs were sprinkled by Brahmā with the water from the vessel that bestows happiness."
Having paid homage to the Enemy of Mura, the one marked by the sea-monster (Viṣṇu) abandoned his golden seats for the ground and took possession of a deer-skin rug.
Among these, some others are described as being common even to slaves:
bowing, excessive silence, modesty, being rich in humility, and the fulfillment of their commands even at the cost of one's own life. (RBhṛs 3.2.160)
Lowering the face, steadiness, avoiding coughing, laughing, and the like, as well as desisting from talk concerning his most intimate amorous sports and so forth.
Now, regarding those of the *sāttvika* nature:
she indeed remains unshakable when her two eyes find their place upon the pair of lotus-feet of Mukunda.
Covered with drops of frost and bearing thorns,
your body today, being perspiring, has produced a fruit of thorns.
Now, regarding the transitory states (vyabhicārin): all those mentioned immediately above are here considered transitory states.
In that regard, joy is as follows:
when the roar of the Lord of Mountains rose high in the sky, those standing in the blessed capital of the Yadus [experienced joy].
There, a dance was performed by the feathers of the young princes and by the joyful actors.
Disgust, as for example:
"Blessed are you, O Sāmba, along with your kinsmen, you who— dusty from the play of the ball—
were drawn by your father and, out of affection, placed upon his own lap."
"Fie on me, unfortunate as I am! For by the flashes of ill fortune that consist of Śaṅkara’s [deeds], even a moment’s joy in being cherished by my father during childhood was not obtained by me."
Now, regarding the permanent emotion (sthāyin):

here, "gravity" (gaurava) refers to the weightiness of the teacher's wisdom arising from the sense of connection with the body. The love for the attendant that consists of that [wisdom] is called "gravity-love" (gaurava-prīti).
In this context, that which is the stable emotion (*sthāyibhāva*) is itself raised up from its very root;

having attained a certain particularity, it is called "love" (*prema*), "affection" (*sneha*), and here also "passion" (*rāga*). It is indeed the same as reverence and joy (*gaurava-prīti*). (RBhrs 3.2.167)
In that regard, there is respect and affection, as follows:
"He does not break her seal with his lips, nor does he raise her face which is drenched with flowing tears."
The steadfast one casts his gaze, which slightly contracts, upon the lotus-foot of the Destroyer of Evil, the one whose mark is the fish.
Love (*premā*), for example:
"Even though Abhimanyu was slain by his enemies after they had forcibly dragged him from the hand of You— who do not permit Your will to be thwarted in the world— [the world still grieves]."
O subduer of the Danujas, the auspicious love of Subhadrā for you has attained such excellence that it has not experienced even a trace of impurity.
Affection is as follows: "Abandon this great trembling; cast off the choking in your throat;
wipe away [your tears] and cast upon me those eyes with their flowing streams of tears."
O you whose banner bears the sea-monster, place your hand—adorned with visible bristling hair—near your father’s side and tell him, "My child, what is this agitation? (RBhrs 3.2.170)
Passion is such that— should the fish-bannered god [Kāma] suddenly drink even poison as if it were nectar at the beck of his father, [it would be so].
If he has no approval for it, he immediately casts that very nectar away as if it were poison.
In these three [stages] alone, the divisions beginning with non-union (ayoga) and union (yoga) are proclaimed as before.
Among these, longing is as follows:
"O fair-faced one, that enemy Śambara, who has achieved the arrogance of difficult-to-overcome calamity, has become like the sky."
When shall we behold our Guru, whose splendor is like that of the king of waters (the ocean), holding the king of conchs (a white conch) in his hand?
Now, regarding separation:
my mind does not desire even the beloved's game of ball,
nor that which is appropriate for her, nor likewise that which is suitable for weapons.
When the Teacher arrived at the city of the Kurus,
he regarded Dvāravatī as if it were a prison.

Success: Śambara’s son Madana, having met his father face-to-face and gazing at him, though steadfast, did not recognize himself, wondering "Who am I?", nor did he recognize the young women. (RBhṛs 3.2.175)

Contentment— upon seeing the Enemy of Mura arrive from the city of Yudhiṣṭhira with Garuḍa mounted upon him, a great surge of joyful excitement arose among the youths in the city of the Yadus. (RBhrs 3.2.176)
Remaining thus— slightly closing his eyes, which were trembling with tears—
the god of love bows daily at the pair of feet of his father.
Whatever is expanded in states such as longing and separation—
excluding agitation and joy— all that should be understood by the wise as belonging to this [category] alone.

Thus ends the second wave, the *prīti-bhakti-rasa-laharī*, within the description of the five primary mellows of devotion (*mukhya-bhakti-rasa-pañcaka*) in the Western Division of the *Śrī-Śrī-Bhakti-Rasāmṛta-Sindhu*. (3.3)
The third wave, known as the aesthetic flavor of *preya-bhakti*,

describes how the stable emotion (*sthāyibhāva*) is brought here to full development in the hearts of the virtuous through excitants (*vibhāva*) and other factors appropriate to it; thus, the *preya* flavor is proclaimed.
In that regard, the objects of focus are as follows:
Hari and his companions are considered the objects of focus therein.
In that regard, Hari states:
"In this case, Hari, possessing two arms and so forth, is the objective support (ālambana), as previously described. (RBhṛs 3.3.3)
There in Vraja, he was as follows: possessing the lovely luster of Indra’s sapphire, with a smile like full-blown jasmine,
and wearing beautiful silk garments resembling blossoming golden ketakī flowers.
With his chest radiant with a garland and his flute resounding, the Destroyer of Sins has come here from Vraja;
alas, he steals away the hearts of our friends!
Elsewhere, for example:

"He is enriched by four arms, which are radiant through their friendship with the Kaumodakī mace and the discus, and which possess a mass of moonlight from the shimmering Kaustubha gem, as well as with the two lotuses."
Having seen Śauri, who surpassed the luster of a captivating emerald and was clad in golden garments,
the sons of Pāṇḍu were filled with the nectar of joy, yet they felt no sense of self-importance.
Well-dressed and marked with all auspicious signs, he was the best among the strong;
he was a master of various wonderful languages, eloquent, and highly learned.
"Of vast eloquence, skillful, compassionate, the crest-jewel of heroes,
clever, wise, patient, beloved by the world, prosperous, happy, and most excellent"— such are his qualities proclaimed here. (RBhṛS 3.3.7)

Now, regarding his companions: those who are equal to him in beauty, dress, virtues, and so forth, who are well-restrained, and whose hearts are filled with confidence, are declared to be his companions (*vayasyas*). (RBhrs 3.3.8)
For example:
"By means of an impartiality that was distressed by fear, yet which bestowed a profusion of devotion through its outpouring grace..."
One should most reverently salute the circle of friends of the Destroyer of Evil, which is interwoven with a multitude of the very essence of trust.
These are generally said to be of two kinds, based on their connection with cities or cattle-pens.
Among them were those connected to the city: Arjuna and Bhīmasena, the daughter of Drupada,
Śrīdāman, the Brahmins, and others— friends residing in the city.
Their friendship was as follows:
On his head, the king, firm-minded, smelled the enemy of sin (the lotus);
on his arms, which were like iron bars, Bhīma and Arjuna were embraced, radiant with horripilation.
The two sons of the Aśvins fell at his lotus-feet with tears,
while the Pāṇḍavas, their minds overcome by intense joy, held him back.
The Blessed One, whose banner bears the monkey, is the most excellent among his city companions.
His form is as follows:
holding the Gāṇḍīva bow in his hand, with thighs as beautiful as the trunk of a king of elephants, and possessing a luster as lovely as a blue lotus.
Mounted upon his jewel-encrusted chariot, that red-eyed king, the possessor of the discus, shone forth most brilliantly.
Friendship, as for example:
"With his forebody surrendered in fearless intimacy upon the lap of the slayer of the enemies of the gods on a great couch..."
This wielder of the Gāṇḍīva bow, his lotus-like face blooming with a smile, shone forth, skilled in the performance of ever-new jests.
Now, as for those connected to Vraja—
the residents of Vraja who were His constant companions, who became dejected at not seeing Him even for a moment, and who were said to have Him as their sole life— these were His friends.
Therefore, among all those of the same age, these possess preeminence.
Their appearance was as follows:
they possessed the beauty of form, age, qualities, grace, and attire like that of Viṣṇu, the younger brother of Indra;
they were marked by lutes, leaf-fans, horns, and flutes that bring delight.
May the companions of Hari— who possess the luster of great Indra-stones, gold, crystal, and rubies, and who are ever full of affection— protect you.
Friendship, as for example:
"O friend, seven nights have passed while you remained here awake; alas, you seem weary from standing—place the mountain now into the hand of Śrīdāman."
The pain pierces us; place it in your hand—why, for a moment, let us now perform at will the massage of your right arm.
Or as it is said in the Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam (10.12.11):
"Thus, for the virtuous who have attained servitude to the Supreme Deity through the experience of the bliss of Brahman,"
Those who had accumulated a mass of merit sported together with the human child, relying upon his illusory power.
Among these is Kṛṣṇa’s friendship, as it is said: "O noble brother, looking on as the multitude of his companions quickly entered the hollow interior of the belly of Aghāsura..."
With my gaunt cheeks washed by trickling, cold tears, I then became for a moment despondent and empty-minded.
Friends, companions, dear friends, and close confidants—
these four types are said to exist within a social circle.
In that regard, his friends—
those slightly older than him in age who possess a friendship imbued with affection—
are always intent on protecting him from the wicked, equipped as they are with weapons.
Subhadra, Maṇḍalībhadra, Bhadravardhana, and Gobhaṭa; Yakṣendrabhaṭa, Bhadrāṅga, and Vīrabhadra, who possess great virtues;
and Vijaya, Balabhadra, and others—these are proclaimed as his friends.
Their friendship is as follows:
"O Maṇḍalībhadra, you run brandishing your stainless sword; O Vijaya, why do you not take up your heavy mace? Do not cause agitation in vain!"
"Do not waste your power, Bhadravardhana! Yonder thundering cloud is plunging toward Govardhana; it is a powerful storm-cloud, not a Dānava in the form of a bull."
Among friends, Maṇḍalī and Balabhadra are indeed the most excellent.
Herein is the form of Maṇḍalībhadra, as follows: Maṇḍalībhadra shines, his limbs like a cluster of pale-red flowers, holding a staff in his hand, adorned with a crest by means of a peacock feather,
bearing [the staff] which resembles a swarm of bees within a circle of light.
His friendship is such that—
exhausted by the heavy play of wandering through the forest during the day,
our friend sleeps happily at night within the dwellings of Vraja.
I shall gently massage his head and whisper stories into his ear; you, Subala, do enough with it—simply fondle his thighs.
The form of Baladeva is as follows:
with a single earring shimmering on one cheek, a blue lotus used as an ear-ornament covered by bees,
a tilaka-mark made of musk, and a radiant garland of gunja berries upon his broad chest.
I took refuge in that hero, who possesses the brilliance of an autumn cloud, who is clothed in dark garments,
whose roar is deep, whose arms are long, and who has brought low his enemies.
Regarding his friendship, it is as follows:
"On the day of my birth, I was detained here in this house by my mother, who was overcome with love for her son, so that she might bathe me."
"Thus, O Subala, convey this message to Mukunda:
'Do not ever go today to the bank of the lake of the Lord of Serpents.'"
Here are his companions—
those who are like younger brothers, bound to him by friendship imbued with affection,
and who serve as protectors for the vast, powerful, and divine regions of the earth.
Maranda, Kusumāpīḍa, Maṇibandha, Karandhama,
and others were his friends, whose sole passion was the friendship of service to him.
Their friendship is as follows:
"O charioteer, perform the task of fanning me with the broad lotus petals; O leader of the troop, brush away these hanging locks of hair."
O Bull, abandon your false prattle; resort to the massaging of my limbs, for our friend has reached a state of great exhaustion in the fierce battle of arms.
Among all companions, this Devaprastha is declared to be the most excellent.
His form is as follows:
wearing a head-ornament (geṇḍu), clothed in garments of white radiance, with his lofty crest bound by a noose, he is powerful.
Resembling the bandhūka flower, with a playful gait like that of a river,
Devaprastha set out for the side of Kṛṣṇa.
His friendship is such that, for example:
Śrīdāmā rests his head upon the broad arm of [Kṛṣṇa],
who is reclining with his body radiant on the bed, while Kṛṣṇa’s left hand holds him by the heart.
In the midst of the beautiful valley, the fortunate Devaprastha, by massaging the feet of his beloved with affection, brings happiness to the son of the King of Vraja.
Then there were his dear friends—
those of equal age who relied solely on friendship as their bond:
Śrīdāmā, Sudāmā, Dāma, and Vasudāmaka.
Also these— Kiṅkiṇi, Stoka, Kṛṣṇāṃśu, Bhadrasena, Vilāsina, Puṇḍarīka, Viṭaṅkākṣa, Kalaviṅka, and so forth.
Their dear friends always delight Keśava with various pastimes, even with the curiosities of wrestling, stick-fighting, and the like.
Their friendship is as follows:
someone laughs at Hari with faltering words and indirect speech;
another, his hair standing on end, embraces him while stretching out both arms.
O slender-limbed one, these dear friends of yours, approaching stealthily with their hands, cover your eyes and bring joy to your beloved.
Among these dear companions, Śrīdāmā is considered the foremost.
His form was as follows:
wearing yellow garments, holding a horn in his hand,
and engaging in friendly rivalry with Mādhava out of affection.
I worship Śrīdāmā, who possesses a copper-colored crown, who is delightful with his dark splendor, and who bears a garland.
Friendship is as follows:
"O hard-hearted one, why have you gone away from us so suddenly on the bank of the Yamunā? By good fortune you have come within our sight; alas, please gladden your friends with firm embraces!"
We say this truly: when you are not seen, even for a moment, what are the cows, who are we, what is the cow-pen, and what is the desired object? Before long, everything becomes inverted.
Now, regarding the dear jesting companions:
the dear jesting companions, however, are even more excellent than those previously mentioned;
they are engaged in absolute secrets and are characterized by a particular state of being.
The Gandharvas Subala, Arjuna, Vasanta, Ujjvala, and others; // RBhrs_3.3.43 //
Their friendship is as follows:
Subala speaks a multitude of messages from Rādhā; behold, the radiant Ujjvala secretly delivers a love-letter from Śyāmā into Kṛṣṇa’s ear with his lotus-hand.
O slender one, your clever companions perform service for you: the cuckoo offers betel-leaf to your mouth, and the stars wear a garland upon your head—thus they serve you with playful affection.
Subala and Arjuna were powerful among their dear companions in playful jests.
In that regard, the form of Subala is as follows: his slender luster surpasses gold; he is beloved by Hari, captivating, and clothed in yellow garments.
I pay homage to Subala, whose eyes are like blue lotuses and who gladdens his kinsmen through his statesmanship.
His friendship is such that, for example,
even in a circle of companions who are experts in all subtle gestures, Mādhava [remains superior].
A certain discourse consisting of signs, difficult for others to understand, took place together with Subala.
The form of the radiant one, as follows:
clad in crimson garments, with upward-glancing eyes,
and adorned with offerings of honey and flowers.
I worship the radiant one, who possesses the luster of a sapphire, who is dear to Hari, and who shines with a necklace of jewels.
Her friendship is as follows:
"O friend, how am I able to maintain my pride when this radiant messenger approaches, and where he meets [the beloved] is not far away?"
"Who, even if she be modest, of noble birth, and devoted to her husband, would not lust after the bull of the cowherds, like a young maiden? (RBhṛs 3.3.49)
This person is especially radiant and is always eager for humorous speech.
For example:
"With its vast shore increased by shimmering, immense waves;
consisting of the nature of most sweet nectar; with its near and far shores difficult to traverse;"
In this world, the race of young women is a river and you are the ocean; therefore, O remover of sins, she approaches you by every possible path.
Some among these are renowned in the scriptures, and some in the world.
Those who move among the gods and those who are practitioners are eternally dear [to him], and thus they are of three kinds;
some among these, being stable by nature like mantra-holders, worship him.
Some, like jesters, make him laugh with their frivolity;
others, being straightforward and possessing the essence of honesty, discipline him.
Some deceive him with the wheel of crookedness;
some who are bold engage in cavil with him;
others, gentle and blessed, delight him with truthful speech. (RBhṛs 3.3.55)
Thus, all these beings, naturally sweet in their various ways,
cultivate the beautiful variety of pure loving-kindness.
Now, the excitants (uddīpanas):
the age, form, horn, flute, and bow of Hari;
his playful diversions, jests, and heroic exploits; his virtues; and likewise his most beloved people.
These include the imitation of the activities of kings, gods, incarnations, and so forth.
Now, regarding age: youth (*vayaḥ*) here is understood as comprising childhood (*kaumāra*), early adolescence (*paugaṇḍa*), and late adolescence (*kaiśora*).
Childhood and early adolescence are to be spent in the cow-pen (*goṣṭha*), while late adolescence is to be spent both in the city and in the cow-pen.
Among those, the *kaumāra* [style] is as follows:
"The *kaumāra* style is to be employed when addressing a beloved; therefore, it is written here in brief. (RBhṛS 3.3.59)
As it is said in the Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam (10.13.11): "Holding a flute against his belly, a horn and a staff in his two armpits,
a smooth morsel of food in his left hand, and the fruits of that [tree] upon his fingers..."
Standing in the midst of his own circle of friends, making them laugh with his own jests,
the enjoyer of sacrifice, indulging in childhood play, feasted while the world of heaven looked on.
Now, regarding *paugaṇḍa*:
*paugaṇḍa* is threefold—namely, the first, the middle, and likewise the remainder.
Among these, the first stage is *paugaṇḍa*: when the lower lip and other parts become beautifully red, the belly becomes thin,
and the conch-like neck begins to emerge— this occurs when the first *paugaṇḍa* is present.
For example:
"O Mukunda, your belly gradually assumes the beauty of a *aśvattha* leaf;
O lotus-eyed one, your neck, like a conch, possesses three brilliant lines."
O moon of the earth, your lip has assumed the luster of a sprouting *kuruvinda* ruby; this unprecedented beauty delights the eyes of your friends—what an extraordinary thing it is!
The variety of floral ornaments, the diverse paintings with mountain minerals, and yellow silk and fine linen garments— these are declared here to be the adornments.
Wandering through all the forests, grazing with a herd of cows,
and undertaking the practice of wrestling, play, dancing, and so forth— this is the activity here.
For example:
In the fragrant forest of Vṛndāvana, he who sports in the protection of the multitude of Surabhis,
who wears a garland of guñjā berries, whose crown is manifested by his crest-lock, and who possesses the splendor of yellow silk garments;
Wearing *karṇikāra* flowers on his ears and a garland of full-blown jasmine on his chest,
this Kṛṣṇa delights his friends here like a dancer, dancing upon the stage of arm-to-arm combat.
Now, regarding the middle *paugaṇḍa* stage:
the nose has a beautiful peak and is elevated; the cheeks are circular in shape;
and the limbs, beginning with the sides, are well-proportioned when one is in the middle *paugaṇḍa*.
For example:
"The beauty of her nose, which rivals the flower of a sesame blossom;
her cheeks, which destroy the pride of a mirror made of fresh jewels."
Here, Hari, having rubbed the boundaries of his flanks,
brings great joy to his friends by his very splendor alone.
Here, she has a crown adorned with a lightning-bright fillet of silk and a cord;
her staff is dark green, three cubits high, with a golden tip and other ornaments.
Her pastimes were at Bhāṇḍīra, and her deeds included the lifting of the mountain, and so forth.
For example:
"Holding a staff three cubits long with its two ends bound in gold,
his splendor was radiant with the beautiful crest of a gracefully tossing yak-tail."
Look, O friend, Mukunda delights the circle of his companions as he plays at their side, wearing a turban bound with a golden-gleaming silken cord.
Even while still in the midst of childhood, this Hari shines resplendent as he plays, appearing as if he already possessed a portion of the excellence of youth due to his wondrously sweet form.
Now, regarding the remaining stage of *paugaṇḍa*:

"The braid with its tip hanging down to the hips, the radiance of playful creeper-like locks, and the fullness of the shoulders"—such [characteristics] exist when the final stage of *paugaṇḍa* has arrived. (RBhṛs 3.3.72)
For example:
"Bearing on his forehead a face adorned with the creeper-like playful locks of hair, and with the flame-like tip of his swaying braid kissing the row of bimba-fruits [his lips];"
With the luster of his lofty shoulders, the remover of sins departs from Gokula, as if bestowing the very splendor of his limbs upon his dear companions of the same age.
A curl on the crown of the head, hands like playful lotuses,
and the vertical sectarian mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍra) and so forth with saffron— these are declared here to be ornaments.
For example:
"Upon his crown is a slight curve; in the palm of his hand, a playfully blooming lotus;
upon his forehead, the fair splendor of an upward-pointing tilaka marked with a drop of musk."
O Keśava, your charming attire today causes even Subala to reel;
how much more so the multitude of cowherd women, who are by nature tender?
In this regard, there is the artful play of words, the essence of ear-whispered secrets shared by playful companions,
and the praising of Śrī by the cowherd boys— such are their activities.
For example:
"Since you, a rogue, know what is in her heart, tell it into her ear;
what kind of abundance of delusion is this now among the group of cowherd girls?"
In this matter as well, O friend, five or six youths from the land of Rohaṇa, the source of radiant jewels,
take delight there, entrusting the burden of conquering the worlds to the Five-Arrowed One.
Now, regarding youth (*kaiśoram*):
youth has already been mentioned previously; it is now described here in brief.
For example:

"Behold, O excellent creeper of the three swollen powers, you who are clothed in the beauty of lightning, radiant with the mass of fragrances from blossoming forest garlands, and possessing the luster of the tamāla tree."
While the cloud that is Damodara nourishes the cātaka birds that are his eyes with the essence of his smiles,
Śrīdāmā shone like a tree whose limbs were covered with the beautiful buds of his body hair.
This Lord generally appears as a youth among all devotees;
therefore, no description of the splendor of his youth has been elaborated here.
Now, as for form (*rūpa*), it is as follows:
"O lotus-eyed one, having adorned your body with ornaments, O wise one, this [body] gladdens us by its very splendor, and our friends alone. (RBhṛs 3.3.81)
Now, as for the horn, for example:
"At dawn, while the excellent horn was loudly crying out upon the terrace of the roof of his own cow-pen..."
Aha! Even the masses of his hairs, being of the same age, woke up at the very same time.
O flute,
do not go like a coward from here to seek Hari, the son of the Sun; for he is not your friend.
Proclaiming this very thing here, the messenger of the flute’s sound delights us upon the mountain peak.
Śaṅkha, for example:
"Hearing the sound of the Pāñcajanya conch, the husbands of the Pāñcālīs, seeing [the enemy] rejoicing, went toward the five-faced one who resembles five faces. (RBhṛs 3.3.84)
For example, as an amusement: [He is seen] with a shimmering saffron silk garment, his fair body adorned with *jāguḍa* pigments,
his hair fashioned into an excellent braid, and his ears graced with jeweled earrings.
O dear friend, having seen Madhuripu here in the very person of Rādhā, Subala was struck with wonder and filled with a smile.
Now, as for the [divine] powers (anubhāvas):
his gratification through sports such as wrestling, ball games, gambling, riding vehicles and mounts, and so forth, as well as through the game of stick-fighting and combats. 3.86.
Sleeping and sitting together on couches and swings;
charming laughter and jesting; and recreation in a body of water.
In the state of union, activities such as dancing and singing are common to all.

In this regard, satisfaction through wrestling is as follows: "O destroyer of sins, you who appear victorious and whose arms itch for battle, you wander among the assemblies of friends praising your own prowess."
Tell me, why do you stand here with limbs rendered powerless, having been forced to cease your performance on the battlefield by the movements of my fierce, staff-like arms?
Speaking of what is appropriate and inappropriate, and encouraging others toward beneficial actions— these,
along with generally taking the lead, are said to be the activities of friends.
The offering of betel and other items into the mouth, the application of forehead marks and decorative pastes,
and the drawing of leaf-designs and sprouts— these are declared to be the duties of female companions.
Defeating him in battle, dragging him by his garment,
snatching flowers and other ornaments from his hand, and adorning oneself with them— these,
beginning with hand-to-hand combat, are declared to be the activities of a dear friend.
He acts as a messenger among the young girls of Vraja; he possesses their affection;
and in the sport with them, he openly takes the side of their friend.

The skill in establishing their respective positions within their own herds without being face-to-face, as well as the playful activities of dear friends involving whispers from ear to ear and so forth; (3.94)
The adornment of Mādhava with forest-grown jewel ornaments,
preceded by the threefold symphony (song, dance, and instrumental music), and the act of tending to the cows.
Massaging the limbs, weaving garlands, fanning, and so forth—
these activities are considered common to female attendants and their companions.
Wise men should understand that other [activities] mentioned previously are also applicable here as appropriate.
Now, regarding the *sāttvika* [emotions],
among them is *stambha* (stupefaction), as for example:
having violently seized Kṛṣṇa as he was emerging from the serpent.
Desiring to embrace Śrīdāmā immediately,
he finds his arms rendered stiff; behold how, overcome by agitation, he is unable to raise them.
Perspiration, as for example:
when the cloud of the Svāti constellation rains with a beautiful sound upon Mukunda, who is the essence of the joy of playful festivals; [the gopīs experience perspiration].
This excellent oyster-shell, the form of Śrīdāma, produces a multitude of pearls from its water of perspiration.
Horripilation, as in the *Dānakelikauṃudī* (37):
"Even in the presence of his elders, Hari embraces you upon his broad lap with a thrill of intense horripilation."
And he rests his serpent-like arm upon your shoulder;
O Subala, tell me, how much asceticism did you perform previously in the field of the Siddhas?
The fourfold group beginning with the change of voice is as follows:
when Mādhava had entered the lake inhabited by the king of serpents,
his friends were then overwhelmed by great trembling.
Their bodies instantly turning pale, emitting hideous, gurgling roars, they fell upon the ground nearby and began to fall into a deep sleep.
Tears, for example:
"Beholding him wandering through the forest with blades of grass as arrows,
she shed a stream of tears as if to bring about his destruction."
Even disregarding her own body, the line of cowherd girls, wearing garlands of lotuses, surrounded Hari on all sides.
Now, regarding the transitory states (*vyabhicārin*):

"With the exception of ferocity (*augrya*), terror (*trāsa*), and likewise lassitude (*ālasya*), all other [transitory states] have been declared by those who know the nature of *bhāvas* to be transitory states (*vyabhicārin*) within the beloved sentiment (*preyasī rasa*). (RBhṛs 3.3.102)
In that regard, during non-yoga (ayoga), there is intoxication, exhilaration, pride, sleep, and stability—excluding [the state of] resolve;
whereas during yoga, there is death, exhaustion, and disease—excluding epilepsy and dejection.
In that regard, joy is as follows:
when the son of the Lord of the Vallavas had indeed approached, having caused the serpent Kāliya to depart.
Through intoxication, their friends stumbled in their steps,
and their voices became powerless, causing their limbs to go limp.

Now, regarding the permanent emotion (*sthāyin*): "The love (*rati*) between two people which is free from agitation and consists of mutual confidence is generally found here [in friendship] when they are of equal status; it bears the designation of both 'friendship' (*sakhyam*) and 'the permanent emotion' (*sthāyi-śabda*). (RBhrs 3.3.105)
*Viśrambha* is a specific form of intense trust that is free from restraint;
this *sakhya-rati*, as it gradually increases, is said to have five stages: *praṇaya*, *prema*, *sneha*, and *rāga*. (RBhṛS 3.3.106)
In that regard, there is the pleasure of friendship, as follows:
"O son of Gāndinī, let Mukunda be informed by you:
'O you who bear the emblem of Garuḍa, when will Guḍākeśa embrace you? (RBhrs 3.3.107)
Affection (praṇaya):
Even when the conditions for agitation and the like have clearly arisen, that state of love which is untouched even by the slightest scent of them is called affection. (RBhrs 3.3.108)
For example:
"Even though his praise was being performed by the gods, headed by Tripurajit,
he manifested the supreme glory of the highest state of Brahmā."
Arjuna, covered in dust, adorned the left arm of Hari upon his shoulder— now bristling with thrills— with moon-like spots on his head.
Love, as it is said:
"O Mukunda, when the Lord, our friend, rises [to power], there is the loss of kingdom; yet when He dwells in the forest, there is residence in another's house and the performance of service."
Let this destiny of the Pāṇḍavas clearly be inauspicious;
nevertheless, the nectar of friendship toward you has increased twofold.

Affection, as described in the Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam (10.15.18): "O great king, others, their hearts moistened with affection, sang softly of the Great Soul's various charming deeds that were worthy of him. (RBhrs 3.3.111)
Or as it is said:

When the dark cloud of Kṛṣṇa rained down the nectar of his playful pastimes upon the swelling clouds that were his friends— whose clear mineral-like bodies were drenched with moisture— a manifest wonder arose.
The Sarasvatī that formerly flowed here has now swiftly vanished from its banks; she who was once ever present before one's eyes has become a river of waterless sands.
Passion, as for example: that row of arrows, difficult to avoid, which was discharged by the merciless son of Kṛpī against Hari with his weapon.
Leaping up as she was being seized in the heart by the wielder of the Gāṇḍīva,
she became like a rain of flowers for his joy.
Or as it is said:
"While gathering flowers fit for weaving a forest garland from all sides in the woods,"
The rays of the bull-like sun, though it was midday, became like moonlight upon the bull.
Next is longing in separation, as follows:
"While studying the science of archery, the middle Pāṇḍava, O Kṛṣṇa, requested an embrace with a voice choked with tears. (RBhrs 3.3.115)
Now, regarding separation, as for example:
"O Protector, you who were the savior here of those [who fled] from the fire of Agha’s belly, from the venomous pool of the serpent, and even from the mouthful of the forest fire."
How is it that our friends have not today recovered from the fever of separation, even though they are supported by this triad which is more manifestly formidable than any other?
Here too, as previously stated, those ten stages beginning with *tāpa* are declared.
In that regard, the torment is as follows:

those who have taken refuge [in you] experience even greater chill in the Bhāṇḍīra forest, and even more heat in the fiercely cold frost; they have reached a state of exhaustion in the current of the Yamunā, the daughter of the Sun.
O enemy of Kaṃsa, this unprecedented and powerful heat born of separation from you inflames the circle of friends headed by Subala.
Emaciation—
[attained] day by day through the exhaustion [of your presence] within the bodies of the rows of Ābhīras in the city, for the sake of liberating King Kaṃsa upon your arrival.
Of the four elements, the earth became diminished for the enemy of the Dānavas;
only the wind attained expansion upon the path of his nostrils.
Vigilance, as follows:
having observed the two lotus-eyes of the commander Varūthapa completely filled with a flood of tears.
There, O Lord of the Yādavas, having grown weary of following [him], she who was like a bee drinking the honey of sleep abandoned him.

When His dear friend, the son of Goṣṭheśvara, had departed from Vṛndāvana forest for the sake of his objective, [the cowherd boys] were suddenly overcome with grief; though they immediately rose up, they fell down again and again.
For my restless mind, like a fickle scale, does not settle anywhere even for a moment, though it wanders and wanders about without support.
Lack of fortitude—
she creates a cessation from her own duty of cattle-tending,
and she exerts millions of efforts toward the forgetting of the arts.
What more need be said here? O best of the Yadus, because of separation from you, even the circle of kinsmen no longer regards life as having any purpose today.
Stupefaction—
those who possess no shelter or belongings, whose limbs are emaciated, shattered, and coarse, whose livelihood is always fruitless, and who are indeed bereft of even shade;
O Mukunda, within your cowherd settlement, the groups of friends shine forth, free from all cries of distress, like trees growing on a mountain peak.
O hero of the Yadus, the circle of cowherd maidens on your bank, their bodily joints loosened by the feverish torment of the heat of separation, toss about for a long time as if afflicted by disease.
Madness—
without the remembrance of you, we have now completely forgotten the entire course of worldly affairs through the delusion of separation.
Alas, these hosts of cowherds plunder on the ground, lie down, laugh, run about, and weep; O Lord of Mathurā, they are acting in some inexplicable way!
He has fainted:
"Now that the Lord of Madhu has obtained the kingdom and sports here in the sweet city of Mathurā."
The entire world rejoiced, yet in Gokula, which was blinded by weeping, there arose constant agitation.
Death— on the mountain slope, the cowherds lie thus, shattered by the series of flames born from the waves of the fever of separation from the Enemy of Kaṃsa, their sprouts of breath weakened.
Even the deer, long accustomed to them through intimacy, now grieve for those who remain motionless, drenching them again and again with tears from their large eyes.
This state of separation has been described in accordance with the manifest pastimes;
for the residents of Vraja, there shall never be a separation from Kṛṣṇa.
And so it is stated in the Mathurā-khaṇḍa of the Skanda Purāṇa: "Mādhava, having entered the interior of Vṛndāvana, always plays with calves and heifers, accompanied by Rāma and surrounded by boys."
Now, regarding success in yoga, as follows:
Having beheld the lotus-eyed one in the abode of the Discus-bearer, the Pāṇḍava,
while assuming a variegated form, manifested the form of a friend.
Contentment, as described in the *Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam* (10.71.27): "Embracing his maternal cousin, Bhīma was filled with bliss; smiling, his senses were overwhelmed by the force of his love."
The twins and Kirīṭin, their eyes brimming with tears of joy, affectionately embraced Acyuta, their dearest friend.
Or as it is said:
"In Kurujāṅgala, having beheld Hari before them,
the multitude of friends from Vraja [longed for] union with their beloved."
With their arms encircled by jeweled bracelets and bristling with horripilation, they embraced him.
Regarding His abiding nature, as stated in the Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam (10.12.12):
"The dust of whose feet is unattainable even by self-controlled yogis after many births of great hardship..."
When that very [Supreme] remains as the object of one's own vision, how can it be described? Therefore, let the good fortune of the residents of Vraja be praised.
Belonging to both [types] and partaking in the sweetness of a single nature, this *preyas* aesthetic flavor nourishes an indescribable wonder of the mind.
Furthermore, between Kṛṣṇa and his devotee, both of whom are affectionate and full of love, there would arise a difference in the nature of their mutual relationship. (RBhṛs 3.3.135)
This [rasa] is indeed the most beloved among all aesthetic sentiments;
it is perceived only by the virtuous whose hearts are touched by friendship.
Thus ends the third wave, on the rasa of *preya* devotion, within the description of the five principal rasas of devotion in the western division of the *Śrī-Śrī-Bhakti-Rasāmṛta-Sindhu*. (3.4)
The fourth wave, known as the rasa of affectionate devotion (*vatsala-bhakti-rasa*):
when the stable emotion (*sthāyī*) of parental affection (*vātsalya*) reaches full development through the determinants (*vibhāva*) and other factors,
it is here called by the wise the "affectionate" (*vatsala*) devotional rasa.
In that regard, the objects of focus are as follows:
the wise declare that for him, Kṛṣṇa and his gurus are the objects of focus here.
Therein is Kṛṣṇa, who is dark like a garland of fresh blue lotuses, with tender limbs,
and whose lotus-eyes are surrounded by bees that are his swaying locks of hair.
Beholding her son sporting in the land of Vraja,
the beloved of the lord of Vraja was drenched by the overflowing of her milk.
Dark-limbed, beautiful, endowed with all auspicious marks,
gentle, pleasant-spoken, straightforward, modest, disciplined, honoring those worthy of honor, a giver, and so forth— Kṛṣṇa, possessing such qualities, is called the "vibhāva" (the excitant).
Thus, because this [rasa] possesses such qualities and is itself that which is to be favored,
its status as the *vibhāva* (the determinant cause) here is proclaimed by virtue of its being the locus of majestic power (*prabhāva*).

Likewise, in the Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam (10.8.45): "He meditated upon Hari, whose majesty is sung by the three Vedas, the Upaniṣads, Sāṅkhya, Yoga, and the Sātvata [Pāñcarātra] traditions, as being born of his own self."
Or for example: "O friend, Viṣṇu is constantly worshipped by me; therefore, I suspect that Pūtanā and the others have been destroyed here, or else those two trees have been uprooted by a storm."
This mountain is visibly held up by Rāma, the lord of the cowherds, along with his companions;
how could anyone imagine such deeds, so difficult to follow, on the part of my mere child?

Now, regarding the gurus: "The gurus are considered here to be [the causes of] the determinants (vibhāvas) through the state of being highly esteemed, by means of imparting instruction, and also through fondling and so forth. (RBhrs 3.4.8)
For example:
