"With a mind filled with abundant grace, longing to cherish [him] on all sides and agitated by compassion..."
With profound reverence, I take refuge in the immeasurable host of qualities belonging to the Teacher of the World.
But they are described here as the Queen of Vraja, the Sovereign of Vraja,
Rohiṇī, and those cowherd women whose hearts were stolen by the Lotus-born One.

Devakī, her co-wives, Kuntī, Ānakadundubhi, and others headed by Sāndīpani— these excellent elders were honored as before; yet among these elders, the Lord of Vraja and the Queen of Vraja were the most preeminent.
In that regard, the form of the Queen of Vraja is described in the *Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam* (10.9.3):
"Wearing upon her broad hips a silken garment fastened with a cord..."
With her pair of breasts flowing with milk from maternal love for her son, the fair-browed woman trembled;
her bracelets on her arms jingled from the exertion of pulling the rope, her earrings swayed,
her face perspired, and the *mālatī* flowers fell from her loosened tresses as she churned.
Or as it is said:
"With her mass of curly hair bound by a cord, the luster of her parting shining with dots of vermilion, she has adopted a method of bodily adornment that is not excessive."

May the Mistress of the Cowherd settlement protect you— she whose two eyes are moistened by tears shed from the mouth of Govinda, who possesses a luster as dark as a fresh blue lotus, and who is clad in variegated garments.
Affection, as follows:
"With a voice faltering and eyes filled with tears, she performs the ritual placement of mantras upon her body; she applies the protective tilaka-mark upon her forehead."
Suckling at dawn, Yaśodā bestows nourishment upon her arms; she shines forth like the very personification of the mass of maternal affection for her son.
The form of the Lord of Vraja is as follows: He shines with hair as fine as sesame seeds and rice grains, and wears garments as beautiful as the fresh leaves of the bhaṇḍīra tree.
I worship the King of Vraja, who possesses an exceedingly large belly, who bears the luster of the moon, and who has a magnificent beard.
Affection, as follows:
"O lady, supporting with her own finger his hand as he crawls with faltering steps across the courtyard..."
With a torrent of tears flowing down his chest,
the Lord of Vraja rejoiced upon beholding his son.
Now, as for the excitants (uddīpanas):
"The stages of life such as childhood, physical form, dress, the restlessness of youth, chatter, smiles, playful gestures, and so forth—these are known by the wise as excitants. (RBhrs 3.4.17)
In that regard, the state of youth (kaumāra)— the initial, the middle, and likewise the final— is considered to be threefold.

Among those, the first [sign] occurs when the first stage of youth (kaumāra) is present: "The thickness, the breadth, and the whiteness of the outer corners of the eyes, the smallness of the teeth, and the manifest softness [of the body]. (RBhṛs 3.4.19)
For example:
"Her moon-like faces, three or four in number, quiver;
the boundaries of her broad waist, hips, and thighs [are visible]."
The prince, as tender as a fresh blue lotus, brought exceeding joy to the two lords of Vraja.
In this [infant state], there was the momentary lifting of his feet, weeping and smiling,
the sucking of his own thumb, and such activities as lying on his back.
For example:
[he saw] his son sleeping on his back, with the soles of his two feet placed upon the tops of the big toes of his lotus-feet.
At one moment she was quarreling here with a smiling face, and at another moment the queen of the cowherd settlement did not cease looking at him even for a sesame seed’s length of time.
In this regard, tiger-claw amulets, protective tilaka marks on the neck, a silk sash at the waist, a thread in the hand, and so forth constitute adornment. (RBhṛs 3.4.23)
For example:
"The circle of the hyena's claws, possessing the luster of a fresh *tamāla* leaf,
and the child adorned with the beauty of *tamāla* leaf-patterns made from lovely *rocanā* pigment."
Wearing a protective amulet and a garland of silk threads shimmering at her waist,
the mistress of Vraja found no satisfaction even after beholding her son.
Now, regarding the intermediate [age]:
having eyebrows that reach the eyes, a straight nose, ears with openings,
and the ability to speak poetically and move gracefully— these occur when one is in the intermediate stage of youth.
For example:
"With eyebrows arched and blocked by trembling curls, with tremulous eyes, with sweet speech, and with the new openings of her ears raised— "
Seeing her son, who was the silken garment of the directions and whose playful movements were composed of no small measure, his mother embraced him within the ocean of nectar in Gokula.
Pearls are placed upon the tip of the nose, fresh butter on the lotus-like hand, and ornaments such as small bells on the waist and other parts; thus is the adornment described here.
For example:
"The mouth was smiling, the tip of the nose was radiant, and it was described as having a cluster of tinkling golden bells."
Seeing her son before her holding a lump of fresh butter in his hand, the wife of Nanda rejoiced.

Now, regarding the remainder: here, when the final stage of childhood has passed, the waist is somewhat slender, the chest possesses a slight breadth, and the head is adorned with the side-locks of a youth (kākapakṣa).
For example:
"His waist was slightly diminishing, while his chest, as if desiring to learn the practice of expansion, began to broaden."
The divine child paralyzed his mother, who bore the appearance of a crow’s wing with its feathers in disarray.
A waist-band, a hood-ornament, and some forest-derived decoration,
as well as small cane-work and jewels, are proclaimed to be the ornaments [of the third stage].
In this [pastime], his activities included protecting the calves near the cow-pens, playing with his companions,
and playing musical instruments such as flutes, horns, and cymbals.
For example:
"With a peacock feather as his crest, holding a hooded snake in one hand and a small staff in the other, he was surrounded by groups of his own age."
O beloved, behold! Your son here, discharging dung in the vicinity of Vraja, is bringing fulfillment to our eyes—alas, look! (3.4.33)
Now, regarding *paugaṇḍa*:
since *paugaṇḍa* and the other stages were already mentioned previously, they are written here in brief.
For example:
"On every path, he whose head is adorned with fragrant flowers and fine silken garments,
and who is beautified by a bodice, is graced by the whiteness of his uneven side-glances."
With his pair of charming anklets tinkling very softly,
my calf approaches from the region of Kaccha upon the land of Vraja.
Now, regarding adolescence: with reddish outer corners of the eyes, a lofty chest like a door-panel adorned with a shimmering pure necklace, and the beauty of a lovely line of body hair;
O Devakī, this jewel of a man, with his dark-limbed form born from the mine of your womb, intensely delights my eye.
Even while sporting with his fresh youth, the delighter of the lord of the cowherds shines like one in the stage of childhood,
possessing nothing but pure affection.
Although he was joined with a delicate youth in his childhood years,
he always shone like a young colt among the most excellent of horses.
Now, as for childhood restlessness:
he breaks the water-jar, scatters the curds upon the courtyard floor,
steals the cream from the whey, and snaps the churning-stick.
Thus, as he incessantly casts fresh butter into the fire,
Hari increases the abundance of his mother's joy.
Or for example:

"Looking repeatedly toward the quarters with apprehension and setting down his steps slowly again and again, this Hari does not come clearly from within the creepers; he is surely coming here to seize the cow."

Stay still at your ease, as if unaware; for I wish to behold his lovely face, with its creeper-like eyebrows arching in the illusion of a thief, its eyes trembling with fear, and its lower lip parched.
Now, the consequential expressions (anubhāvas):
the smelling of the head, stroking the limbs with the hand,
bestowing blessings, giving commands, fondling, and protecting.
Giving beneficial advice and so forth are proclaimed as the qualities of affection.
In this context, there is the smelling of the head,
as described in the Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam (10.13.33):
"Her heart was flooded with the nectar of love arising from the sight of Him."
Their affection awakened and their anger gone,
they lifted the children up with their arms, embraced them, and smelled the tops of their heads, thereby attaining supreme joy.
Or as it is said:
"Having smelled her entire head, including the hair, which was smeared with milk dripping from her breasts,"
With her hand, she repeatedly wiped the limbs of the cowherd’s son on the courtyard of the master of the herd.
Kissing, embracing, calling out, addressing by name, and reproaches— these are the actions shared here with friends.
Now, as for the *sāttvika* [emotions]:
there are nine *sāttvika* ones here—namely, the flowing of breast milk, paralysis, and so forth.
In that regard, the flowing of breast milk is described in the Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam (10.13.22):
"Their mothers, hurried up by the sound of the flute..."
Lifting them up with their arms and embracing them tightly,
they regarded the nectar-like wine of the milk flowing from their breasts out of affection as the Supreme Brahman, and caused their sons to drink it.
Or as it says in the *Lalitamādava* (1.46):
"Yaśodā [washed] those [trees] whose leaf-rows were thickened by the mineral pigments of the mountain caves, and which possessed all the fragrant pollen."
With the floods of milk released from her jar-like breasts, which contain the honey-sweet nectar of affection, she performs for you a new consecration.
For example, [the verse beginning]: "With limbs stiffened, she is not able to embrace him by any means; with eyes flooded by a torrent of tears, she is not even capable of looking at him."
And though her throat was choked, she was unable to teach what she had heard;
the mistress of Gokula remained agitated while holding Lord Acyuta.
Now, regarding the transitory emotions (vyabhicārin):
among them, those accompanied by epilepsy (apasmāra) are said to be the "pleased" (prīta) transitory emotions.
In that regard, joy is as described in the *Śrī-daśama* (10.17.19):
"The highly fortunate Yaśodā also, having lost and then regained her child..."
Having embraced him and placed him on his lap, he shed a stream of tears again and again.
Or as it says in the *Vidagdhamādhava* (1.20):
"Having surpassed the splendor of the moonlight from the moon’s pollen, and the beauty of *nalada*, blue lotuses, and sandalwood..."
On all sides, the great festival of your touch brings coolness and sweetness to me.
Now, as for the permanent emotion (sthāyī):
that very love (rati) which, having fallen away from agitation and the like, exists toward a benefactor out of compassion, is here called the permanent emotion of parental affection (vātsalya).
But for Yaśodā and others, parental affection (vātsalya-rati) is naturally mature;
it appears sometimes as love (prema), sometimes as endearment (sneha), and indeed, at times, as passion (rāga).
In that regard, affectionate attachment (*vātsalya-rati*) is as described in the *Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam* (10.6.43):
"The noble-minded Nanda, taking his own son who had returned from the dead..."
Having smelled his head, O best of the Kurus, he attained the highest joy.
Or as it is said:

"Today, at the onset of evening, the flute—with its holes arranged [to produce sound]—desires to hear its own resonance once more; raining down a profusion of notes, it overflows with redoubled longing."
Entering the courtyard from the house, and from the courtyard back into the house again, the wife of the lord of Vraja, distressed, repeatedly gazes along the path of Govinda.
Just as in love— for instance:
"Having seen You there being praised by the circles of the kings of sages, she was freed from her agitation."
The mistress of Gokula, her breasts flowing with milk, placed Kṛṣṇa upon her lap in the land of the Kurus.
Or as it is said:
"Even though Devakī’s act of giving birth had been revealed, and even though he was being proclaimed by the people as the son of Vasudeva, his face was being wiped clean [of all doubt]..."
When Govinda arrived at the field of Kuru out of eagerness to seize the sun, the love of the two lords of the cowherds reached a state of supreme exultation.
Like something oily, as follows:
the Ganges was produced by the streams of milk falling from the mountain-like breasts with the luster of nectar,
and the Yamunā by the lotus-eyes that became dark like collyrium.
O Queen of Vraja, you have clearly grown weary at the meeting of those two who have fallen from afar and from mid-air; you truly long for the sight of their son’s face.
Like passion— for instance:
"O Mukunda, if the Mistress of the Cowherd settlement gazes upon you while the fire of chaff, though situated above her, remains fixedly burning within the chaff."
Even the ocean of nectar is clearly filled with formidable *kālakūṭa* poison;
for if you were not present there, your lotus-face would not be beheld.
Now, longing in separation, as for example:
"Alas! When will the face of our child—which puts to shame the autumnal moon—bring a festival for our eyes?"
Thus, as Acyuta dwelt in the courtyard of Vraja,
the earth quickly triumphed over the daughters of the gods.
Or as it is said:
"O brother, son of Gāndinī, send word to my brother's son."
O Hari, while dwelling among her rivals, Kuntī longs to see you.
Separation, as described in the *Śrī-daśama*:
"While listening to the deeds of her son being described, Yaśodā shed tears, her breasts flowing with milk out of affection. (RBhrs 3.4.62)
Or for example:
"When Hari had gone to the royal city, behold her face with its smoky curls disheveled, her body emaciated, causing wounds upon her frame through harsh rolling on the ground."
The chief queen of the great lord of the earth in the cow-pen is now ruined; crying out "Alas, my son! My son!
she painfully beats her breast with the palms of both hands.

Even when many [causes] are present, some among them here— such as anxiety, despondency, world-weariness, dullness, dejection, agitation, madness, and delusion— reach an extreme intensity upon separation.
Herein lies the reflection: "The mind has become sluggish with heavy exhaustion;
the pair of eyes remains for a long time fixed with pupils slightly turned upward and motionless."
With sighs that cause her milk to flow and boil,
O Queen of the cowherds, you are surely being overwhelmed by the agitations of separation from your son.
Despair:
"While my son’s lotus-face was still closing in childhood, I did not behold its beauty as it was being polished by the onset of fresh youth."
Alas, that son of Śvaphalka has hurled a thunderbolt upon my head; he did not allow me to enter this palace while it was occupied by my newly wedded bride.
Disgust [arises]:
"Fie upon this wretched life of mine, even though it possesses limitless fortune, since today my breasts, dripping with nectar, do not smell the head of Hari!"
Fie on that fickle man who plunders even a hundred million cows that constantly yield fresh nectar, yet whose curd is not fragrant with the scent of the Surabhi cow!
Stupidity—
O lotus-eyed one, that which served as an ornament for your hand-lotus while you were staying in the cow-pen;
Beholding him, whose senses were as steady as a staff,
your mother became one who possessed the form of a staff.
Wretchedness:
"Alas, O Creator! Yaśodā, casting aside her teeth, begs you for grass with tears."
Even for a single moment today, abandon your stinginess regarding my sphere of activity; bring me my calf.
Restlessness—what indeed does it do? This shameless one stands in the palace;
"This is the Lord of Vraja," says this deluded person here with joy.
Ah! Having abandoned his son, who is dearer to him than life itself, that hard-hearted man enters the cow-pen at will and finds happiness.
Madness—Where is my son? O *nīpa* trees, tell me; O deer, did he wander here? O bees, speak the news of him in my vicinity!
Thus, O Lord of the Yadus, Yaśodā wanders in every direction, tormented by a heavy burden of delusion, asking about you again and again.
Delusion:
O mistress of the household, why do you cause distress upon the shore of your mind?
Cast your gaze even slightly forward; your son stands right before you.
"O housewife, do not leave this home empty"—
thus does your father Nanda, the lord of the Yadu clan, lament in distress for your mother.
Now, regarding success in yoga:
having beheld Hari, who has attained union upon the stage of the arena and whose sight is the desired object of the eyes;
In an instant, the queens, beloved of Ānakadundubhi, drenched the hem of his new tunic with their breast milk.
Contentment, as in the first [chapter] (1.11.30):
"Placing their son upon their laps, with milk flowing from their breasts due to affection, their souls overwhelmed by joy, they drenched him with the waters of their tears. (RBhṛs 3.4.74)
Or as it says in the *Lalitamādhava* (10.14):
"With streams of water falling from her two eyes and also from the pair of her breasts..."
Aha! The mistress of the cowherd king’s house affectionately consecrates her own son.
Stability [of the mind], as in the *Vidagdhamādhava* (1.19):
"Ah! O Mukunda, having fixed her eyes upon this mass of beauty here, which possesses the fragrance of a lotus, she [looks] at the moon of your face."
From the mouths of her jar-like breasts, your Mother, out of excessive joy, repeatedly showers streams of milk that moisten her garment.
Even some who are experts in dramaturgy accept this aesthetic flavor (rasa).
Thus they have said [SD 3.201]: "The wise know *rasa* to be clearly characterized by wonder and affection (*vatsala*).
Here, the stable emotion (*sthāyin*) is affection, and its objective basis (*ālambana*) is considered to be one's son and so forth. (RBhrs 3.4.78)
Furthermore:
"If the emotion of love for Hari is not perceived, there would be a lack of nourishment for the *preyas* sentiment;
however, for the *vatsala* [sentiment], the concealment of that [love] causes no harm. (RBhṛs 3.4.79)
This triad of rasas, beginning with *prīti* (affection), has been described as most wonderful;
yet, in some cases, a state of commingling among them is also proclaimed.
The friendship of Saṅkarṣaṇa was joined with affection and tenderness,
while Yudhiṣṭhira’s tenderness was accompanied by both affection and friendship.
The affection of those beginning with Āhuka was mixed with parental tenderness;
the affection of the aged Ābhīrī and others was mixed with friendship.
The friendship of Mādreya, Nārada, and others is blended with affection;
the love of Rudra, Tārkṣya, Uddhava, and others is mixed with friendship.
Thus some spoke regarding the descendants of Aniruddha;
in this way, the mixing of entities should be understood among certain others as well.
Thus ends the fourth wave, on the *vatsala* (parental) rasa, within the description of the five primary rasas of devotion in the Western Division of the *Śrī-Śrī-Bhakti-Rasāmṛta-Sindhu*. (3.5)
The fifth wave, known as the mellifluous rasa of devotion (*madhura-bhakti-rasa*),
having been nourished within the hearts of the virtuous by its appropriate determinants (*vibhāva*) and other factors,
becomes the mellifluous devotional rasa; it is the mellifluous attachment (*madhurā rati*).

Because its utility has ceased, because it is difficult to master, and because it is a secret, this aesthetic flavor (rasa) is being written down in an abbreviated form, though its limbs are extensive.
In that regard, the objects [of meditation] are as follows:
in this case, the object is Kṛṣṇa, and his beloveds are those with beautiful brows.
In that regard, Kṛṣṇa says: "Hari, as the locus of incomparable, supreme beauty, playfulness, and the wealth of charm, is considered the sweet *ālambana* (the objective support)."
As it is said in the *Śrī-Gītagovinda* (1.11):
"Bringing joy to all by his enchanting grace, he brings about the festival of the bodiless god of love with limbs as dark and tender as a row of blue lotuses."
O friend, in the springtime, the charming Hari plays like the personified god of love, embraced on every limb from all sides by the beautiful women of Vraja who follow their own will.
Then his beloveds— those waves of affection intermingled with ripples of love, preeminent in their ever-fresh excellence of sweetness— [spoke].
Bow down to those most wonderful young maidens who worship Hari out of their own innate delight.
Among these beloved consorts of Hari, Vārṣabhānavī is the most excellent.
Her form—
her gaze steals the loveliness of the cakorī bird startled by passion; her face has subdued the fame of the moonlight of the full-moon night.
Behold, Rādhā shines forth— the glory of the foremost among those who have shaken off all imperfections through purification, and the vessel of honey for the sweetness [of love].

Her delight: even when I speak jestingly, she remains with her face turned upward, clearly not placing [her ear] even against the edge of her own ear, though it is created for the festival of supreme bliss.
Even while displaying a certain lightness through her playful, disdainful words, Rādhā,
out of the weight of her friendship, bestowed upon me a joy a hundred times greater.
In that regard, attachment to Kṛṣṇa is as described in the *Śrī Gītagovinda* (3.1):
"Even the enemy of Kaṃsa [Kṛṣṇa] has cast off the fetters bound by the latent impressions of worldly existence..."
Having placed Rādhā in his heart, he abandoned the beauties of Vraja.
Now, the excitants (uddīpanas): here, the excitants are said to be the sound of the flute and so forth. (RBhrs 3.5.11)
As it says in the *Padyāvalī* (verse 172,
attributed to Sarvavidyāvinoda):
"The disgrace of insulting one's elders..."
And the householder’s life is something truly dreadful; alas, alas! it makes one forget everything before the flute of Murārāti.
Now, as for the consequents (anubhāvas): the consequents are said to be the glances, the bowing of the head, the looks, the smiles, and so forth.

As it is said in the *Lalitā-Mādhava* (1.14): "Having drunk the nectar in the city of the celestial river— the moonlight of Rādhā’s smile— where the Yamunā, rippling with dark waves, has been made into a confluence with the celestial Ganges."
With the emergence of our suffering licked away by even a tiny fragment of the flooding frost of inner contentment,
we have now traversed the seven worlds and are seated above them all.
Now, regarding the *sāttvika* [emotions], as in the *Padyāvalī* (181): "Granted,
the body is thrilled with horripilation and the eyes are filled with tears..."
O friend, your words are faltering and your chest is trembling;
I have understood that the sweetness of Mukunda’s flute-song makes your heart, O moon-faced one, tremble like nectar.
Now, as for the transitory mental states (vyabhicārin): all of them should be understood as transitory states, with the exception of indolence (ālasya) and ferocity (aughrya).
In that regard, there is world-weariness, as in the *Padyāvalī* (221): "O Five-Arrowed One, do not release your five arrows upon the body."
O Wind, do not sprinkle my limbs with the thick essence of nectar, for they have been disgraced by the breaking of her affection; today, life itself is no longer able to sustain them in any way.
Joy, as described in the *Dānakelikau mudī* (34):
"The splendor of his own limbs, surpassing the beauty of blue lotus petals, was being tasted by the bee-like eyes of the young women of the blue lotuses."
The rogue of the mountain forest, whose playful waves leap over the intoxicated young elephant, devours my fortitude.
Now, as for the permanent emotion (sthāyin):
here, the previously mentioned sweet love (madhurā ratiḥ) becomes the permanent emotion.
As it is said in the *Padyāvalī* (158):
"The beauty of his face is sweet with the art of the dancing of his creeper-like eyebrows;
his ear-ornament is entwined with the buds of the *kaṅkelli* tree."
"Who is this person, appearing like a brand-new touchstone, who, O friend, subdues me with the sound of his flute? (RBhṛs 3.5.20)
In some place and at some time, this love of Rādhā and Mādhava is never interrupted by any emotions, whether of the same or different kinds.
For example:
"Far from here the queen shines; all around her is a circle of friends;
before my eyes is Candrāvalī; and above the mountain is a demon."
On the left, upon Rādhā’s body concealed by flowering creepers, the beauty of Mukunda’s flickering sidelong glance wanders like a flash of lightning.
The fierce, dark night of ignorance obstructs the courtyard where Śaṅkhacūḍa has been shattered;
the breath of the most eminent Brahmins pours down the frost of peaceful hymns of praise;
and before us, Rāma, radiant as the moon, triumphs, bringing forth that which is worthy of Kṛṣṇa’s delight.
Even then, the lotus of Rādhā’s heart did not wither, but remained in full bloom.
It is considered to be of two kinds, distinguished as separation (*vipralambha*) and union (*sambhoga*).
In that regard, *vipralambha* (love-in-separation):
"That [love] consists of *pūrvarāga* (love at first sight), *māna* (love-in-anger), and likewise that consisting of *pravāsa* (separation due to travel) and so forth;
*vipralambha* is said here by the learned to be of many kinds. (RBhṛs 3.5.25)
Among these, *pūrvarāga* (love at first sight) is as follows: "The state of two people who have never met before is called *pūrvarāga*. (RBhṛS 3.5.26)

As it says in the *Padyāvalī* (181): "O friend, on one occasion as I was walking along a path, I suddenly beheld one whose body was dark like a fresh rain-cloud, traveling toward the bank of the Yamunā."
I do not know what he did with his glance; since then, this mind of mine has become restless and no longer finds attachment to any household duties.
As it is said in the *Śrī-daśama* (10.53.2):
"Just as the lotus-eyed Rukmiṇī was sleepless and her mind was fixed upon Him,
so too am I fixed in my mind upon Him and find no sleep at night."
"I know that, out of hatred for me, Rukmiṇī prevented my marriage."
Now, as for pride:
pride is indeed well-known in this context.
As it is said in the *Śrī-Gītagovinda* (2.1):
"While Hari was sporting in the forest with a common affection toward all women, Rādhā, having set aside her own excellence out of the power of jealousy, went elsewhere."
In a certain bower of creepers, where the thickets were made resonant by swarms of humming bees, she, though distressed and hidden away, spoke in secret to her friend:
Now, regarding separation: separation is the falling away from association. (RBhṛs 3.5.31)
As it says in the *Padyāvalī* (verse 350):
"Of her who rests one cheek upon the hollow of her hand, her face bathed by the ceaseless flow of tears from her eyes..."
From the auspicious day of Mādhava’s departure onwards, how could there be even a moment of sleep for that lotus-eyed woman?
As it is said in the *Prahlāda-saṃhitā*, in the words of Uddhava:
"Even the Blessed Lord Govinda, afflicted by the arrows of Kandarpa, neither eats nor sleeps, for he thinks of you day and night. (RBhrs 3.5.33)
Now, as for enjoyment (sambhoga): the enjoyment of two who have united is proclaimed as "enjoyment" (sambhoga).
As it is said in the *Padyāvalī* (199): "Then,
by Rādhā, who was intent on supreme passion and whose state of being blossomed through the skill of embracing,"
Adorned with a crest of peacock feathers, he spent that festival of amorous dalliance together with her.
Through the vision revealed by the authoritative scriptures such as the Śrīmad-Bhāgavata,
I have manifested this primary aesthetic flavor of the fivefold devotion.
Though bearing the splendor of the form of Gopāla, may he who expands the state of Raghunātha be pleased in the western quarter of the ocean of nectar, the eternal Self.
Thus ends the fourth wave, titled "The Sweet Flavor of Devotion," in the Western Division of the *Śrī-Śrī-Bhakti-Rasāmṛta-Sindhu*.
Thus [ends] the *Śrī-Śrī-Bhakti-Rasāmṛta-Sindhu*.
The Western Section, which defines the primary rasa of devotion, is completed.
The Northern Section (4.1): the description of the rasa of devotional humor.
May the Lord, the eternal Self, who experiences love through the weight of devotion in the first wave and has accepted the company of Vraja, always bestow satisfaction upon me.
In this fourth part, called Uttara, of the ocean of the nectar of aesthetic flavor (rasa), there are seven types of secondary flavors (gauṇa-rasa): friendship, enmity, and mutual coexistence.
And for that reason, nine semblances of rasa (rasābhāsa) are proclaimed here as waves;
previously, they were described as having no fixed substratum, arising occasionally and in any place whatsoever.
The seven secondary aesthetic sentiments (bhakti-rasa), beginning with the comic (hāsya) and so forth, are to be described in order.
Indeed, among these five types of devotees already mentioned,
the objective support (ālambana) for those with secondary devotion is considered to be either one or many, depending on the case.
In that regard, the rasa of humorous devotion (hāsya-bhakti-rasa) is defined by the learned as follows:
when the sentiment of love for the Lord (ratir bhagavati) reaches a state of laughter through the aforementioned excitants (vibhāva) and other factors,
it is called the rasa of humorous devotion.
In this [treatise], Kṛṣṇa is the primary subject, as are others connected to him;
generally, the wise have declared that those who take refuge in him—whether elders or children—are the subjects described.
Furthermore, due to the particularity of their *vibhāvanā* (extraordinary causes) and other qualities, they are in some instances considered preeminent.
Thereupon Kṛṣṇa said:
"Mother, I will not go near this terrifying, decrepit, and withered creature; he will carry me away, hiding me under his arm by means of a trick."
Having spoken thus, as Hari gazed with startled eyes at the wonderful child,
the sage’s laughter became exceedingly manifest, even though he had restrained it.
Now, regarding that which follows from it: "And that which is declared to have activity directed toward Kṛṣṇa as its object—that here is what follows from it. (RBhṛs 4.1.9)
For example:
"I give curd and molasses; open your mouth"—having heard these words of an old woman standing before him, he stood with his tender lips parted.
Perceiving that a fresh flower had been offered by her, the cowherd boys laughed heartily and uncontrollably at Hari as he lowered his face.
Or as it is said:
"O Lord of Sages, having beheld the hand of this dark child of mine, tell me truly: alas, will he be long-lived, or will he become the master of ten million cows?"
When I had spoken thus today, O Blessed One, why is this face of yours— upon which a bold smile has suddenly appeared— being covered by you with your beautiful garment?
The excitants of Hari are such things as his speech, dress, and conduct;
the ensuants, however, are the quivering of his nose, lips, and cheeks, and so forth.
Joy, languor, dissimulation, and so forth are to be understood as the transitory states (*vyabhicāribhāva*).
Here, it is specifically this *hāsaratī* (the erotic sentiment of laughter) that is declared to be the permanent emotion (*sthāyibhāva*).
The sixfold *hāsya-rati* consists of *smita*, *hasita*, *vihasita*, *avahasita*, *apahasita*, and *atihasita*; for the [six] beginning with Jyeṣṭhā, there are two each in successive order.

Due to the variety of factors such as the specific context of the situation, even for one who is superior, laughter and the like may occasionally occur; thus it is said by those who understand emotional states.
Among these, a smile (*smitam*) is that which does not reveal the teeth and causes the expansion of the eyes and cheeks.
For example:
"Where shall I go? This wicked old woman, wishing to seize me while I carry the curd, is running after me with speed; O Subala, protect me quickly!"
When Hari, fleeing in terror, uttered these faltering words, the host of sages in heaven had their lotus-faces blooming wide.
Smiling:
that very [laughter] becomes a smile when the tips of the teeth are slightly visible. (RBhṛS 4.1.18)
For example:
"This Hari standing before you is my very self, your son;
look!"—thus spoke she, her eyes reddened with agitation, having been made to trust by the words of Acyuta.
When her son, having been scolded with faltering words by his matted-hair mother and driven out, first went to the circle of his friends, their lips were washed white by the luster of their teeth.
A smile—
when it is accompanied by sound and the display of teeth, that indeed is called a smile.
For example:
"Stealing the thick curd, you fear it will be in vain in the meantime;
here, with its display of sighs, the matted-haired one sleeps."
While Keśava was speaking thus, the old woman, feigning sleep, let out a loud, boisterous laugh that revealed her rows of broken teeth.
The *avahasita* (laughing smile):
and that *avahasita* has blossoming nostrils and contracted eyes.
For example:
"Is this intense red ointment on your eyes a thick mineral dye? Or, my son, have you put on a black garment upon your body this morning?"
Having heard these words of the mistress of Vraja, the messenger’s nose began to quiver; with her eyes shrinking and a suppressed smile, she was unable to restrain herself from laughing.
The derisive laugh (apahasita) is that which is accompanied by tears in the eyes and trembling of the shoulders.
For example:
"The divine sage in the sky, his head-like arms trembling slightly as he raises them,
whitens the clouds with the radiance of his teeth."
When the divine Child of Vraja was clearly acting out the roles of Brahmā and the other gods, that old woman, through her rhythmic chanting, made him dance; he then directed his gaze toward her.
Excessive laughter—
when it involves a thousand claps and the casting about of the limbs, they know that as excessive laughter.
For instance:
"O old woman, you have a face wrinkled with folds; seeing that you are so well-suited, this excellent monkey, eager to marry you, is making me go."
"With these [qualities], my mind is overwhelmed; indeed, there is nothing superior to you, O Destroyer of Bali," said the girls with their attendants, laughing aloud at her resonant voice.
Even if laughter itself is not directly expressed anywhere,
it is nevertheless perceived through the power of the determinants (vibhāva) and other factors.
For example:
"Your breasts hang like pods; the shape of your nose vies with that of a female frog;
your eyes are like those of an aging iguana; your lips resemble glowing coals; and your waist is like the belly of a drum."
O daughter of Jaṭilā, what woman on earth is more crooked than you?
O fair-browed one, by the merit of the beautiful women of Vraja, your flute is not capable of stealing away their steadfastness.
In that [treatise], this rasa of humor (hāsya) is extensively elaborated within the expansion of the Kaiśikī vṛtti,
with the various manifestations of the erotic (śṛṅgāra) and other rasas explained in many ways.
Thus, in the *Śrī-Śrī-Bhakti-Rasāmṛta-Sindhu*, in the Uttara-Vibhāga,

within the exposition of the devotional aesthetic of humor (*hāsya-bhakti-rasa*), this is the first wave on the devotional aesthetic of wonder (*adbhuta-bhakti-rasa*). (4.2) This concludes the section titled "The Devotional Aesthetic of Wonder."
When that wonder-filled love (*vismaya-rati*) is brought to a state of relish within the heart of the devotee through excitants (*vibhāva*) and other factors appropriate to itself,
it becomes the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) of wondrous devotion (*adbhuta-bhakti-rasa*). (RBhrs 4.2.1)
In this context, every kind of devotion is applicable as a basis for wonder;
its object is Keśava, who is the cause of supermundane action.
The specific movements and so forth that serve as excitants (*uddīpana*) for that [rasa] are considered its actions (*kriyā*),
such as the expansion of the eyes, paralysis, tears, horripilation, and the like.
Agitation, joy, stupor, and so forth would be the transitory emotions (*vyabhicārin*) therein;
the stable emotion (*sthāyin*) would be wonder and delight arising from superhuman deeds.
And that [wonder] is said to be of two kinds: direct and inferred.
In that context, "directly" means as follows:
"Directly perceptible through the senses is that which is seen, heard, recited, and so forth. (RBhṛs 4.2.5)
In this regard, it is observed as follows:
[the sun], though but one, simultaneously occupies all palaces while exerting its various efforts.
Upon beholding Mukunda at Dvārakā,
the sage became motionless, his body released from all agitation.
As it is said in the Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam (10.69.2): "How wonderful! Indeed, with a single body, he simultaneously and separately married sixteen thousand women in their respective homes."
Or for example:
"Where is that infant Govardhana of yours, whose moon-like face is scented with breast-milk; and where is this mountain, which obstructs the clouds with its peaks?"
O friend, look! With the Lord of Mountains itching from being scratched by his left hand, he seems to be sporting; alas, what a magical illusion this is!
I have heard that whatever weapons the soldiers hurled, the Lord cut each one individually with three arrows.
Having thus reflected upon the power of the enemy of Kaṃsa in battle, the king’s eyes widened and he was covered in horripilation.
It was proclaimed as follows:

"Behold! The children, clad in garments resembling gold and possessing the luster of clouds, have become four-armed; and as I speak the word 'Vatsas,' I have been rendered helpless by the splendor of the pillar."
I shall tell you a marvel; listen, sirs! Each one of you is being praised on all sides by world-eggs, each of which is seated upon a lotus. Alas! (RBhṛs 4.2.10)
Inferred, for example:
"The children of Vraja, having opened their eyes, look again and again at Bhāṇḍīra tree before them with incomparable wonder."
There, they beheld themselves and the multitude of animals released from the forest fire, and their minds were struck with wonder.

The performance of an unpleasant act and the like does not cause wonder even if it is extraordinary; yet, for one who is dear, that very same act produces at least some degree of astonishment, even if it is not uncommon.
"How much more so for one dearer than the dearest, who is the most supreme among all the worlds?"—
in this regard, the sweetness of the favor of passion is proclaimed amidst such wonder.

Thus ends the second wave, on the rasa of the wonderful devotional sentiment (*adbhuta-bhakti-rasa*), within the section on the description of secondary devotional sentiments (*gauṇa-bhakti-rasa*) in the Uttara-vibhāga of the *Śrī-śrī-Bhakti-rasāmṛta-sindhu*. (4.3) Now follows the description of the devotional sentiment of heroism (*vīra-bhakti-rasa*).
That very enthusiasm and delight, which is the stable emotion (sthāyibhāva) appropriate to its own determinants (vibhāva) and so forth,
when brought to the state of being relished, becomes the heroic devotional rasa (vīra-bhakti-rasa).
Through the virtues of combat, generosity, compassion, and [moral] discipline, one is called a hero in four ways;
it is this very fourfold [set] that is declared here to be the objective support (ālambana).
However, this enthusiasm may arise in all devotees whatsoever.
In that regard, the hero of battle (yuddha-vīra) is described here as follows:
"One who displays enthusiasm for combat for the sake of pleasing Kṛṣṇa—whether he be a friend or a special kinsman—is called a hero of battle in this context. (RBhrs 4.3.4)
Whether Mukunda is the opponent or remains a spectator,
another excellent friend may appear here through the influence of His will.
In that regard, Kṛṣṇa says:
"O Mādhava, having forcibly overcome you— who pride yourself on being unconquerable and who are so fickle— "
I would now curse my circle of friends, were it not for you who have turned away from the battle.
Or as it is said:
"At that time, on the bank of the Yamunā, he was being gazed upon with wonder by his circle of friends, while the splendor of the onset of his adversaries was made manifest by his impetuous fury."
Even though their friendship was unbroken, the martial display of Śrīdāman, who roared with boar-like pride, and the enemy of Bakī became more intense.
The excellent friend, as follows—
the skillful Dāma, casting aside countless searches for the group of friends on all sides, today gradually whirled his staff around.
Even the son of the Lord of Vraja, having offered his praise,
regarded him as if he were trapped within a cage of sticks, his hair standing on end with thrill.
Generally, even for those who are naturally brave, an exceedingly wonderful enthusiasm for the sport of battle sometimes arises even from their own side.
And so it is said in the *Harivaṃśa*:
"Likewise, O best of the Bharatas, the powerful Madhusūdana, while sporting with the wielder of the Gāṇḍīva bow, defeated that foremost of the Bharatas in the presence of Kuntī. (RBhrs 4.3.10)
In this context, actions such as brandishing weapons, clapping, competing, displaying prowess, and seizing missiles,
when performed by those standing as opposing combatants, serve as excitants (uddīpana).
In this regard, it is said:
"O Dāmodara, you boast here that you have conquered the mighty Piṇḍīśūra by trickery; do not make such vain boasts in battle against one whose limbs are weak."
Intoxicated and stealing away the pride of the serpents that are your heavy arms,
this peacock with its slightly dark plumage dances nearby with a deep, resonant cry.
If the powers such as katthitā and the rest are proclaimed to exist within one's own nature,
then likewise there is self-aggrandizement, shouting, abuse, and leaping about.
Even when without allies, the desire for battle, not fleeing from the fray,
and granting fearlessness to those who are afraid— these and others should be understood by the wise as [qualities of a hero].
In that regard, there is an example:
"O slayer of Keśin, why do you urge me on so excessively with persistence, even though you know Bhadrasena?"
To fight here with an army equal in strength to my own, which is exceedingly weak, my arm— the opponent of divine bolts— is ashamed.
Boastfulness, as for example:
"O Lord of cowherds, moon of the ocean, who maintains such majestic pride, you bind your girdle with exultation, suited for the practice of battle with your arms."
Victorious is the frequent, longing display of self-importance by Sudāman as he dances, his round face covered with bristling hair from the roar of joy.

In all four types of heroes, there are exclusively sattvic transitory emotions (vyabhicāribhāvas), such as pride, agitation, fortitude, shame, thought, joy, dissimulation, indignation, longing, envy, recollection, and so forth. (RBhrs 4.3.17)
The delight in the enthusiasm for battle is declared to be the stable emotion (*sthāyibhāva*) therein;
whether it is innate or acquired through such factors as one's own power and allies, that persistent desire to conquer in battle is termed "enthusiasm for battle" (*yuddhotsāha*). (RBhrs 4.3.18)
In that regard, there is delight in aroused enthusiasm by one's own power, as follows:
"Though clearly summoned by Puruṣottama for the instruction of his own father, he did not wish to go."
Slightly dark-complexioned and possessing a thirst for battle,
he raised his staff and whirled it around.
Delight in innate enthusiasm according to one's own power, as for example:
"O wretched Bhadrasena, do not fear upon seeing my staff-like arm shaped like a trunk!"
"Having easily defeated Rāma today with a mere playful effort,
I, Śrīdāmā, shall challenge Kṛṣṇa himself."
Just as Mandara, having secured the support of Mukunda, churned the ocean with the force of its powerful strength while agitating the host of friendly deities— so did he act.
Deafening the people with his formidable roars, that hero Bhadrasena, with his steady voice, alone brought joy to Hari in the assembly.
One whose enthusiasm and delight are unassailable by any companion, as in: "While I, of terrifying prowess, am leaping forth, do not suffer defeat from this battle."
Thus, at the word of Mitra, Varūthapa went to Hari while speaking [of him] along with Virūpa.
Delight in innate enthusiasm through companionship, as follows: "The skillful Sudāmā, with the arms of one desiring battle, himself desired the victory of Dāmodara."
In this matter, the powerful Subala provides assistance, provided that the jewel is well-fashioned from excellent gold.
For a hero, even a friend can be an adversary; however, for Kṛṣṇa, there is no enemy at all.
Because he causes agitation among his devotees, he is the objective basis (*ālambana*) in the Furious Sentiment (*raudra-rasa*).
His distinction from the [sentiment of] Passion (*rāga*) lies in the absence of [worldly] attachment in his gaze and other faculties, despite the presence of the Furious Sentiment.
Now, regarding the hero of generosity:
there are two kinds of heroes of generosity; among them, one is the giver of much, while the other is said to be the renouncer of even that which is difficult to obtain when it is presented.
In that regard, the "giver of much" (bahu-prada) is he by whom everything is given away suddenly, even his entire possessions;
for the sake of Dāmodara’s happiness, he is called the giver of much.
In this context, the excitants (uddīpanas) of the recipient are considered to be glancing and so forth;
[furthermore, they include] the state of being a giver of more than what is desired, and speaking preceded by a smile. (RBhrs 4.3.27)
Steadfastness, courtesy, fortitude, and so forth are declared here to be the consequent emotions (anubhāvas);
while deliberation, longing, joy, and so forth are to be understood as the transitory mental states (vyabhicāribhāvas).

In this [sentiment], however, delight in the impulse to give is declared to be the stable emotion (*sthāyibhāva*). An intense and enduring desire to give is termed "the impulse to give" (*dānotsāha*). (RBhṛS 4.3.29)

Although this [giving] is said by the wise here to be of two kinds when it is abundant, one is that which pertains to worldly prosperity (*ābhyudayika*), while the other is that which consists of the bestowing of those [very things]. (RBhṛs 4.3.30)
Among these, the *ābhyudāyika* [gift] is as follows:
"That by which one's entire property is bestowed for the sake of Kṛṣṇa’s exaltation upon supplicants such as Brāhmaṇas and others, that shall be the *ābhyudāyika*. (RBhṛs 4.3.31)
Just as the Lord of Vraja, with a pure heart, bestowed a multitude of black cows here for the sake of his son's birth-rite, so did he [the sage] bestow them.
The gods on earth proclaimed loudly that even Pṛthu, whose fame was like that of Nṛga, had now become concealed, for they were so satiated by him.
Now, regarding that which has him as its recipient:
he by whom one's entire possession—the locus of one's "I-ness" and "mine-ness"—is given to Hari, who is known [as the Self], is one for whom He is the recipient (tat-sampradānaka). (RBhṛs 4.3.33)
That gift is said to be of two kinds: through joy and through worship.
In that regard, the gift of affection:
the gift of affection is that which one should give to someone who appears as a kinsman or the like.

Just as he [gave] the *cārcikya* banner, the Vaijayantī flag, a cloth resplendent with vast gold, a series of ornaments set with rubies, and variegated elephants, chariots, and horses, all with a variegated [cloth].

Having given away his kingdom and even his own family to the Blessed One, the Pāṇḍava, desiring to give yet another great gift but seeing nothing else anywhere, became distressed at that sacrificial assembly.
Worship and gift—
worship and gift are those which are given to him who has assumed the form of a brahmin.
As it is said in the eighth [chapter] (8.20.11):
"The wise ones, who are conversant with the injunctions of the sacred tradition, perform the sacrifice for Him with solemn rites."
"Whether he be that very Viṣṇu, the giver of boons, or another supreme being, O Sage, I shall grant this desired land to him."
Or as it is said in the *Daśarūpaka* (by Dhanika on 4.72):
"By him alone was the hand of Hari—reddened by the saffron from the bosom of Lakṣmī’s breasts—made into a begging bowl, even though he was the stronger. (RBhrs_4.39)

Now, he who renounces even a difficult-to-attain object when it is present— by him that boon, such as equality with Hari (sārṣṭi) and so forth, was not desired, even though it was being offered by Hari himself, who was content [with his state]. (RBhrs 4.3.40)
In this context, there may be a reversal of the causal factors for both [the hero and the heroine] from the perspective of the former;
the excitants (*uddīpana*) in this case include Kṛṣṇa’s compassionate speech, smiles, and so forth.
The *anubhāvas*— such as the firmness of describing its excellence and so forth—
are here predominantly manifested as belonging to *dhṛti* (fortitude) alone.
In this [treatise], the stable emotion (sthāyībhāva) declared by the wise is delight in renunciation;
such mature desire for renunciation is termed "enthusiasm for renunciation" (tyāgotsāha). (RBhṛS 4.3.43)
As it is said in the *Haribhaktisudhodaya* (7.28):
"Desiring a [suitable] place and established in austerity, I have attained you, the secret of the gods and the lords of sages."
O Master, even while searching for glass, I have found a divine jewel; I am fulfilled and ask for no further boon.
Or as it is said in the third [canto] (3.15.48): "They do not even consider Your favor to be ultimate, much less anything else that carries fear with the raising of Your eyebrows."
O Lord, those who have taken refuge at Your feet are experts in Your narrative,
which proclaims Your holy fame, and they are connoisseurs of its aesthetic flavor.
This very person, possessing a particularly high degree of mature passion,
would follow the path of the third type of hero, the *dhurya* and others.

Now, the hero of compassion (*dayā-vīra*)— one who offers his body in pieces due to a heart moistened with pity, and who bestows it upon Kṛṣṇa whose compassion is unrestrained— is here called a hero of compassion. (RBhṛs 4.3.47)
The excitants (uddīpanā) are said here to be the manifestation of their suffering and so forth,
as well as the habit of protecting those in distress even at the cost of one's own life.

In that [state], consolatory words, steadfastness, and so forth are the primary [emotions] (*vikriyā*); longing, excessive joy, and the like should be known by the wise as the transitory emotions (*sañcārin*). (49)
In this [rasa], the stable emotion (sthāyibhāva) declared is "compassionate energy" (dayotsāha).
Here, "compassionate energy" is said to be an enthusiasm that bears an abundance of compassion.
For example: "With folded hands like a budding lotus, I repeatedly bow to the Hero whose banner is the peacock,
who, desiring to give half of his body to the enemy of Kaṃsa— who was a Brahmin in disguise— [gave it] to that very person."
"Alas! I am choked with a stammering at the very start of speaking; oh, my wise [son] has joyfully split open the auspicious [sacrificial post] with a saw, along with his wife and son! (RBhṛs 4.3.51)
If Hari possesses knowledge of reality, compassion does not truly belong to him;
yet in the absence of that [knowledge], he clearly falls within the category of a hero of generosity.
Because he is a Vaiṣṇava, he always directs his delight toward Kṛṣṇa;
and since devotion has been established by him toward this one in the form of a twice-born, he possesses the status of a devotee.
The wise Vopadeva and others, speaking of the inclusion of this [heroic sentiment] within the heroic sentiment of generosity (dāna-vīra), describe the hero as being of three kinds.
Now, regarding the hero of dharma (dharma-vīra):
one who is always firmly established in that dharma which consists solely in pleasing Kṛṣṇa,
and who is generally steadfast and tranquil— he is called a hero of dharma.
In this context, the excitants (uddīpanas) are said to be the hearing of authentic scriptures and so forth;
the consequents (anubhāvas) are right conduct, faith in the existence of the afterlife, fortitude, self-restraint, and so on.
The enduring emotional state (*sthāyībhāva*) here is said by the wise to be "delight in the enthusiasm for Dharma" (*dharmotsāharati*);
for the virtuous, the singular devotion to Dharma is considered "enthusiasm for Dharma" (*dharmotsāha*).
Just as—
O Puruhūta, you who are ever invoked, by performing the seven-threaded sacrifices for the sake of delighting in your city;
The cheek of that daughter of Danu, resting upon the lap of Śacī’s left hand, was for a long time fashioned by the son of Pāṇḍu as a subduer of demons.

Sacrifice (yajña) is a specific form of worship; it is when one meditates on the limbs of Viṣṇu, such as his arms and so forth, as the abodes of Indra and the other deities, and an oblation is offered into them.
But this Yudhiṣṭhira, the best of great devotees and an ocean of love, performs sacrifices directly by his very command.
Some wealthy people and others, while clearly praising the three kinds of heroism beginning with generosity, do not consider the heroism of the Dharma to be such.

Thus ends the third wave, the Marvelous Devotional Flavor (*adbhuta-bhakti-rasa*), within the section on Heroic Devotional Flavor (*vīra-bhakti-rasa*) in the latter division of the *Śrī-Śrī-Bhakti-Rasāmṛta-Sindhu*, by the commentator on the *Daśarūpaka*. [4.4]
The fourth wave, known as the aesthetic flavor of compassionate devotion (*karuṇa-bhakti-rasa*),
having been brought to full maturity in the hearts of the virtuous by its appropriate determinants (*vibhāva*) and other factors,
is indeed the aesthetic flavor of devotion called compassion, which consists of the delight in sorrow. (RBhrs 4.4.1)
Although this [state] possesses uninterrupted great bliss, Kṛṣṇa is to be known as its beloved, because He is the state of attaining the supreme object of love. // RBhrs_4.4.2 //
Likewise, one's own dear person who has not yet attained the happiness of devotion to Him—
these three types of objects are to be known as the supports (ālambana) by virtue of being its [compassion's] domain.
Furthermore, he is threefold: the knower of that [object], the devotee of that, and the one who serves as its locus.
He too should be understood according to his propriety (*aucitya*), and is generally devoid of [the specific emotional states] such as *śānta* (quiescence).
In this context, the object's actions, qualities, forms, and so forth, constitute the excitants (*uddīpana*).
The external manifestations [of grief] are dryness of the mouth, lamentation, drooping of the limbs,
and such things as labored breathing, crying out, falling to the ground, and striking one's chest.
In this context, there are eight *sāttvika* [emotions]: torpor, despondency, languor, dejection, anxiety, dejection, longing, and agitation; as well as fainting, madness, and death.
Furthermore, there are transitory states (*vyabhicārin*) such as laziness, forgetfulness, disease, and delusion. (RBhṛS 4.4.6)

When *rati* (attachment) undergoes transformation in the heart through a portion of *śoka* (sorrow), it is called *śoka-rati*; that very state is here declared to be the stable emotion (*sthāyī-bhāva*).
In that regard, Kṛṣṇa is described in the Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam (10.16.10) as follows:
"He [the serpent] was encircled by the coils of the serpent, his movements unseen."

Seeing this, the cowherds, his dear friends— whose own selves, friends, wealth, wives, and desires were all dedicated to Kṛṣṇa— were deeply distressed; with their minds overwhelmed by grief, sorrow, and fear, they fell to the ground.
Or as it is said:
"When Piñchacūḍa plunged into the terrible lake of serpents, her upper garment was washed by the mass of her warm, falling tears."
The queen of the king of the cowherd settlement entered a difficult and precarious state that paralyzed the functioning of all her senses.
His beloved person was as follows:
"In the contest for the attraction of Kṛṣṇa’s beloveds, fashioned by Śaṅkhacūḍa,
the moon-like face of Nīlāmbara repeatedly assumed a dark blue hue."
One's own beloved, as described in the *Haṃsadūta* (54):
"The toe-nails of him whose feet shine with their tips brushed by the crest-jewels of Brahmā— himself distressed by the theft of the young maidens of Vraja— "
Upon seeing them for a moment, that celestial sage, overwhelmed by manifest supreme bliss, grieves intensely even for those embodied beings who have attained liberation.
Or as it is said:
"O Mother Mādrī, where have you gone now? Alas! O Father Pāṇḍu, where are you? This ocean of the nectar of intense bliss was not within the range of your vision."
Thus the younger brother of Nakula lamented loudly upon beholding the intensely radiant splendor of the pair of lotus-feet of Govinda, while he himself was overwhelmed with joy.
The emergence of laughter and the like occurs sometimes even without passion; however, there could never be the possibility of sorrow arising from this [laughter].

In proportion to the abundance or the deficiency of passion (*rati*), sorrow (*śoka*) likewise becomes more abundant or diminished; because it is inseparable from passion, this [sorrow] possesses a certain extraordinary distinction.
Moreover:
"The ignorance of Kṛṣṇa’s sovereignty and other attributes was not produced in them by nescience (avidyā);
rather, it was produced solely by a particular excellence of the rasa consisting of supreme love."
Therefore, sorrow, manifesting and repeatedly attaining intensity,
spreads a certain inscrutable course for happiness.

Thus ends the fourth wave, the Wave of the Sentiment of Compassionate Devotion (*karuṇa-bhakti-rasa*), within the Description of the Secondary Sentiments of Devotion (*gauṇa-bhakti-rasa*) in the Uttara-vibhāga of the *Śrī-śrī-Bhakti-rasāmṛta-sindhu*.
Now begins the fifth wave, titled the Sentiment of Fierce Devotion (*raudra-bhakti-rasa*).

When the passion of anger is brought to full development by its own appropriate determinants (vibhāvas) and so forth within the heart of a devotee, that becomes the aesthetic flavor of the heroic emotion of wrath (raudra-bhakti-rasa).
The object of anger is threefold: as beneficial, as harmful, and as both. In the case of the "dark" (kṛṣṇa) [anger], female friends, old women, and others have become its substratum;
likewise, all kinds of devotees are its substratum in both the beneficial and the harmful.
In that regard, there is the anger of a female friend toward Kṛṣṇa;
when a great harm has been done by Kṛṣṇa, the anger of a female friend arises toward her friend.
As it is said in the *Vidagdhamādhava* (2.37):
"Though we are indeed stained by internal afflictions and shall today go to the city of Yama,
he nevertheless does not abandon his smile, which is fond of the accumulation of deceits."
Alas, O wise Rādhikā, how could your love be so profound for this rogue of the cowherd hamlet, who is wrapped in deep deceptions?
In that regard, the anger of the old woman is as follows: "The anger of the old woman arises when she perceives Hari in connection with her daughter-in-law and others. (RBhṛs 4.5.5)
For example:
"O young woman-thief, the garment on your breast is clearly visible to the bride; alas, why do you prattle 'no, it is not'?"
"O residents of Vraja, listen! Why do you not raise a cry of alarm?
By the son of the Lord of Vraja, fire has been set in my son's house!"
Except for the great wrestler Govardhana, among all the other inhabitants of Vraja,
a mature love for Govinda shone forth in everyone.
Now, as for the "beneficial" (hita):
the beneficial is of three kinds—namely, the heedless, the reckless, and the envious.
In that regard, "inattentive" refers to one who, although performing the duty of protecting Kṛṣṇa, is distracted by an obsessive attachment to that very task;
he who is occasionally negligent therein is said here to be "inattentive."
For example:
"Arise, fool! Do not delay in vain; fie on you who consider yourself a scholar!"
O friend, that son of yours, bound between two *kraṭyat-palāśa* trees, wanders about.
Now, regarding the reckless person (sāhasī): "He who incites [others] toward a cause for fear is called reckless. (RBhrs 4.5.11)
For example:
"Govinda has clearly departed for the grove of palmyra trees at the mere words of his dear friends," having heard this distinctly.
With her gaze fixed upon the parted space between her eyebrows, the wife of the Lord of Vraja beheld these first of the children.
Now, the envious woman—she is said to have pride as her wealth, her mind overcome by intense envy. (RBhṛs 4.5.13)
For example:
"Churned by the agitation of my wicked pride, what shall I say to you? Go far away; otherwise, I shall blaze up in your very presence."
Alas, what a pity! Though your feet were once massaged by the tips of the feathered ends of your beloved’s hair, you now have a face as red as the dawn.
Now, regarding the "unfavorable" (ahita):
it is of two kinds, distinguished as being unfavorable to oneself and unfavorable to Hari.
In that regard, "detrimental to oneself" means:
that which obstructs one's connection with Kṛṣṇa would be detrimental to oneself. (RBhrs 4.5.16)

As it is said in the *Uddhava-sandeśa* (74): "May the son of Gāndinī not violate the boundaries of those born in the Yadu clan, he who, robbing Kṛṣṇa by his pitiless strength, seeks the slaughter of the cowherd women."
Thus, as I proceeded on my journey to Madhupura, the piteous lamentations of those terrified cowherd women rose up on high from that place.
Now, as for the enemy of Hari—
his adversary, that is said to belong to the faction of his foes.
For example:
"He who displays contempt even for Hari, whose lotus feet are radiant, being consecrated by the rays of the crest-jewels upon the heads of the Vedas..."
This Pāṇḍava hurls [the discus]—terrible like the staff of Death—with force;
having clearly raised his left foot three times above his crown.
In this context, derisive laughter, sarcastic speech, side-long glances, disdain, and so forth—directed toward those who harm or benefit Kṛṣṇa—are the excitants (uddīpanas). 4.5.20.
Squeezing of the hands, clashing of the teeth, redness of the eyes, biting of the lips,
excessive knitting of the brows, and the slapping and striking of the arms.
Silence, downcast countenance, sighing, averted gaze, reproach, shaking of the head, and a reddish hue at the corners of the eyes; // RBhrs_4,5.22 //
In this context, the following are declared to be the *anubhāvas*: the knitting of the brows, the trembling of the lips, and so forth;
herein, all the *sāttvika* states, such as paralysis (*stambha*) and the rest, attain manifestation.
Agitation, dullness, pride, despondency, delusion, and fickleness;
envy, ferocity, as well as indignation, fatigue, and so forth—these are the transitory mental states (vyabhicāribhāvas).
In this [sentiment], the stable emotion is the passion of anger; that anger is considered to be threefold:
*kopa*, *manyu*, and *roṣa*. Among these, *kopa* is directed toward an enemy. (RBhrs 4.5.25)
*Manyu* is declared to be threefold among one's kinsmen—as equal to, greater than, or less than [themselves];
however, *roṣa* is the anger women feel toward their beloved, and for this reason, it deviates from that [threefold classification].
Beating with the hands and so forth are said to be the actions in anger (*kopa*); silence and so forth in indignation (*manyu*);
and the reddening of the corners of the eyes and so forth in rage (*roṣa*). (RBhṛ 4.5.27)
In that regard, concerning the enemy, as follows:
Having besieged the city of Unmada in battle, while the King of Magadha— whose refuge is unfathomable courage— was shouting something at Hari, whose face was [distorted] with fury;
The wielder of the plow cast forth a gaze, tawny like a fiercely burning ember, which scorched the wilderness of the spreading host of his enemies.
He is worthy of worship, as it is said in the *Vidagdhamādhava* (2.22):
"While she was crying out, the powerful one immediately covered her mouth with his sprout-like hand."
As she runs away, filled with fear, she blocks my path ahead with her outstretched arms;
while I roll at her feet, she repeatedly bites my lip in anger.
O Mother, O fierce one, how can I protect myself from her crest-ornamented crown?
Likewise, for example:
"O foul-mouthed one with matted hair, by your words the embers burn in my vital organs and on the surface of my forehead."
O low-born daughter of mine, when did Giridhara ever touch his daughter out of passion?
In the case of deficiency, for example:
"Ah! This beautiful necklace, which used to dwell upon the slope of Hari's neck, now shines upon the crown of my own breast."
"O, look! This young bride, though she is like a cluster of soot from her own family, deceives me with her forehead mark."
In this [state of] pride (*manyu*), such a favoring of passion (*rati*) does not exist;
nevertheless, it has been shown here merely as an illustration.

Because anger is naturally inseparable from worldly attachment (*rati*), the anger of enemies such as Śiśupāla, who are the objects of wrath, cannot attain the status of the aesthetic flavor of devotion (*bhakti-rasa*). (RBhrs 4.5.33)

Thus, in the *Śrī-Śrī-Bhakti-Rasāmṛta-Sindhu*, in the section on the secondary devotional moods (*gauṇa-bhakti-rasa*) within the Uttara-vibhāga, this is the fifth wave, the *Raudra-bhakti-rasa-laharī* (The Wave of the Furious Devotional Mood),
titled "The Description of the Terrifying Devotional Mood" (*bhayānaka-bhakti-rasākhyā*). [4.6]
The sixth wave:
When *bhaya-rati* (fearful attachment) reaches its full development through the *vibhāvas* and other factors to be described hereafter,
it is proclaimed by the wise as the *bhakti-rasa* named *bhayānaka* (the fearful).
In that regard, the objects of focus are twofold: the "dark" and the "cruel.
The "dark" refers to those who have committed offenses against those worthy of compassion, as well as their kinsmen.
These are proclaimed to be cruel due to constant affection, and are characterized by seeing, hearing, and remembering the attainment of what is undesirable for them.
In that regard, Kṛṣṇa’s compassion toward those worthy of pity is as follows:
"Even though your face is parched, abandon the great trembling that agitates your heart;
resort to the natural state of the universe, for there is not even the slightest cause for you to feel resentment."
O King of Bears, by you who have impetuously displayed your prowess upon one smeared with heat,
the earth has instead been fashioned for me into a mere stage filled with the curiosity of battle.
Or as it is said:
"O Destroyer of Mura, who among those before you is a wretched serpent? Do not direct your wrath toward one so insignificant."
O Guru, this transgression was truly committed through ignorance;
I am without refuge and utterly deluded—protect me, protect me! Be gracious.
Cruel toward kinsmen because of what they see, as for example:
"Alas! What shall I do? O Gopendra, forcibly restraining him within the interior of the house, protect the child!"
Behold, the demon-horse, shaking my mind along with the circle of the earth, leaps over the mountain peaks!
From hearing, for example:
"Hearing that the arrogant demon Turaga was indeed entering Gokula in a rage..."
Immediately, the Queen of Vraja became distraught with anxiety for her son’s protection, her lotus-like face parched.
From remembrance, as for example:
"Desist, desist, O Mother! Even now, this body of Pūtanā, when remembered, causes trembling."
Who, as if to swallow him whole, blinded the boy with a roar and manifested a terrifying body of immense proportions.
In the case of fear (*vibhāva*), the knitting of the brows and so forth are considered its excitants (*uddīpana*);
[its ensuants are] the parching of the mouth, sighing, and looking back over the shoulder. (RBhṛs 4.6.9)
In this state, there is self-concealment, rolling about, seeking refuge, and actions such as crying out; these are sattvic qualities, though they are devoid of tears.
In this context, the transitory emotions (*vyabhicāribhāva*) include terror, death, agitation, haste, dejection, despondency,
delusion, epilepsy, apprehension, and so forth.
In this [state], the stable emotion (sthāyībhāva) is the frustration of desire arising from offenses;
and therein, the state of being offended occurs in many ways due to terrifying things.
The fear born from that [object] would not exist elsewhere without the people who are to be protected—
those who are terrifying by their appearance, by their nature, or by their power.
Fear directed toward such objects generally arises in this world for women, children, and others who possess only simple affection. (RBhṛs 4.6.14)
Pūtanā and others are terrifying by their very form; wicked kings are so by their nature; but Indra, Śiva, and the rest are terrifying by their power.
Kaṃsa and others are always struck with absolute fear of the Blessed One; because they are devoid of delight, they are not considered suitable objects [of compassion] here.
Thus ends the sixth wave, the *bhayānaka-bhakti-rasa-laharī*, within the description of the secondary *bhakti-rasa* in the Uttara-vibhāga of the *Śrī-śrī-Bhakti-rasāmṛta-sindhu*.
[4.7] Now follows the description of the *bībhatsa-bhakti-rasa*.
When the aesthetic sentiment of disgust (*jugupsā-rati*) attains nourishment through its own determinants (*vibhāva*) and other factors,
it becomes the aesthetic flavor of devotion (*bhakti-rasa*); this is designated by the wise as "the loathsome" (*bībhatsa*).
In this [state], the wise consider the objects of focus to be the peaceful and so forth which are based upon it.
For example:
He who was a scholar on the path of wandering for pleasure, having taken the vow of initiation into desire,
first exercised the sovereign rule over the entire city of the *ṣiḍgas*.
It is strange that this man, while proclaiming the virtues of Hari with tearful eyes,
turns his face away and spits out in disgust upon seeing the face of a woman.
In this regard, there are spitting, contorting the face, closing the nostrils, running away,
and various other transformations such as trembling, horripilation, and perspiration.
In this context, the transitory emotions (vyabhicāribhāvas) include languor, fatigue, madness, delusion, despondency, dejection, despondency, restlessness, agitation, and dullness.

In this [aesthetic state], disgust (*jugupsā*) and delight (*rati*) would be the stable emotions (*sthāyin*); and that disgust is said by the wise to be of two kinds: that born of discernment (*vivekaja*) and that which is common (*prāyikī*).
In that context, "born of discrimination" (*vivekajā*):
for a certain particular devotee who has developed a longing for Kṛṣṇa, there arises a loathing toward the body and so forth; that which arises from discrimination is called "born of discrimination."
For example:
[in this body] which consists of thick blood, is bound by skin, and possesses a putrid odor mixed with flesh;
How could a wise person take delight here in this body, when even a mere atom of delight in the Blessed One has arisen? Alas!
Now, regarding the "common" [aversion]:
that aversion which generally arises in everyone toward everything due to the experience of impurity and stench is considered the common aversion. (RBhṛs 4.7.9)
For example:
"Dwelling in my mother's womb— drenched, with a body rendered inert, amidst a thick mire of impurities and drenched in blood and urine— "
I experience agitation of mind due to my inability to perform service for You;
therefore, O Ocean of Mercy, show Your compassion toward me, this enemy of Kaṃsa.
Or for example:
"In this place, hideous with the stench of putrid excrement wafting from the snorting nostrils [of the dead], swarming with insects,
and where the eyes and life-force are blown away by the impact of the dung-heaps of diseased herds falling upon the thresholds..."
Alas! We have been cast into this hell named Kārā by Yama, the ruler of Magadha; yet, O destroyer of hell, having regained our memory, we live here once more.
Only for one who has attained delight in the Dark One (Kṛṣṇa) is the mind always thoroughly purified;
it becomes agitated even at the slightest unpleasant thing, and therefore, there is the favor of delight in Him.

The fact that the comic and other such sentiments are proclaimed to possess the status of *rasas* even in a secondary sense should be understood by the wise as being according to the opinion of the ancients.
These five, beginning with tranquility (śānta), are considered the aesthetic flavors (rasas) of devotion to Hari;
among these, the flavors such as the comic (hāsya) and others generally assume the status of transitory emotions (vyabhicāribhāva).
Thus ends the seventh wave, the *bībhatsa-bhakti-rasa*, within the description of the secondary *bhakti-rasa* in the Uttara-vibhāga of the *Śrī-śrī-Bhakti-rasāmṛta-sindhu*.
[4.8] This concludes the section concerning the establishment of friendship and enmity among the *rasas*.
Now, in this eighth wave, the mutual friendship and enmity among these rasas, beginning with the peaceful (śānta), are described in their proper order.
In the *śānta* [rasa], the best of friends experience the sentiments of love (*prīta*), disgust (*bībhatsa*), righteousness (*dharma*), and heroism (*vīra*);
and this marvelous sentiment (*adbhuta*) is present in all four of these, beginning with love.
His enemy is pure, a hero in battle, fierce and terrifying.
The *bībhatsa* (disgustful) rasa arises from a friend who is pleased; the *śānta* (tranquil) likewise arises from both types of heroes (*vīra*).
The *vairī* (enmity), *śuci* (purity), and *yuddha-vīra* (heroic in battle) rasas each have a single determinant emotion (*vibhāvaka*), namely the *raudra* (furious).

The beloved [hero] evokes the sentiments of the pure (*śuci*), the comic (*hāsya*), and the heroic in battle (*yuddha-vīra*); the best of friends evoke the same; enemies evoke the tender (*vatsala*), the loathsome (*bībhatsa*), and the furious (*raudra*); and Bhīṣma is as before.

The *vatsala* rasa has a friend as its excitant (*ālambana*), a smile as its ensuant (*anubhāva*), and compassion as its transitory emotion (*vyabhicāribhāva*); likewise, the *karuṇa* (pathetic) has fear of Bhīṣma;
the *śatru* (hostile) has purity; the *yuddhavīra* (heroic in battle) is joyful; and the *raudra* (furious) is as before.
The Comic (hāsya) is thus proclaimed to be his friend, while the Pure (śuci) is said to be his beloved friend.

The Envious (dviṣ), the Compassionate (vatsala), the Disgusting (bībhatsa), the Tranquil (śānta), the Fierce (raudra), and the Terrifying (bhayānaka)— some say these are his friends, while others say the pair of Heroic (vīra) rasas are his enemies.
The Comic is friendly, the Disgusting is pure, the Erotic is beloved and affectionate; the Pathetic is said to be its opposite, as is the Terrible.
The hero of the marvelous (adbhuta) rasa has five allies, such as the peaceful (śānta) and others;
its opposites would be the furious (raudra) and the loathsome (bībhatsa).
For the heroic sentiment, however, the marvelous, the comic, the lovable, and likewise the affectionate are its allies;
the terrifying is its adversary, and for some, the peaceful sentiment is also [an adversary].
In the *karuṇa* (pathetic) rasa, the *raudra* (furious), the *vatsala* (affectionate), and the *hāsya* (comic) are observed as its allies;
likewise, the *sambhoga-śṛṅgāra* (erotic love-in-enjoyment) and the *adbhuta* (marvelous) are its enemies.
The compassionate is said to be the opposite of the furious, and the heroic is the opposite of the best of friends;
however, for the comic, its opposites are the erotic and the terrifying.
The terrible, the loathsome, and the pathetic are the best friends;
let the heroic, the erotic, the comic, and the furious be proclaimed as enemies.

The sentiment of disgust (bībhatsa) may become the peaceful (śānta); likewise, the comic (hāsya), the friend, the enemy, the pure, and the beloved—these others should be understood through their application by means of logical reasoning.
In that regard, the duty toward a friend is as follows:
those who are beyond the categories already mentioned are considered by the wise to be neutral (taṭastha).
Through its union with a friend, it thoroughly experiences the taste of flavor.
But when two [elements] are mixed in equal measure, it would be difficult for them to be held by a balance;
therefore, the wise maintain that their union occurs through the relationship of primary and subordinate.
Whether the dominant rasa in a work be primary or secondary, the wise should treat that rasa which serves as its subordinate element as if it were a true friend.
Now, first of all, the status of being the primary elements (aṅgin) is described here for those who are principal,
wherein both friends who are primary and those who are secondary assume the state of being subordinate members (aṅga).
In that regard, for one who finds delight in the Peaceful One (Śānta), there is a state of being a limb [of Him], as follows:
"What indeed shall I massage with my hands the pair of lotus feet of Him, whose nature is the dense consciousness and whose splendor is like the sparks of the fire of life? (RBhrs 4.8.20)
In this case, there is the status of being a subordinate (aṅga) for the primary element within the primary subject;
specifically, that of the *bībhatsa* (the loathsome), as in: "I am here [composed] of phlegm, semen, and blood..."
O Śiva, Śiva! I am a wicked soul, delighting in my body which is but a vast bag of skin; I am sluggish even in remembering the Supreme Self, whose nature is bliss.
In this case, the primary [sentiment] subordinates the secondary;

and therein, when one is delighted, the marvelous (*adbhuta*) and the loathsome (*bībhatsa*) are likewise subordinated, as in: "Having abandoned delight in this body, which is bound with flesh and drenched in blood..."

With a mind overflowing with joy, when shall I repeatedly serve that Supreme Brahman— who is dark as a rain cloud— seated upon a golden throne, the abode of incessant evil thoughts, by means of the skillful movement of the breezes from my moving and beautiful chowries?
In this case, [the relationship] is between the primary and the primary, as well as between the two secondary ones.
Now, regarding the peaceful one who has attained delight—for example: "By virtue of being free from ignorance, I immediately..."
When shall I worship the Lord whose eyes are like lotuses, who is as beautiful as a blue water-lily, and who is faultless in his practice of sweetness?
Here, [the rasa] of the primary [hero] is [present] in the primary [context];
in that very same context, there is also the *bībhatsa* (disgust), as for example:
"Remembering the lotus-feet of the Lord, the Vaiṣṇava wanders about dancing."
But he who, even at the sight of lotus ponds, feels a profound sense of shame;

In this case, the subordinate [rasa] occurs in relation to the primary one; specifically, the *bībhatsa* (disgust), *śānta* (quiescence), and *vīra* (heroic) [may be subordinate] therein, as for example:
