"He displays a contortion of his face at the onset of the passion for union with a young woman."
O Lord, the mind is not satiated even by a meditative absorption consisting entirely of bliss;
nor does it harbor a longing for supernatural powers, even when they are being attained;
rather, it attains its highest thirst for worship at Your feet.
Here, [the figure of speech] occurs between two primary things, or between two secondary things;
now, for the case of the "dearer" (*preyasi*) compared to the "pure" (*śuci*), as in:
"Truly, the cowherd women of Vraja are the foremost among the fortunate."
Those flickering [flames] lick up even the lower part of the peacock-feather crest.
In this case, the primary [cause] occurs in relation to the primary [effect];
that is, the laughter occurs in that very same place, as for example:
"O charming girl, enough with the tremors of your eyes; turn back and go to Vraja."
"You imagine me to be such as you do, but I am not so; what is the use of much talk?"—
as Mādhava spoke thus, Subala, his eyes wide with power, beheld the face of the young woman under the guise of a fresh vine.
In this case, there is the secondary [meaning] within the primary;
specifically, regarding the "pure" and the "laughable," as in:
"The lovely bank of the daughter of the Sun, with its rising *vañjula* trees..."
Here enters Subala, disguised in the dress of Rādhikā;
beholding Kṛṣṇa with impetuosity, he rises up and covers his own face, whose cheeks are blossoming with a smile.

In this context, [the rasa of] the Heroic (vīra) is the primary [rasa] in relation to the primary and the secondary; whereas the Pathetic (karuṇa) is [the primary rasa] in relation to the Affectionate (vatsala)—as in:
"Without a parasol in the forest, constantly with his sandals cast off..."
He protects my calves; alas, my mind is burning with grief!
In this case, there is the subordinate [flavor] within the primary;
therein, the comic [flavor] is as follows:
"Your son, stealing a large lump of fresh butter from my inner chamber—"

Having performed the ritual placement [of mantras], she withdrew her gaze from the face of the sleeping child; thus addressed by the family elder, may Goṣṭheśvarī— who casts a smiling glance at the face of her son with knitted brows— ever be for your welfare.
Here too, [the rule applies] when the primary [sentiment] is present;

in that very case, [there is subordination] of the Frightful, the Marvelous, the Comic, and the Pathetic, as for example: "Trembling, with sweat upon her forehead where the curls are matted, her eyes wide and staring..."

May the Queen of Vraja protect the universe— she who stands for a long time with her eyes upturned and shedding tears, while Lord Hari, whose broad cheeks expand and who wears hundreds of playful facial expressions on his left arm, holds the king of mountains upon it, drenching her garment with the flow of her tears.
In this case as well, among the four secondary [types],
there is no primary friendship in the *vatsala* alone; therefore, in this *vatsala*, its status as a [dramatic] element is even less established.
Now, an example of the "Radiant" (ujjvala) beloved:
Behold Mukunda, having placed his arm upon the lovely head of Subala, whose body is accustomed to my own dress and conduct.
O slender one, while he is clearly wearing the cloak of horripilation, you deliver my message into his very ear.
In this case, there is the primary [feeling] in relation to the primary;
therein, it is the comic (hāsya), as for example: "I am your sister, O merciless one; why do you not recognize me?"
"O slender-limbed one, bestow upon me an embrace full of affection," said Hari,
who was disguised in the dress of a young woman; at that, Rādhā smiled knowingly in the presence of her elders.
In this case, there is the subordination of the secondary to the primary.
In that very context, regarding the *preyas* and *vīra* [rasas], as for example:
"This Mukunda, with restless glances upon the moon-like face of Candrāvalī..."
He casts a sidelong glance, smiling with love,
toward his friend from nearby; placing his serpent-like arm upon his friend’s bristling shoulder, he incites the demon Vṛṣa with the roar of the enemy of elephants (the lion).

In this context, regarding the primary [rasas] and the primary and secondary [rasas]: now, as for the status of the secondary ones as the principal— this is the example that has been given for the secondary rasas, such as the comic (hāsya) and the rest.
Thus, the status of these as primary members (*aṅgin*) and that of the others as subordinate members (*aṅga*) is clearly established;
nevertheless, only a small portion is written here for the sake of a minor distinction.
Then, indeed, there was the state of being a limb for that [limbless] one who was pure, as follows:
when the garment’s hem was forcibly seized by Tri-vakrā, who was blinded by passion.
Hari placed Vinata’s face, with its cheeks blooming, before the people.
In this case, when the secondary (gauṇa) is the principal subject (aṅgin), the primary (mukhya) becomes its subordinate (aṅga).
As in the case of the Heroic (vīra) being subordinate to the Amorous (preyasa):
"Having beheld the commander-in-chief Bhadrasena defeated..."
"O Viśāla, how is it that you come before me to fight?
Even a hundred beautiful women cannot move one whose thighs possess such fierce majesty;
O Śrīdāman, who are you here? (RBhrs_4,8.38)
Here too, when the subordinate [rasa] is the primary [subject], there is the subordination of the principal [rasa]:
in the *raudra* (furious) rasa, the *preyas* (affectionate) and *vīra* (heroic) rasas are subordinate, as in: "O delight of the Yadus, [you who are] arrogant in censuring..."
Desirous of slaying Śiśupāla in battle,
the sons of Pāṇḍu seized their excellent weapons with eyes like intensely red lotuses.

In this context, regarding the primary and secondary [sentiments]: in the marvelous (*adbhuta*), there is a subordination of the beloved (*preyaḥ*), the heroic (*vīra*), and the comic (*hāsya*), as for example—[in the verse]:
"The enemy of Pralamba, who was surrounded by Mitrāṇīka and esteemed as a teacher in the mace-weapon..."

Having witnessed the skill of Śrīdāmā— who, having defeated him with a frail staff, was singing boastfully before him during the festive display of their playful combat— Kṛṣṇa shone with blooming cheeks, bristling hair, and wide-open eyes.
In this context, the subordination of the primary to the secondary, and of two secondaries [to one another],
as well as the subordination of other secondaries, should be understood by poets; likewise, the subordination of primary and secondary rasas should also be known.

That rasa which is either primary or secondary, being capable of transcending all [other rasas], becomes the "limb" (aṅga) when it proceeds as a transitory emotion (sañcāribhāva), nourishing the principal sentiment (aṅgin).
And thus the masters of dramaturgy recite:
"There should be only one predominant rasa which is the primary stable emotion;
other rasas, by following that one, would be transitory (vyabhicārin)."
And in the *Śrī-Viṣṇudharmottara*:
"Among the various rasas combined together, that one whose form appears most prominently should be considered the stable rasa (sthāyī-bhāva); the others are regarded as transitory (sañcārī)."
Born from a slight manifestation and having attained a state of variability,
the subordinate [feeling], while nourishing its primary master, dissolves back into that very same [master].
Arising through the excellence of its cultivation and having attained preeminence by means of the primary [feeling],
even the secondary [feeling] assumes the status of the principal when its own master is in a state of contraction.

But the primary [Vāsudeva], having assumed the status of a subordinate member like Upendra, nourishes Indra while making the secondary [Saṃkarṣaṇa] the principal possessor of the limbs, his own inherent glory remaining concealed.

In the mind of the devotee, which has been perfumed by the manifestation of beginningless latent impressions, this [Self] shines forth indeed; it does not become dissolved, unlike a transitory secondary attribute.
The primary subject shines forth here, independent and sovereign, augmenting itself through those constituent elements and emotional states, both of the same class and of different classes.

Whichever primary deity one’s own devotee constantly takes as their personal refuge, that very deity shall become the presiding principal (aṅgin) therein; even another primary deity may then assume the status of a subordinate limb (aṅga).
Furthermore:
"The status of being a subordinate element (aṅga) with respect to the principal element (aṅgin) consists in its being the cause for the intensification of aesthetic relish (āsvāda).
Without that [intensification], its occurrence leads only to futility. (RBhrs 4.8.51)
Just as when sweet milk-rice is being eaten, the consumption of grass and such might somehow occur during that chewing, yet it would still be considered the eating of grass.
Now, regarding the action of an enemy:

the union of flavors with their enemies inevitably produces a state of hostility, just as well-prepared drinks and the like become unpalatable when mixed with alkaline or bitter substances. (RBhṛs 4.8.53)
For indeed— O most devoted to Brahman, much time has passed in vain for me through this vow of meditative concentration; alas!
I beheld with the corner of my left eye that very Brahman, embodied as intense bliss.
In that regard, there is a sense of distaste for the radiant [state] because of its tranquility;
even for a moment, one should contemplate that Lord of Indirā, who is affectionate toward ten million ancestors and whose feet are worshipped by gods and sages.
My mind desires to see the Lord marked by the nail-scratches of beautiful women.
There, O friend, embrace me with your two arms, radiant with joy and as long as a bolt; then,
having smelled your head, Kṛṣṇa, I shall sport with you.
Here, the *preyas* (the pleasant) is subordinated to the *vatsala* (the affectionate):
"Him whom all the Vedas declare to be the Supreme Lord,
while the Sātvatas call him the Blessed One."
Alas, how could my tongue wish to revile you, who are his daughter, O rash woman?

In this matter, O messenger, you who are as flickering as the play of lightning, being beloved by that affectionate one, go today itself and delight Mādhava with me, for he is rich in the wealth of fresh youth.
There, a certain amorous woman, residing on Kailāsa, embraced the radiant Acyuta with playful charm after joining him with the blessing, "May you live long," which was characterized by tranquility.
In this regard, [the author says]:
"If, by some means, even a trace of a connection with the pure were to somehow exist in the affectionate, then it would lead only to extreme distaste. (RBhrs 4.8.60)
"I am not made of flesh and blood; truly, I am worthy of you.
O dark-limbed one, out of compassion, accept me who have been pierced by your sidelong glance."
In this case, the *śuci* (the pure) is opposed by the *bībhatsa* (the loathsome);

in this same way, other instances of the opposition between aesthetic sentiments (*rasa*) should also be understood by the wise. Generally, such opposition results in what is known as the "semblance" (*ābhāsa*) of a sentiment.
Furthermore:
"In this case, when one of two [alternatives] is described as being sublated,
even when both are stated as being remembered, and even when they are expressed with equality," (RBhṛs 4.8.63).

When there is an intervention by another rasa, or when the beloved stands as a neutral witness, or when there is a distinction between the object and its locus, or when the union is with a subordinate or an enemy—
as in such cases— the conjunction of an enemy does not produce a sense of distaste.
In that context, when one [of two alternatives] is described as being sublated, as in the *Vidagdhamādhava* (2.18):
"The sage, having withdrawn his mind from sense-objects for a moment, desires to fix it upon that [Self]..."
This [mind] is childish; it seeks to dwell upon sense-objects, and thus the yogi draws it back.
Alas! For even the slightest stir of its activity, the yogi yearns intensely in his heart.
Behold, this deluded mind indeed desires to depart from his very heart.
In this case, there is subordination because of the description of the excellence of the tranquil and pure one.
Regarding the state of being remembered— for example:
"He is indeed the one who, through his playful jests,
brings about the outburst of laughter for the people of Vraja."
Now being dragged away by the Lord of Serpents,
he utters lamentations for us, alas!
Regarding the expression of equality, for example:
"O Rādhā, you who have rested the sixteen digits, who are free from conceptual construction and veils, and whose nature is bliss, shine like the knowledge of Brahman. (RBhrs 4.8.68)
Or as it is said:
"Like Śānti, Rādhā, making me sleepless and fixing my eyes upon her without blinking, dwells within me as I am absorbed in meditation in a mountain cave. (RBhrs 4.8.69)
When there is an intervention by something else in between, for example:
"Who are you, O Śāntā? Why have you come here into the intermediate space, and from where do you have eyes to see the Supreme Brahman?"
Because of her exceeding beauty, what else could have disturbed his soul, that he entered into the plantain tree with a sense of duality through the power of love?
In this case, there is an intervention by the marvelous;
when there is a difference in the object,
as in the Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam (10.60.45):
Enveloped by skin, beard, body hair, nails, and head hair, and filled within with flesh, bones, blood, worms, feces, phlegm, bile, and wind—
a living corpse— she, utterly deluded, clings to her beloved.
That woman who has not smelled the nectar of your lotus feet...
Or as it says in the *Vidagdhamādhava* (2.31):
"O friend, from the moment this gaze of ours became fixed upon her lovely face, radiant with beauty, and upon that pair of charming eyes..."
We speak the truth: until that time, the moon and the blue lotus shall remain so, for as one repeatedly recalls the god of love, this [moon] causes a crookedness in the face and brings about shame.
In both cases, [the rasa is] the pure (śuci) and the loathsome (bībhatsa), provided there is a difference in the substratum; for example:
"Having seen the victorious [hero] undefeated on the stage..."

On the land, they assumed the forms of the cowherd boys of his own age, displaying their martial prowess; yet upon the bodies of his enemies, they manifested a multitude of horripilation and a deep blackness.

In this regard, although there is a difference between the objects and the substrata of the *vīra* (heroic) and *bhayānaka* (terrifying) sentiments, the association of the primary [sentiment] with a primary enemy indeed results in enmity alone. (RBhrs 4.8.74)
In that regard, regarding the distinction of objects, for example:
"O father, release the bolt-fastening; do not delay!
I am going to the house of Kāśī; my heart has been stolen by a dark youth. (RBhrs 4.8.75)
In this context, [the emotion arises] from one who is pure and another who is pleased;
regarding the difference in substrata, for example:
"When shall my chest, smeared with the saffron from Rukmiṇī’s breasts..."
I shall serve the supreme Brahman, which is eternal bliss, through direct perception.
In this regard, certain devotees whose minds are devoted to the path of knowledge perform [the worship] of Śānta with pure [materials];
they do not admit any distaste for Śānta when his substratum is distinct.
Furthermore:

Just as between two servants of a master, even if they are naturally hostile to one another, their union in a single place may lead to the prosperity of their master; so too, the union of the two limbs with the possessor of the limbs (the body) leads to its nourishment. (RBhṛs 4.8.78)
For example:
"O dearest one, this son of yours, Keśin, who is as delicate as a mallī flower, has become heavy like a mountain; thus my mind trembles."
May it be auspicious for the bound soul; raising my arms and repeatedly trampling this wicked one, may I make the community exceedingly prosperous.

In this context, the *vīra* (heroic) and *bhayānaka* (terrifying) sentiments nourish the *vatsala* (affectionate) sentiment, as in the verse beginning: "Trembling on the forehead where the sweat-dampened curls are powdered... (BRS 4.8.31). RBhrs_4,8.80 //

In that regard, the sentiments of humor (hāsya) and compassion (karuṇā) nourish only the paternal affection (vatsala). Moreover: even those two sentiments which are mutually hostile [in ordinary life] [become harmonious] when directed toward the sons of Dharma and others.
There is no fault in those two [the self and the object] perceiving manifestation through the distinction of time and so forth.
When the Great State has ascended, there can be no union with those who are hostile and devoid of flavor; this was demonstrated previously in the radiant union of Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa.
In some inexplicable, great power, upon the crest of the Great Being,
the immersion into the series of aesthetic flavors arises solely for the sake of relish.
In that regard, concerning the objects of the aesthetic sentiments (*rasa*), as it says in the *Lalitamādhava* (3.4):
"The preceptors of the Daityas, their friends the eminent wrestlers, [beheld] a distortion in his mouth..."

Upon seeing Mukunda on the stage, the wicked attained swelling pride, the hosts of sages the dissolution of their meditative heat, the mothers tears of joy, the warriors a thrill of horripilation, the lords of the gods an indescribable inner wonder, the servants a dance, and the dark-eyed women a sidelong glance. (RBhrs 4.8.84)
In terms of his character (*āśrayatva*), it is as follows:
he is free from pride even toward his own burden-bearing bull; he utters a roar of defiance at children who attempt to lift heavy loads;
he smiles when yogurt is sour; he spits at those who are fawning; he displays boldness toward his friends; and he has bloodshot eyes toward Indra.

May that Lord protect you—he who, weeping in the cow-pen and distressed before his elders, cast away the sacrifice for Hari; who trembled before the young women with wide-eyed gazes and stood bristling with joy while bearing the mountain.
Thus ends the eighth wave, titled "The State of Friendship and Enmity among the Rasas," in the Uttara-vibhāga of the Śrī-Śrī-Bhakti-Rasāmṛta-Sindhu.
The ninth wave is titled "Rasābhāsa" (the semblance of rasa).
Previously, it was taught that when the characteristics of rasa are deficient,
those very rasas are proclaimed by connoisseurs of rasa as *rasābhāsa* (semblances of rasa).
Metals are of three kinds: secondary metals (uparasa), secondary-derivatives (anurasa), and non-metals (aparasā).
These are declared to be, respectively, superior, middling, and inferior.
In this context, the secondary sentiments (uparasa):
"But when the stable emotions, the determinants, the consequents, and so forth, attain a state of transformation,
the [eight] sentiments such as the peaceful and others are considered to be twelve secondary sentiments."
Among those, the *śānta* (tranquil) is a secondary flavor (*uparasa*):
because of the state of Brahman, and through the yoga of the preeminence of non-duality within the Supreme Brahman;
likewise, the *śānta* indeed becomes a secondary flavor of the *bībhatsa* (disgustful), the *bhūta* (terrible), and so forth.
Among these, the first is as follows:
"The bliss that arises in Samādhi, which is purified by the perfect tranquility of consciousness when [the Self] is perceived— that very same bliss is found in You, the Ancient Person."
The second is as follows:
"In whatever object my gaze falls, that very thing I perceive as you."
Apart from you, who are stainless and the seed of both the higher and the lower, there is nothing else whatsoever.
Then Prītoparasa said: "Out of extreme audacity before Kṛṣṇa, out of contempt for His devotees,
and out of perceiving the supreme excellence of another deity who is not Your own chosen one— "
And through such acts as transgressing established boundaries, the state of being another's beloved is considered to arise.
Among these, the first is as follows:
"Even though his dancing was disregarded by the families of the virtuous, he who brings about a state of helplessness in embodied beings remains unrestrained."
"O Lord, cast Your glance upon me here," said the clever young boy with unimpeded speech, thus revealing his own affection.
Now follows the secondary rasa of love (*preyānuparasa*):
The secondary rasa of love arises through friendship alone, through the slighting of Hari, Mitra, and others, and also through the field of battle and so forth. (RBhrs 4.9.9)
Among these, the first is as follows:
"Addressed as 'friend,' he trembled with fear;
deceived by a joking word, he offered praise."
As he sought to embrace him with both arms, that king fell prostrate before Hari like a staff.
Now, the secondary flavor (uparasa) of *vatsala* (affection):

"From the recognition of an excess of capability, from the absence of effort such as fondling, and from the intensity of compassion and so forth, there arises the secondary flavor of the fourth [rasa]. (RBhṛS 4.9.11)
Among those, the first is as follows:
"I beheld the destruction of the Mallas, who were as formidable as mountains, brought about suddenly by your son."
I do not feel agitation until that limit is reached, even as I enter into that most protracted assembly.

Now follows the secondary rasa of erotic passion (śṛṅgāra). In that regard, there is a perversion of the stable emotion (sthāyibhāva): for indeed, when love is observed between two people, it belongs to only one of them.
That which constitutes the multiformity of a single, persisting entity when it is observed in various states is merely the multiformity of its manifestations;
this multiformity is here figuratively attributed to the persisting entity itself.
In that regard, there is delight in one [of the two],
as in the *Lalita-mādhava*:
"Her gentle smile, though natural, is interrupted..."
And though it was innate, the wave of her glance was concealed;
yet, as the fire of the passion-afflicted wives of the twice-born began to smolder,
a certain woman suddenly became the sprout of the *gātrī* plant.
In this context, indeed, absolute non-existence (atyantābhāva) of passion is intended;
for if there were only its prior non-existence (prāgabhāva), there would be no pure uparasa.
Delight in many places, as for example:
"O friend, seeing Kāmapāla performing his amorous play right before me upon the ground..."
O virtuous lady, today you have been split in two by the remembrance of Mukunda’s dust as you hear it.
Some, however, maintain that even when the hero possesses equal passion toward many heroines in every respect, there exists the secondary rasa (uparasa) called *śuci*.
The deformity of the excitant (*vibhāva-vairūpyam*)—the absence of cleverness and brilliance is the deformity of the excitant;
it exists even in creepers, beasts, Pulinda women, and old women. (RBhṛs 4.9.18)
In that regard, the *latā* (creeper-like woman) is as follows:
"O friend, having heard the flute emitting honey, the tender girl was then glanced at by the Slayer of Madhu."
This row of creepers, bristling with buds, reveals in my heart the blossoming of passion.
The beast, for example:
"Behold, O fortunate ones, the deer with their lofty pride today on the sandy bank of the daughter of the sun (the Yamunā)— how wondrous they are!"
Those [women] who, purified by his sidelong glances, cast their eyes— filled with the passion of love— upon the body of Keśava.
O Pulindī,
look— on the banks of the Kālindī, the Pulindī is covered in horripilation; seeing the natural flickering of Hari’s eyes, she reels.
O old woman, for example: she whose hair has been made black with collyrium, and who has fashioned high breasts from a pair of *bilva* fruits.
Behold, O Gaurī, this old woman, casting the corner of her eye, smiles at the Destroyer of Evil (Śiva).
If the stability [of the emotion] here were to consist in its being of a single color (rāga),
then this would serve as an illustration even when the excitant (vibhāva) possesses a variety of colors.

Because of its purity, brilliance, and elegance, as well as its graceful attire, it is described as the *vibhāva* (excitant cause) of the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*); otherwise, it would be a mere semblance (*ābhāsa*) thereof.
Now, regarding the discordance of the ensuants (*anubhāva-vairūpya*):
"The transgression of the rules, vulgarity, and even impudence—these are declared by the wise to be the discordance of the ensuants and so forth. (RBhṛs 4.9.25)
In that regard, the transgression of the convention (*samaya-vyatikrānti*) is as follows:
for women such as the *khaṇḍitā* and others, it consists of anger arising from the beloved and so forth;
for men, it consists of smiles and the like when they are struck by the beloved and so on.
The alteration of these commitments is their transgression.
Among these, the first is as follows: "O Hari, although I am today pierced by the nails of my beloved, casting aside all shame,
favor me with a glance of compassion, making me the servant of her who dwells on Kailāsa."

Now, regarding vulgarity (*grāmyatva*): the employment of words such as "child" (*bāla*), the prolixity of tasteless expressions, and [references to] "itching of the hips" (*kaṭī-kaṇḍūti*) and so forth—these are declared by the wise to be vulgarity. (RBhṛs 4.9.28)
Among these, the first is as follows:
"O cowherd boy, why do you always tear away the lower garment of us young serpent maidens, who dwell in the lotuses, with the sound of your flute? (RBhrs 4.9.29)
Now, regarding boldness (*dhṛṣṭatā*): boldness consists of manifest entreaty and the like, as well as sexual enjoyment and so forth. (RBhṛs 4.9.30)
For example:
"O beloved, this is a grove on Mount Kailāsa; I am beautiful and in the bloom of youth;
you are clever, O Govinda—what more need be said? (RBhrs 4.9.31).
In the same way, wise men should understand that laughter and the other secondary emotions (gauṇabhāvas) are themselves cited as examples for another sattva.

Now, the secondary sentiments (anurasa): the seven sentiments beginning with the comic (hāsya), as well as the peaceful (śānta), are considered secondary sentiments when they are produced by excitants (vibhāva) and other factors devoid of any connection to Kṛṣṇa, such as food and the like. (RBhrs 4.9.33)
In that regard, the sentiment of laughter (hāsya) has its subordinate flavor (anurasa) as follows: "Alas! The harsh female monkey performed a violent dance with the knitting of her eyebrows."
By which the herd of cowherds shone,
their faces suffused with a profusion of laughter.
Now follows the *adbhutānurasa* (the flavor of the marvelous):
Within the grove of Bhāṇḍīra, there was much disputatious debate on the Vedānta system by the circle of parrots.
Listening with his eyelashes motionless,
the celestial sage stood with his body covered in horripilation.
In the same way, the illustration of the *vīra* and other [mudrās] should be understood here as well.
If these eight, while remaining in their external states, attain manifestation through Kṛṣṇa and others acting as the determinants (vibhāva) and so forth, they proceed along the path of experience.
Now, regarding the *aparasā* (inferior) [laughter]:
if the opposites of that [superior laughter], such as laughter and the rest, have come to depend upon sense objects, then they are considered *aparasā* by the wise. (RBhṛs 4.9.38)
There, Jarāsaṃdha, beholding Kṛṣṇa fleeing with his tremulous eyes darting about, laughed repeatedly and mockingly from afar.
In this way, others as well—such as the marvelous (*adbhuta*), the pathetic (*karuṇa*), and so forth—are to be understood.
However, some have declared that the "semblances of rasa" (*rasābhāsa*) are the highest forms of rasa.
For it is thus:
all entities are manifestations of that [Self], and certain things are manifestations of rasa;
all these are called "rasas" by those who are experts in the aforementioned rasas, because they are tasted.

The four styles (vṛtti), beginning with Bhāratī, which indicate the abiding of the aesthetic sentiments (rasa), are described in the definition of the drama because they are the mothers of the dramatic art.
Out of fear of the bulk of the original work, I have composed this concise compendium of the splendor of the aesthetic flavor of devotion.

May the Eternal One, who, though assuming the splendor of the form of Gopāla, is ever-expanding with the ecstatic mood of Raghunātha, be pleased in this northern portion of the ocean of the nectar of rasa.
Thus ends the ninth wave, on the semblance of rasa, in the Uttara-vibhāga of the Śrī-Śrī-Bhakti-rasāmṛta-sindhu.

Thus ends the fourth section, titled "The Description of the Secondary Flavors of Devotional Rasa," in the illustrious *Śrī-bhakti-rasāmṛta-sindhu*. This *Bhakti-rasāmṛta-sindhu* was composed by one of humble form while residing in Gokula, in the Śaka year reckoned as the number of Rāma’s limbs (1673).
